TURNED OFF!
There,:ang up the bill:;;;C, m—ii-sug-,-and: give 113 my pipe and
a light; Aint I ready for suppei ?" No, thank'e. I wants no supper
to-night; _ _ 'Twill be. time enough when I'm 'ungry to turn to the victuals
and drink, - To-night all I want is the bacey. and to sit by the fire and think. What about? Wor it that ye wor axin? Lor bless 'er, poor

soul. I forgot, I 'sant as yet bin and told 'er— and yet I'd as lief be shot, Like our lad as went out for a soger last year in the Injin fight, As tell 'er the poor old missus, why I can't eat no supper to- night ! Yet, tell 'Cr I maun, same as Joey was forced to stand there stock still, And face them davils of Injins as they swarm'd on 'im down the 'ill, And the longer yer waits for to do it, why the wusser it be, I 'spose, So. I'll just get my pipe well started—that's it—and then orf I goes! Well, missus, I'se got news for yer, but yer maun't, now, take it amiss. When we lost our Joey yer bore up,ancl so ye maim do ower this, Net as this 'ere time, lot bless yer, it's oily-thing like as black— It's only my Lord's goin' a tourist', and I—well, lee got the sack! There, don't say no 'ard things, missus, it ain't my Lord's s- fault, ma.bbe ; E's allers bin fair enough spoken,and her Leddyship, so 'as she But as the folks says at the ortice ('tis them in course 'as to speak), They must begin savin' somewhere, and I corsts 'em twelve shillin' a week. There's them fellers, yer says, in powder, and her Leddyship's pair o' cobs, As she spanks with to church in the summer, or a goin' to 'aye tea with the nobs. And the chap as they calls 'er "tiger " (tho' why puzzles my old crown!) And them deer we gets never a taste on—why, yer says, don't they put them down? Or them horchids my Lord's sl crazed with, each blossom, as Fee 'eard said. If yer reckons one year wi' another, corsting ower a guinea a end! And the pheyzants as stands in a pot, too, by the time they'se ready for killin'— Why doan't they, yet says, put them down, afore they docks my twelve shillin'? There, I can't tell yer, missus says passon, some things 'ere on earth below, It's no sort o' use to inquire on ; yer isn't supposed to know: And this 'ere be one on 'em. mebbe ; and passon, es no bad chap, And things ain't a goin' so easy as they used to wi"im, maybap! Still, my feyther, 'e served my Lord's feyther, as afore him 'is feyther, 'e Werked, too, for my Lord's grandfeyther, as I 'ave for this 'tin, yer see, Ever since just a lad from Coll idge 'e took to the title and 'states. And it's 'ard when yer nigh agen sixty, to be turned like a tramp from the 'gates ! But there. I'se too old for them meetins they talks on, the younger chaps, And flags, and brass bands, and what not, and spoutin' from four2orse traps • Says passon, the Lord 'as willed it. so,I 'ad best, too, be whim'; And the werk'us, mebbe, at sixty, is as good,arter all, as twelve shillin' ! —Corn/j2ll Magazine.

' I

- Hew sweet are the slumbers of him who can lie down on his pillow and review the transactions of every day without condemning himself! Those with whom we can apparently become well ac- quainted in a few moments are generally the most difficult to rightly know and understand.— Hawthorne. Miss Tattleton, entering se ldenly "It's raining, girls."—De Spoonville, rising hastily: "You will excuse me. I want to be outside, don't you knosy, if it's rain- ing girls." Perseverance can sometimes equal genius in its results. There are only two creatures," says the Eastern pro- verb, "which can surmount the Pyramids—the eagle and the snail!" "Just think, darling, a week ago we were utter strangers, and now we are engaged."—" Ah, yes, Mr. Hobson, dear; it was a case of love at first sight."— "Mr. Hobson? Why don't you call me by my first name. dierling ?"—" Because, my 'precious," the girl replied shyly, "I don't know what it is." Elderly masher (trying to scrape an acquaintance) : "Charming day, madame. Travelling alone?" Lady (vivaciously) : "Oh, no. I'm going down to Newport to be tried for bigamy. Those two gentlemen in the front seats are my brothers, those in the rear deputy sheriffs, and my two husbands are in the smoking car.' —Á meriean. "So you have got a Wife," said Jones to a newly- married man. "I don't know—don't know," replied the man, with evident hesitation. "Sometimes I think I've got her, and sometimes I think she's got me. You see, I've only been married a few Months, and I can't tell just vet how the confounded combination is going to turn out." Do not command children under six years of age to - keep anything secret, not even the pleasure y -al may be preparing as a surprise for a dear friend. The cloudless heaven of youthful open-heartedness should not be over- cast, not even by the rosy dawn of shyness—otherwise children will soon learn to conceal their own secrets as well as yours. At a Scotch police-court an old roman—the solitary prisoner—was brought before the presiding bailie. "As I'm the only ane, yer lordship micht let me aff," she pleaded slyly. "Na. Tibby," severely sipoke the Bench, "that will I no'. Just because there's only you, I'll gie ye!t as het an' strang as I'm allowed by statoot to dae. I've been nearer gettin' a pair o' white gloves than ony magistrate that ever sat in this court, an' wad hae haen them bit for yer gettin' fou' an' fetchin'. Forty days wi' hard labour, without the option o' a fine." "Will you kindly allow me to stand ?" asked a gentle- ma.n, as he got into a railway carriago at, Waterloo Station, en route to Epsom, and whieh carriage already contained the specified number. "Certainly not, sir !" exclaimed a passenger occuping a corner seat near the door. "The way these trains are overcrowded is shame- ful !" "As you appear to be the only person who objects to my presence," replied the gentleman, "I shall remain where I am." "Then I shall call the Etilard, and have you removed, sir !" Suiting the action to the word, the aggrieved passenger rose, and, putting his head out of the window, vociferously summoned the guard. The newcomer saw his opportunity, and quietly slipped into the corner seat. "What's up?" inquired the guard, as be opened the carriage door. "One over the number," replied the newcomer, coolly. "You mdst come out, sir, the train's going on," and, without waiting for any further explanation, the guard pulled o it the aggrieved passenger, who was left wildly gesticulating on the plat- form. He didn't see the fun on the Downs. Beer TIME FOR TAXING A BATH.-011 this point there is ecnsiderable difference of opinion. The general idea ' is that the best and most convenient time for taking a bath is just after getting out of lied in the morning ; and there can be no doubt that a cold bath then does act as an invigorating tonic to the system. Dr. Richardson, however, and other eminent authorities on hygiene main- tatn that this theory is incorrect; and that it for any reason it be impossible to carry out complete ablution twice a day, which is beyond question the best plan, then general ablution is best just before going to bed. "There is no practice," says Dr. Richardson, "more ob- : jeetional then to go to bed closely wrapped up in the dust and dirt that accumulates on the surface of the body during the day ; nor is there anything I know so - conaucive to sound sleep as a tepid douche just before ; getting into bed. I have many times known bad sleepers become the best of sleepers 'from the adoption of this Simple rule. If the body be well sponged over before . going to bed, the morning ablution, though it is still bet- ter to carry it out, need not of necessity be so general; the face, neck, chest, arms, and hands may be merely , well sponged and washed at the morning ablution. Sourneit's IDEA OF SHELLEY. —Here ig a man at Keswick who acts upon me as my own ghost would do. He is just what I was in 1794. His name is Shelley, son _ to the member for Shoreham; with £l,OOO a year en- tailed upon him, and as much more in his father's power to cut off. Beginning with romances of ghosts and murder, and with poetry at Eton, he passed, at Oxford, into metaphysics; printed half-a-dozen-pages, which he entitled "The Necessity of Atheism ; " sent one anony- mously to Coplestone, in expectation, I suppose, of con- verting him; was expelled in consequence; married a girl of seventeen, after being turned out of doors by his father; and here they both are, in lodgings, living upon £2OO a year, which her father allows them. Ile is come to the fittest physician in the world. At present he has got to the Pantheistic stage of philosophy, and in the course of a week, I expect he will be a Berkeleyan, for I babe put him upon a course of Berkeley. It lies sur- prised him a good deal to meet, for the first time in his life, with a man who perfectly understands him, and - does him full justice. I tell him that all the difference between us is that he is nineteen, and I am thirty-seven; and I dare say it will not be very long before I shall suc- ceed in convincing him that he may be a true philo- sopher, and do a great deal of good, with £6,000 a year; the thought of which troubles him a great deal more at present than ever the want of sixpence (for I have known such a want) did me. * * * God help us! the world wants mending, though he did net set about it exactly in the right way. div.head: SUFFOCATED IN A SEWER AT WIDNES. HORRIP,LE FATE OF THREE WARRINGTON
div.p: SUFFOCATED IN A SEWER AT WIDNES. HORRIP,LE FATE OF THREE WARRINGTON
MEN.

The inhabitants of *lanes were startled on Mon- day afternoon by one of the most awful occurrences that has taken place in the town for many years. No less than three men were suffocated in a sewer, two meeting their death in a gallant 'attempt to rescue their comrades, and a fourth had a narrow escape from sharing their fate. It appears that about eight men, who are servants of the London and North-Western Railway Company, were em- ployed in cleaning out a length of the sewer known as Bower's Brook, which drains several chemical works, and empties itself into the Mersey at a point near the works of Messrs. Gossage and Son. The length of sewer being operated upon commenced at the man-hole at the iron bridge, which spans the canal at the Old Marsh, and ended at a man-hole about fifty yards distant. The node of working was as follows. A bucket of peculiar shape is at- tached to a rope, that runs through the sewer, and this rope is fixed to a winch, which being turned, drags the buckbt along the bottom of the canal. The sediment is thus disturbed, and the force of the stream, or a flush of water from the canal, carries away' the refuse to the river. On Monday Robert Whitworth, of Orford-st., Warring- ton, descended into the sewer, which is seven feet deep, and made fast the bucket. to the rope. Afterwards he and William Clare, of Aiken-at., Warrington, followed in the path of the bucket in order to dislodge the sedi- ment that adhered to that portion of the sewer left un- touched by the bucket. At the outset, the atmosphere was clear ; bat, after travelling some yards, Clare said "I smell something strong." Whitworth replied" So do I; come on let's be going along," and as the noxious vapour seemed to be travelling behind them, they went forward as quickly as they could. At the resin works man-hole there was no ladder to enable them to reach the surface, and they pushed on towards the "four foot man-hole" where there was such a convenience. They had only traversed a few more yards when Clare fell down and cried "Oh God help us, Robert! I'm done." "I cannot help thee, Bill," replied Whitworth, "I'm done myself." As well as he could Whitworth shouted, and hi.s cries being feebly heard on the surface; John Monaghan, of Sankey, and John Tyrer, of Winwick, des- cended into the sewer to see what was the matter. The suspictons of the other men were aroused, and they fol- lowed in the wake of their comrades, and were horrified to find all the four men lying at the bottom unconscious. With all possible dispatch the.men were brought into the open air, but this was a work of no little difficulty, as the manhole was only about 18 inches in diameter. The unfortunate men presented a shocking appearance; and Dr. O'Keeffe and several other medical gentlemen, together with several policemen and others, who had been summoned to the scene, displayed great energy in attempting to restore animation. Whitworth was the only one who showed signs of life, and he was removed to the Commercial Hotel, where he eventually recovered to a considerable extent. The dead bodies of his fellow-workmen were shortly afterwards conveyed to the same house.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest upon the bodies at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday at noon. 'Mr. Preston, of Llme-st station, represented dee Railway Co., and Mr. Worthington; district engineer, of Manchester, was also present. Theproceedings were also watched by Dr. Affieck, the District Alkali Inspec- tor. Mr. Tomas Atherton was forernan of the jury. Alfred Tyrer, of Winwick, said John Tyrer wa.s his brother. He was 37 years of age, and was a labourer for the London and North-Western Railway Company. He was a single man. Joseph Clare, of Winwick, deposed that William Clare was his brother, and lived in Aiken-st.; Warrington. He was a labourer for the Railway Company and was 27 years of axe. He left a widow and one child. William Thomas Mitchell, of 14, Kent-st., Latchford, deposed that John Monoghan was his father-in-law. He lived at Back-lane, Sankey. Dr. O'Keeile said he was called to see the men vrho were lying on the canal bank beyond the Iron Bridge. Efforts were made by himself and other medical men to restore animation, but without avail. nip . foreman of the jury (Mr. Atherton) and three police constables worked most energetically in endeavouring to restore animation. Death was,the result of asphyxia by sulphu- retted hydrogen. The sewer was known a:3 Bowers Brook. For the purposes of trade,.portions of the brook had been culverted over. The place where the men lost their lives belonged to the Railway Company . The distance from whore the men entered the sewer to where they were taken out was about 30 yards.—By Mr. Preston Before it en- tered the works the brook was comparatively pure water. There was no asphyxiating vaptur before the brook entered the works._

- Robert Whitworth iof 51, Orford-st., Warrington, said he had worked as a labourer for the Railway Company for five years. He had been in the sewer in question nearly every day during that period. Besides himself and the deceased there were working on the job John Clare, James Bate, Joseph Holden, and Thomas Sankey. John Slaw was the foreman but he was away at St. Helens at the time of the accident. He then gave evi lence bearing out the above narrative. By Dr. Affleck : It was necessary for men to go into the sewer, to see that the bucket did its work. Some- times the sewer snielt strongly ; at other times it was quite sweet. He did not see what could be done to pre- vent such accidents. The gas followed them; they did not produce the gas by wading through the water. There was no gas in the water. By the Coroner: Had there been a ladder at the Resin Works man-hole they might have escaped that way. By a Juryman: When the black water from the Cop- per Works came in contact with the drainage from the Alkali Works, the liquid became green and gas was given off. Joseph Holden, of Sankey Bridges, said he was a labourer for the Railway Company. He had worked at the sewer for eight years. When working the man-holes were always open, so that there would be a current of air. If a man felt he was being over-powered by gas at the Resin Works hole, he would have to shout for as- sistance to get out. He dad gone down an,d found the sewer in such a state that he had had to come up again. They formed their juigment on the amount of danger by the smell and the colour of the water. There had been more gas ix the sewer thisyearthan everbefore. The sediment which was stirred up was sluiced into the river withwater from the canal. In a dry season,when the canal was low, they did not flush the sewer at all. The canal water was only used on instructions from Mr. Shaw, the foreman. In the absence of Mr. Shaw, the deceased man Tyrer gave instructions. Six weeks ago the de- Ceased man Clare afid James Bate were overcome by gas at the same place, and had to be assisted out of the sewer. One was able to resume work at noon, and the other not until next morning. He had seen the patent breathingapparatus used at the works of Messrs Hutchin- son and Co. They did not use such apparatus, nor was a none tied round them.

The inquiry- was then adjourned until Tuesday next, as the Coroner was compelled to leave to fulfil an impor- tant engagement. The usual orders for the burial of the dead were, however, given to the relatives in atten- dance.

WARRINGTON RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIA- TION AND THE GAS QUESTION. On Monday evening a meeting of tha Committee of the Warrington Ratepayers' Association was held in the offices, King-st., the subject for consideration being the gas question. Mr. James Smethurst pre- sided, and there were also present Councillors J. Shaw Green (secretary), and F. Dixon: Messrs. S. ljaVies, John Roberts, T. Jones, W. Roberts, 11. Thornton, T. Flood, J. Dobson, and W. Walker (as- sistant secretary.)—The CHAIRMAN referred to let- ters which had appeared in the papers referring to the Association, and said the writers of the letters were evidently ignorant of the amount 'of time the Committee had spent in considering the position of the ratepayers of Warrington. With regard to the Gas Committee his feeling was that the Committee had acted very wisely in retaining the services of Mr. Paterson, who had been an efficient servant to the Borough of Warrington for a long time, for the small sum of £lOO a year. He knew that the ar- gument would be used apt Mr. Paterson was of opinion that Mr. Haddock was a suitable person for the position of manager. If he thought the payment of £lOO was a pension he would oppose it tooth and nail, but he con- sidered it was wise to retain the services of Mr. Paterson —one so able to give advice to a young man. Compli- cated matters would arise in which Mr. I'aterson's ad- vice would be given, and would be very beneficial to the ratepayers, With regard to the question of leakage he thought the Gas Committee ought to take the bull by the horns and take up the mains which leaked. If the mains were bad they ought to be taken up and f,resh ones put down, especially when there was such a Ihrge leakage as there was at the present time. He was satis; , fled that a public meeting ought to be called to consider the question, especially as so much had been promised by one party or other. He also believed with the Commit- tee of the Ratepayers' Association that a statement of the gas accounts ought to be published separately and distinctly; a statement of the Longford scheme ought likewise to be published. (Hear, hear.) They had been waiting for it for some time. It had been promised, but it was not yet forthcoming.— Mr. Joux Ton' said the Gas Committee of the Corpora- tion ought to give them a full statement—an annual statement of their doings—to which they were entitled by the Corporation Clauses Act of 1871. The statement, however, had not been given, and as consumers and rate- payers they had a right to ask for what the Act gave them. They asked for it nobas a privilege but as a right. There ought also to be a reduction in the price of gas. (Hear, hear.) The price of gas in Warrington was higher than it was in other towns, the quality was in- ferior, and scarcely fit to be mentioned by the side of some of their neighbours' gas. There was another matter he should like to refer to, namely, the perpetual annuities. He did not blame the Town Council for this; the blunder was on the part of the Government in forc- ing Town Councils to purchase them as perpetual annui- ties. In 1871 the Government could not foresee the cheapness of money in 1883, and if they would refer to the "Gas World" they would find that other gas cor- porations were exactly in the same position with regard to these perpetual annuities, and were applying to the Local Government Board for provisional orders to com- pel the annuitants to sell at a certain price fixed by Act of Parliament, and he maintained that the Gas Com- mittee of Warringtoa ought to do the same, and re- arrange their finances in the Gas Committee. These were all important and vital questions for the ratepayers to consider. The power against them was great, and he was astonished when he tooled over the names of the members of the Corporation to find lviw few of the mem- bers' hands were clean in that respect. It was time they had a change, not only in the constitution of the Gas Committee ; they ought to have a re-organization of both I Gas Committee and gas managers from the highest to the lowest. Mr. Toft concluded by proposing "That a town's meeting be held at once to impress upon the Gas Gommittee the necessity of advertising for a manager, and getting the best man for the best wages." DILLON, M.P., SENT TO GAOL.—Mr. John Dillon's appeal from the sentence of six months' imprisonment passed upon him at Mall, on the 11th May, carna on Wed- nesday before the Louth County Court Judge (Mr. Kis- bey, Q.C.) at Dundalk. Mr. Dillon had been convicted of conspiracy to incite tenants not to pay their rents, the charge arising out of a speech which he made at Tullyallen on the tith April. After the Crown counsel had read the passages in the speech on which the prose- cution relied, Mr. Dillon said he had heard many Eng- lishmen use the same expressions. No denial was offered to the evidence tehdered by the police, and Mr. Dillon contented himself with a short speech. , He said it had never been attempted before to charge a man with conspiracy and bring fonward as evidence a single speech, and expressed his belief that the Crown riad pre- sented their case in this careless way because they felt that they could secure a conviction without any trouble. The sentence was confirmed.

DAYIRS seconding the proposal, it hard on the frog. was agreed to. Anyway I could remember the graceful strokes of that frog, and only wanted a chance to put my own limbs through the same movements. I have gone into these little details to show that if you intend to learn from the frog you had better tie a chain to him and keep him in a dog kennel when you don't want him to swim. For fear that I should forget the exact stroke, I hastened into the other room, and, planting my stomach on a chair, I took several minutes' practice, which resulted in my having any amount of confidence in my own powers. As we have a good sized plunge bath in this town, I thought it would be better to practice in than a slipper bath, which I had used formerly. At any rate, I con- sidered it would be plenty large enough for a few weeks, by which time I intended to swim a length in about three strokes, and then I could take the Straits of Dover, or something of that sort. A friend of mine, who could swim, undertook to act as master of ceremonies, and we took down with us a piece of rope, and an inflatable necktie. My friend stood on the side of the bath, and held one end of the rope, the other end being tied round my body, and in this manner I acted the man frog to perfection, and my friend pronounced my strokes to be faultless. I believe I could manage the Atlantic very well after this style, if the ropist could manage a balloon. The next act in the performance was fastening the inflated necktie—a thing like an enormous German sausage—on my neck,for the purpose, as my friend said, not of supporting me so much as giving me confidence in my own powers. "You had better dive in," said my friend; "it looks so very undignified walking down the steps." So I resolved to dive. • I dove. I feel thankful that this is written in the pest tense. I sprang up, turned the seventh part of a somersault, and reached the water at an angle of nothing. There must have been a very peculiar sound or some- thing as I touched the water, for everybody in and about the bath was waiting anxiously for the pieces to float around, when a head energed from the water, with two eyeballs protruding from it in such a manner that, you could almost have hung your hat on them. It made its way steadfastly towards the steps, and gradeally rose out of the water, followed by a body, upon which the glow of health shone up to the 99th degree. Need I say who that noble,figure (blushing along its entire front at the immoderate mirth of the spectators) belonged to ? I think not. I cannot recommend the inflatable necktie for learners to dive in. It has a tendency to make a dive floppy ;'otherwise I could swim with it very well. But all these are nothing but side issues. lily ffiend asked me if I had zufficient confidence to swim without any artificial support. "For instance, said he, "have you confidence enough to dive off the springboard at the deep end and swift:et° this end?" My reply was a practical one. • Was Ito acknowledge that I had studied frogology, and listen to his kind advice for nothing? Scarcely. I walked to that springboard and dived from it with. out any bother. If my description of the result of that dive is confused I must aela the reader to bear with me, and get him to imagine himself under the same circumstances. When I had been under the water for What seemed about half an hour I rose to the surface, and the swim- ming commenced ; at least it ought to have commenced, but somehow I clean forgot all about imitating the frog. I tried to catch hold of the roof, but as this was too far off I tried to shout for somebody to bring something for me to stand on; but everybody seemed indifferent. About this time I was seized with an inordinate thirst, and though I drank copiously I wasn't refreshed. I then went down under the water to see if I could find a way out, but this project failing I again rose to the sur- face, and as the people on the side didn't offer to take any notice of me I commenced splashing the water at them right and left with both hands. I was just about to go down on a second search for an underground passage when something grabbed hold of my hair from behind, and I was bourne to the side and dragged up. I have since calculated that at the speed I went it would have taken me about three years to reach the other end of the bath, that is barring accidents. I desire to pause here to put the inexperienced reader up to a wrinkle. Don't drink so much water. It was no wonder that I didn't get along, for when I came to stand up on terra firma I emptied nearly a gallon of water off my stomach, by which you will see that I'd been considerab'y overballasted. I won't describe the taste of that water, as that isn't the subject, and, besides, I have felt sick several times through merely thinking about it; but if you will believe me, although it is pretty thick, considered as drinking water, a swimmer doesn't derive much nourishment from it. I could easily fill another column with a condensed account of the recollections that whirled through my brain when I was in the water, but as some of them would lose their value if often repeated to me across the hearth, I refrain. Although I regard the first lesson as rather a tough one, I don't intend it to be the last by any means. If you chance to see a man asking the bath manager sometime next week to let about half the water off, so that it isn't more than four feet at the deep end, you can walk up and introduce yourself to me right away. There will be no offence.

With characteristic kindness Mr. John Crosiield, J.P., on Saturday entertained at his residence some three hundred guests, who had been invited to spend the afternoon at Walton Lea for the purpose of viewing the extensive and beautiful grounds.' and of, in other ways, enjoying themselves. The guests were principally the day school teachers, as- sistant teachers, and pupil teachers of W arrington, but invitations had also been extended to the local clergy and ministers of all denominations, and various ladies and gentlemen. Amongst those who accepted the invitation, some of whom were the private guests of Mr. Crosfield, were Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Alderman Davies, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, the Rev. H. G. Smith, the Rev. F. L. and Mrs. Good, the Rev. 0. P. Whalley. the Rev. G. E. Young, the Rev. E. Moore, Dr. and Mrs. Adams, Dr. and Mrs. McFall. Major and Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. and Mrs. Thos. Morris, Councillor J. Shaw Green, and Coun- cillor Robert Heaton. The arrangements for the party were put in the charge of Mr. George Riley, the school attendance officer, who saw to the necessary preliminary work, and who, on Saturday, was kept busy in looking after the requirements of Mr. Crosfield's guests. The guests commenced to assemble at Walton Lea shortly after three o'clock in the afternoon, and from that time until evening there was an almost incessant , coming and going of visitors. The weather was delight- ful, and, as the grounds at Walton Lea are both exten- sive and wonderfully well kept, it was a great pleasure to stroll about them at one's sweet will. The conserva- tories, vineries, ferneries, and peach houses were in- spected, and there were numerous expressions of admir- ation to be heard. The beautiful order in which every- thing appeared to be kept reflects no little credit on Mr. Kipps and the gardeners at Walton Lea. At four o'clock in the afternoon most of the visitors then present sat down to an excellent tea that was served in a large marquee. A staff of waiters paid every attention to the wants of the visitors. Mr. R. H. Pearson's band was present, and during the afternoon selections from vari- ous operas were played. After tea the band played for dancing, which took place in the field adjoining the lawn. Games of tennis and cricket were also played. Shortly before separating those who still remained in the grounds were calledtogether, after which Mr. CORNET (headmaster of Wycliffe Day Schools) said that he did not think it would be well to part, after spending such a pleasant day with Mr. Crosfield, with- out tendering him the best thanks they were able to give for his generous and kindly hospitality, in asking them a second time to his residence. (Hear, hear.) They all knew the deep interest Mr. Crosfield took in all institu- tions connected 'with Warrington, but in none had he taken so deep an interest as in elementary education. For many years he had been associated with one school in particular. He had fostered the growth of education in that school, and had taken a very just pride in the results which had been obtained. But while he had helped that school in particular, and bad watched its growth, he had fostered similar institutions in the town, which were very much indebted to him; their presence there that day was another proof, if it were needed, of the interest Mr. Crosfield took in the work in which elementary teachers are engaged. He proposed that the best thanks of the teachers of Warrington be tendered to Mr. Crosfield for his kindness to them. (Applause.) Mr. Twos (headmaster of the People's College), in seconding the resolution, said that Mr. Crosfield, and his father before him, were the best friends, or amongst the best friends, education ever had in Warrington. The People's College was particularly indebted to Mr. John Crosfield; in fact, so was every school in the town more or less. Not long arm the last school that was erected in the town received' a very handsome donation to its building fund from Mr. Crosfield. He had great pleasure in seconding the resolution which had been proposed by Mr. Corney. (Applause.) The motion having been put and heartily agreed to, Mr. CROSFIELD, in reply, said: am very much obliged to the two gentlemen who have just spokea for moving this vote of thanks to me. I need not tell you that the pleasure to me is quite as great, if not greater, 1, than it is to you, to see you enjoy yourselves on an after- noon like this, with the help of gardens, flowers and music, after your dry labours are over, for I canna call them anything else, from week to week and month to month all the year round. I have always felt a sympathy for the day school teachers, because I know how wean- some and trying their work often is; and, not being Sunday school teachers, they miss the treats the latter often get. I believe Mr. Riley is to blame for your coma ing here to-day, because he has told me several times that he has been attacked by several of the young ladies—(laughter)—who asked him "Are we going to Walton Lea this year?" As you know, Mr. Riley has such a persuasive manner about him —(renewed laughter)—that, although I am a very obstinate man as a rule, I could not resist him, and I said "Very well. If the day school teachers en- joyed their out last year they shall have it again." (Applause.) It has been a very great pleasure to all of us to see you here this afternoon enjoying yourselves in this manner in the open air, and I am sure it is calcula- ted to do you good both mentally and bodily. The two , gentlemen who have just spoken have told you quite truly that I have always taken a deep interest in educa- tional matters, because I believe that no man can confer a greater benefit upon his country than by helping to • educate the children; the fact is that education is the greatest blessing we can have, especially when we grow up to manhood and womanhood. (Applause.) lam confident that the future generations of Warrington will be a vast deal better in every respect owing to the splen- did schools we now have in the town. I always feel in- debted to the teachers of the day schools in Warrington, because!• believe that their labours will have a beneficial effect upon future generations. As I said before, lam very pleased to see you here this afternoon, and I hope, if we are spared, that we may meet again. (Ap- plause).

div.head: GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
div.p: A GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS, Author of "Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," "Wild Gqorgie," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XXIII. ONLY ON WAY.

Irene is sitting alone in the drawing-room; she is piaying dreamy melodies and thinking of Sergius Lens- koff ' • .her thoughts about him are the only pleasing ones she has to dwell on, for her own home, once so happy, has grown terribly changed of late. Lady Fedora seems pre-occupied, and passes the greater portion of her time in her own room; and Geoffrey—' well Irene but rarely sees Geoffrey now. In fact she would be dreadfully unhappy but that her overwhelminglove for Sergins'Lenskoff seems to fill every other void in her life. On a sudden, while she sits there, the door opens, and Marks tells her that Mr. Stanhope wishes to speak to her in his study. A rush of blood comes into Irene's face as she heap this. Naturally she at once thinks it is about the prince he would talk to her; the more se as it is a subject to which Mr. Stanhope has never as yet alluded. Prince Sergius has been a good deal in Eaton- • square since the dinner at the club, but he has come more in a tacitly understood sort of way, and has not been acknowledged as Irene's betrothed. She goes very slowly down to her father's study, seeking vainly to steady her disturbed nerves as she goes. Mr. Stanhope is writing a letter when she enters. "Sit down, my child," he says, keeping her waiting in torture while he finishes his missive, addresses an envelope, &c. Then he draws his chair somewhat nearer to her, and begins rather solemnly. "Irene, I want you to help me in a matter in which we are all deeply interested, but which I can make nothing of without your assistance." Irene opens her beautiful eyes very wide and looks at him in some surprise. It is not then of Bergius Lenskoff he is going to speak. Ferdinand —her thoughts jump at once to Ferdinand,.

_ But no, again she is mistaken, for Mi. Stanhope, after another short pause, which he employs in clear- ing his throat, says : It is about Geoffrey I wish to talk to you." "What has Geoffrey done 2" asks Irene, utterly , mystified, since she has no idea that Geoffrey's pre- ' dilection for Phyllis is known to Mr. Stanhope. "He has done nothing yet, it is to prevent him ' from doing that Which will be most disadvantageous to himself and all of us, that I want you to talk to Phyllis Knight." Good gracious!" exclaimed Irene, who, though utterly aghast, was yet beginning to comprehend the position of affairs. Good gracious, what do you want me to do 2" "You know, I suppose," Mr. Stanhope went on, "that by Simon Knight's will Phyllis cannot marry for two years. I want you to skew her how wrong it is of her to encourage Geoffrey, how ungrateful to us who have done so much for her; and to tell her that If she wishes to act as an honourable woman she will set him free and persuade him to start off abroad on a long foreign travel." "0, papa, how can I do this 7" "You must, Irene—must. It is the only course left. ou are the one person who has an influence over this girl ; she will listen to you. ,What use for me to make sacrifices, and God knows how great the sacrifices are, for the sake of my family, if Geoffrey is to be perniitted to contract a low marriage --as well have an elder son who is in a trade at once, to allow such a thing Your mother is anxious that you should marry—well, we won't enter into that now, the subject is painful to me • but someone in a very different rank of life to Phyllis Knight has offered for your hand. If I waive strong prejudices that you may be in a high position, I cannot allow Geoffrey to drag the family into the dust. I saw him at Wandsworth this very morning. He will in no wise listen to reason from me. In your hands then everything rests—our position in the world your own. You must use your influence over Phyllis I" Irene had sat very still listening to her father, her hands over her face the while, as though she dared not watch his agitation; she withdrew them however, when he had finished speaking, and looking up answered him— " I will try and do what you wish, papa, but it is difficult, since Geoffrey is too angry with me just now to let me talk to him." . _ . . . .

• "Nat to him, Irene, not to him. You must go to Phyllis. Use your influence with her, and make her break with Geoffrey." "Is this quite right and honourable?" asked Irene, looking very,:straight at her father with her frank eyqs. His glance sank beneath them. "How was it, he wondered, that right and honour were so strongly developed in his children? They had scarcely inherited them from him, and perhaps in their constant reference to right and honour, to a great extent Henry tanhope's punishment con- sisted."

Geoffrey had engaged himself, perchance in. a ras' h moment to Phyllis Knight; at all events, he told his father that it was because his honour was deeply in volved, that nothing would prevent him from carry- ing this engagement into the strongholds of marriage., It was in consideration of this resolve of Geoffrey's that Mr. Stanhope, almost in despair when he saw how desperate the situation was, arrived at the con- clusion that the only. thing to be done was to press Irene into the service and get her to induce Phyllis Knight not only' to withdraw her claim on Geoffrey, but to make him understand that under no circum- stances would she consent to be his wife. And now Irene met' him with a question as to whether this striving to , work on Phyllis would be right and honourable ; it was well nigh more than the hardly- tried father could stand, and he cried out in his anguish, "Since when have you learned to weigh my words and set up your own squeamish notions of what is just and honourable, when I tell you what you are to do ?" It was the first time in his life that Henry Stanhope had ever spoken harshly to Irene, and her eyes filled with tears. He did not seem to notice them, how- ever, but went on. "Am Ito be driven into an early grave by my own children, Ferdinand's vices, Geoffrey's low marriage, and you—" "Please, papa, don't talk like that," cried Irene, now fairly sobbing; "of course, you know better than I do; I will do whatever you tell me." This sudden giving in to his will sober Stanhope as by magic, and drawing his daughter to- wards him, lie kissed the pretty eyes as though he wished to swallow her tears and with them every drop of sorrow that might fall in her life. "What I am asking you to do, my .pet, is not half as serious as you think," he said, changing his tone into the -caressive one he usually employed when talking to Irene ;"I only want you to go and see Phyllis Knight, and represent to her how foolish and imprudent both for herself and Geoffrey this marriage will be. Phyllis is a sensible young -Woman, and, if I mistake not, she will more or less fall into your views. Especially she will understand that it is impossible she can ever be- come the sister-in-law of a prince. This last shot of Henry Stanhope's took effect, and Irene's flee was suffused with blushes. "He'- father then intended to give his consent to her marriage with Sergius Lenskoff r and for the first time a sense of pride coming to her as she felt ths possession of a new dignity, she feared that to have Phyllis Knight for a sister-in-law would be indeed a serious drawback to her own,happiness. It was evident that Henry Stanhope had not been in the diplomatic service for nothing, he knew right well how to overcome scruples that might else have proved rather serious obstacles. And so, after only a few m6re wdrds, the father and daughter parted; he would leave the manner of carry- ing out this design of 4iis entirely to Irene; her feminine tact he knew wAld stand her in better stead than any advice which in his man's wisdom he might give her. Henry Stanhope did not calculate -what hours of mental torture this work he had set her would cost Irene, or he would probably have paused before he gave such a task to the child he loved so well that he had at one time contemplated the sacrifice of his own life rather than that of her happiness. , Brought up since infancy with Phyllis Knight for an almost constant companion, how was Irene going to present this girl with the very bitterest cup that can be - offered, to a woman's lips; even that she her Self should say the words that are to separate her for ever from the man she loves ? For no one, not even he himself, knew as well as Irene did how intense was the love Phyllis had for Geoffrey.. • After She left her father's study she went into her own room, locked the door, and sat down to think. What should she do, how carry through to the bitter end this hateful task?
Twice she got up to -ring the bell and summon the maid who generally accompanied her when she wont to Wandsworth, but she sank back again

fnto her seat. She could not go to-day; she felt ag if she had not the courage to face Phyllis with such a request on her lips. Poor little Irene, it seemedl almost as if she were goingthrough all Phyllis's suffer- ings in imagination,and making them her own; and yet she could not form any idea what Phyllis's feelings had been of late, or how much she had changed since the reading of her father's will. _ At last, after a long struggle with herself, lasting for at least half an hour, Irene got up, and this time actually rang the bell. Lady Fedora was lying down with a bad headache, consequently it was the very best moment to go te Wandsworth, and the sooner a disagreeable thing was over the better, she decided— " Yes, she would go." But when the maid answered her summons instead of telling her, to put on her bonnet,she inquired if Mr. Stanhope had gone out yet. "No, he was just going downstairs out of her ladyship's room." \ Irene ran out after him. "May I have the carriage to go to Wandsworth,' papa, as mamma is too ill to go put ? " she asked inl the most natural tone she could assume.

"Yes, yes, my child, I will order it for you 3 Simmons and the brougham." So Irene ' would be able to go to Wandswor without the maid, who she felt would be terribly .01.. the way during the ordeal she had to go through with Phyllis. Arrived at Wandsworth after . a drive which her thoughts had been too painful to enjoy,she stopped en the -Common, told the coachman to put up at the Three Griffins, and walked across to the Brick House. She found Phyllis where Geoffrey had found her in the office, and this time she was not paying her men, but leaning over big green ledgers, though from the tardy way she was adding them up, ; it was evident that thoughts not of figures were filling her mind. *She started to her feet when. she saw Irene, and uttered a cry—th.gre was that in ' her foster sister's face which betokened trouble. ' "What is it, what is it, Irene, dearest? DistresS and annoyance seem to have come on the Stanhope& —do not tell me that the family worry has evei , , reached you." "What ik, you mean by distress and annoyance, ' Phyllis—what have you heard ?" , ' 0, Irene, it is all occasioned by this mad love Of, Geoffrey for me. I knew it would never end in ant good. It has killed my poor father and Mr. Stars.' hope is naturally most displeased at it. After all it is not likely that he and Lady Fedora should be, otherwise than very angry at the idea of Geoffrel marrying me, and yet— ' So Phyllis had entered on the subject herself,l Irene's task would thus be far easier than she had eir- !, pected. She knelt down beside her friend, who was still sitting before her ledgers, and laying her pretty hand against her shoulder, she said in a low voice, "Yes, it is making is all very unhappy. lam so sorry." "Unhappy, you, Irene, how does it make you unhappy? sl thought you always seemed glad that Geoffrey loved me." "0, I am glad—yes—at least I should be if papa—" .f "Go on dear—if papa—" 1 " Well;he seems inclined to visit it on me." ' "On you ! How ? " "I hardly 'like to tell you, Phyllis, but he is dreadfully angry--" " I must know, Irene; doonot spare me. Tell me all the truth. It, would not be fair to let me marl Geoffrey without letting rim know how much miser/ that marriage would bring about. Others besides my poor father might die." Phyllis looked unnaturally cool; it was, however, no sign with her that strong emotions were not raging within.

" Since I must tell you then, dear," began Irene, hiding her face completely among the folds of Phyllis'd dress as she spoke, "I do think if you mart/ Geoffrey it will kill papa." i , "You cannot think how awful he looked thia'n morning, and what dreadful things he said. IR is. making every sacrifice for the sake of h. family he -told me, even going to let me marry th prince, though why it is a sacrifice to papa to let rat 'marry the prince, I can't think, but he says it will be a useless one if you marry Geoffrey." ' "Yes, yes, I fully understand—but the Stanlu family must not be allowed to sink. We—you a. I—lrene, must uphold it," muttered Phyllis, in sort of cold whisper, " woman's duty is sacrifie You must marry Prince Sergius; while I—" "Phyllis t" and Irene looked up now, " 7 you talk in this strange tone? I do not uncle] these incomprehensible words ; what do you mean do ? "

Phyllis bent her head and kissed the girl who wag looking up it her with wide open tearful eyes. 'I must think about it, love; such a grave deci- sion as I have now to make cannot be arrived at rashly. There are more interests .at stake tho,u mine, you knoW." - "Alas, yes," said Irene, very sorrowfully. She had partially gained the object for which she , camp, yet she almost regretted that she had done She rose from her knees, and the two girls 50 looking at each other for several seconds. "Now go,' my darling," said Phyllis at last. "Tell Mr. Stan- hope he may trust me, but I must be alone Of awhile, to think carefully over the responsible act am called on to take in life." Irene shivered and gave a gasp; she could 110 speak,. she had no words to say. She only. ki - Phyllis, and then walked slowly—somewhat humbli —away. The part of princess was at that moment certa. being played by Phyllis. - Irene did not go near the Three Griffins, or send fa the carriage, but wandered about fife common alon • till the shades of evening, creeping up all aroun' reminded her that she must summon Simmons, an' return to Eaton-square. Meanwhile, no sooner had she left the Brick Ho': than Phyllis locked the door leading from the offifr', to the yard, and sat doW2.l' once more among 11' ledgers, but now they were all closed. A long, log time did Phyllis sit there; there were dark ring° about her tearless eyes when she got up at last, and began to pace the room excitedly, as she re., geated over and over again, "There is only one way—one way—my God,telP me to follow it." (To be continued.)

FATAL AFFRAY BETWEEN TURKISH REGIMENTS.

COVRTANTTIQOPLE, SATURDAY.=On Monday last, while the Sultan was on his way to the Mosque for the Bairatn 'ceremony, a soldier of the Arab regiment insulted a man' belonging to the Albanian regiment. On the following 'day the whole Albanian regiment left its barracks, near Yildiz Kiosk, and marched neainat the neighbouring bar- racks, occupied by the Arabs. and on approaching it (Mened ore, the Arabs immediately following Six Men were killed and thirty wounded. Other regiments arriving stopped the fighting, and both barracks were immediately surrounded. The Albanian soldiers were disarmed, and will be sent away. Ismail Pasha, their L commander, has been conveyed on board a Turkish vessel and is to be exiled to Terzan. Ismail Baker Pasha. f. the Yikliz Commandant, has,also been dismissed. The Lord Chancellor took his scat shortly after 4 THE GERMAN EMPEROR'S DEATH.—ADDR.ESS 01`. SYMPATHY. _ _

The NlAmnia of SALISBURY rose to meet an address of i sympathy to the Queen and to the Empress of Germany, owing to the loss that both had sustained by the death of the late Emperor of Germany. The Emperor Frederick had been distinguished by great experience, proved aptitude, flowage in war, high reputation for culture, and for a-knowledge of The arts of pear" and a deep sympathy for the highest and best aani rations of his people. All these things seemed to tit him ror a career of power and of splendid capacity for good. but the expec- tations which had been formed had been dashed to the ground by an Inscrutable &scree. Even in his short reign he had left an example that they might cherish, for he had shown tinder eircurosts flees of singular trial the devotion to duty and the indomitable spirit by which his race had made the greatness of Germany and its own. The Emperor bad died at his post with the devotion eta soldier, without having uny of the encouragement which lightened &soldier's cAling. In agreeing to the address the House would be rendering homage to one of the highest and noblest matures that ever adorned a throne. awl 'GRANVILLE, in seconding the motion, said that death had seldom struck a blow at so shining a mark. Having had opportunities during the last 37 years in England, in Russia, and in Germany, of closely observ- ing the late EmpePor, he could not, even if he wished, recall any defeet which marred the deceased monarch's straightforward and noble character. There was wide- spread sorrow Itt the death of this dashing soldier and beneficent ruler, especially in France, which had so freely achnosiledged the merits of one who was lately their successfnl but generous foe. Deploring the loss of this strong guarantee of European peace, he yet thought there was no solid ground for believing -that peace would be rudely broken. After graceful allusion to the courage' dignity, and devotion of the German Empress, he trusted 'God would give her strength to hear this overyiheltning blow. The address was adopted. -

REFORM OF TFIE PIOTISE OF tORIIS. Lord Sat-Imm; in calling the attention of their lord- shipstothe subject of the reform of the Flouse, said he proposed to lay on the table a hill which, warned by experience, ho had made extremely simple. After enter- ing at length into the history of the question, the noble lord detailed the particulars Of the bill. It proposed the oration of *life peers, not, more than five in one year, and the number limited to fifty. He held that they should be Chosen from the legal. mili- tary, naval, and diplomatic professions, and that a 'Privy Councillor was a 'fit subject for a life peerage. The Queen should also have power to appoint to be a peer of Parliament a person of any special qualification. Restrictions to prevent this power of creating life peerages from being abused were indicated, as well WI the course to be taken with regard to black sheep; and the Premier said the bill was simply designed for strengthening the 'House of 'Lord.. and giving it the power of removing that which was objectionable. adding that which was powerful and.stmng, and enabling it to do its duty better to the country. The Earl of RoseaturPregardr:d this as a modest mea- sure, introdueed in a Singularly modest,speech. The " revolt of the eldest sons" was a most significant sign of the favour in which 'reform was held. It was extra- ordinary that the noble Marquis had nothing more to propose than that a Rear-Admiral, a Major-General, s Privy Counsellor, or an ambassador should be wade life peer. It would be said by many observers that the creation of these life pears would have a tendency to de- 'grade hereditary peers. He believed that the process of expurgation proposed would prove a dead letter. No no would take upon himself the invidious function of censor without a good prospect of success. The Duke of ARGYLL went, out of his way to attack 'Mr. Gladstone.--EarI`GRANYTI.LIt expressed the opinion that the Duke of Argy:l's utterances tended to show that measures of great importance had been delayed by their Lordship's House. The bill was read a first time, and their Lordships ad- ;ourned at 6 40 p.m. HOUSE OF 'COMMONS.—Motrosr.

div.head: LATE EMPEROR.
div.p: THE LATE EMPEROR.

At 4 45 Mr. NV. H. Steturn rose in a very full House, the Prominent members being clad in mourning on either side, to move votes of condolence with the Queen and the German Empress cn the death of the German Emperor. Mr. Smith 'first alluded to the visit of the late Emperor to this country on the occasior of the Jubilee celebrations, and to the admiration and regard which he evoked from the people of this country, and proceeded to deliver a panegyric upon his qualities as a ruler and as a man. He was listened to amid impressive silence.

Mr. fitanteroete, in siesemeling the address, said : It is proposed we should express to her Majesty our share in ! the sorrow she has sustained, and also take measures Mr conveying to the German Empress the expression of our sympathy with her in her trial,. which probably is the greatest that can in any circumstances happen to any human being, and whichiin her case has been illus- trated by a devotion, courage, and patience during the trial of fluctuations and suspense and pain of a twelve- month, and a devotion second only to that of her illus- trious husband. lam sure we feel that on this occasion we are discharging very much more than a mere formal duty. (Clieers,) ' For in truth, if we did not entertain that sentiment we should differ from the whole of Europe., and from the entire civilised world, which regards the event which has just taken place, and the; survivors or 'that event, in the whole course of the experience with whichewe have been made familiar from day to day with a pitying, as well as an admiring sorrow. I greatly 'doubt whether there ever has been a case in which one so exalted in rank and station as was the Crown Prince of .Germany, and subse- quently the German Emperor, has had such claims, I do not Eitty merely upon the admirationebut upon the sym- pathy and pity of the world. (Cheers.) It is touch- ing to reflect on the enhancements of a great trial, which were due to the eincumstanees under which it occurred, the peculiar slowness hand suhtilty of the disease, the extraordinary strength. of the consti- tution of the sufferer, and the great advance in the resources of medical art which enabled .its most skilful professor to procure for the illustriens,Prince a consider- able hut an ineffectual prolongation of life. That pro- longation, which we fondly hoped might be a precursor of his recovery, was in truth but an addition to his suffer. ings. Our recollections of the EmpereriErederick reach hack over a long series of years, and It was iin'Cthe very first period of his happy marriage that'he made a deep impression upon the minds of the people of England. rhey felt that their interest in him was a personal in- terest, and was not founded only on what would have been in itself sufficient to commend it, namely, his near association with our own beloved Sovereign, -hut likewise upon the qualities in early life .he displayed, the high intelligence, the wonderful simplicity and gentleness of character, the kindliness Which made him open to the access of all men, and these qualities ,as time went on were destined to be followed up by afresh development of qualities higher still. When he came baek to this country after the war of 1870 it was im- possible not to be profoundly struck with the fact that one who in his youth had displayed in so peculiar a ,legree all the modesty of youth, and who had on the field of chattle obtained tilt,' very highest distinction, and Shown-that in skill and !valour he was worthy to take his .place amongst the heroes of the world, when he , 4.ettne back it seemed as if all were conscious of that except himself. (Cheers.) His charficter remained precisely the same in its unassuming gentleness, and its total aixse..nce of pretension as it had been before the opeportemity of inenifesting to the world the elkeeep he was so .well entitled to make upon its admiration. There may be a di,position to murmur upon the part of some that the reign of the Emperor Frederick was so short But there is another view which, I think, will change4hat murmur into ehankfulaess, that after all hie ascent to the Throne made him still more conspicuous in the eyes of the world, and caused a yet deeper im- pression of the invaluable qualities of his mind and character to be made both upon the German people and upon mankind at large. (Cheers.) It was well said of hire that in the course of a shert time on the ,Throne he fulfilled a long life, and there was no expectation, however fond, that had been enter- tained before he 'became Emperor which was not fully realised by all. We heard daily of his share in the labours of the State, and of wise and compres hensive views on the condition of Europe which were at the very earliest date made known to his "nation and the nations around. So we have to hope that as far as human sorrow can be alleviated either by the expres- sion of sympathy or by glorious recollections, or by' yet more glorious hopes, that that consolation will be so- }used by those who are now mourning over the death of Us. German Emperor. One wish remains to us, and Ova is thio—ths; the roconootion of his veil croaks.
overruled

his singular union of wisdom and valour, and of wisdom with virtue, and virtue with his known attach-extent to the liberties of his country. and his resiort for its constatution which made him so secure a guardiati el the privileges of the people no less than of the hanouc of the Throne, and all the winning personal qualities which in him showed forth the most beautiful and ap- propriate of all associations, of the extreme of gentleness with the highest manhood, and again that hely recollec- tion that he had displayed upon the bed of suffering a fortitude greater in degree than that of many a soldier and perhaps many a martyr. All these things constitute a great and noble inheritance to the great German people. And we trust that that Freest nation through long periods of strength, prosperity, and virtue will cherish the recollection of the Emperor whom they have lost as amongst the precious possessions that can accrue to the lot of any people on earth. (Cheers.) The Marquis of 4ARTINGTON said notwitstanding any political differences on that side of the House, speaking for everyone with whom he was associated, that he entirely and fully concurred with every word which had fallen from the right hon. gentleman, and thanked him for the eloquent expression he had given to the sentiments which prevailed in every part of the House. (Cheers.) The Speaker then put the motion and declared it carried netn. con.

THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. The House resumed Committee on the Local Govern- ment Bill. An animated discussion took place on Mr. Pickersgilf's amendment to transfer the visitation of prisons from Quarter Sessions to County Councils. The amendment was opposed by Mr. Ritchie and Mr. Matthews. Mr. B. FOWLER, amid Opposition cheers, said there was a desire on the Ministerial side of the House to put the County Councils in a secondary and subordinate position, and the sooner the Committee came to close quarter 3 on that principle the better. The.amendment would be of advantage as a precedent whim the bill came to be pplied to Ireland.—Sir W. HATECOURT also noticed a disposition on the part of hon. members sitting behind the Government to distrust the County Councils and minimise their powers, until they will be tittle more than the old turnpike trusts.—When the Committee divided there were for the amendment, 187; Against, 259; ma- jority against, 72. Several clauses were agreed to, but Clause 6, referring to the power of Quarter Sessions to visit lunatic asy- limos, was struck out.—Mr. CHAVLIN. to allow a full opportunity of discussing what body ghoul(' have the appointment of chief constables and control of the police. moved that progress be reported.--This was done. - The Wine Duty Bill passed through Committee; And the Victoria University Bill was read,a third time. The House adjourned at 12 35.

elosure, and again he was ed by the Chairma r, I on the ground that theyoint at issue had not been suffi- ciently discussed. The ruling caused loud derisive laughter, and cheers on the Opposition benches. The sitting was suspended till nine o'clock. COLONIAL Srocxs,--On business being resumed Sir GEO. BADEN POWELL called attention to Colonial Go- vernment inscribed stocks and their value for trust investments and moved " that, in the opinion of this House, the suitability of Colonial Government inscribed stpcks for trust investments should be more adequately recognised." The income tax returns showed that whilst the income derived in this country from foreign securities had fallen by £2,600,000 in the 11 years from 1872 to 1883 the income derived from Colonial Government PeCUritieg had risen by £3,600,000. That showed that the investing public had great confidence in colonial securities, and when it was said that the Colonies had borrowed at a rapid rate it must be remembered that they were dealing with rapidly-developing communities.—Mr. Osnotont MOR- GAN, in seconding the motion, thought that a wide scope should be allowed in trust investments in the direction of Colonial Government Stocks. Such a step, besides other advantages, would tend to improve the relations which existed between the mother country and the Colo- nies. Nothing would tend more to promote the Imperial Unity,which he for one advocated. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. GOSCHEN said he was not quite sure that the mag: nitude of the debt .of the Colonies was one of the argu- ments in favour of this motion which would commend itself to the House, whatever weight it might have in comparing their credit with that of foreign countries. He must point out that they were not simply asked by the motion to authorise investments in Colonial Stocks, but where wills had been made, and trusts had been established, excluding Colonial Funds that the Legisla- ture should step in and authorise the inclusion of those funds. If they were to legislate in the direction sug- gested by the hon. member the courts would be averse to undertaking the discretion which would be left to them, and it would be to a great extent, if not entirely, inoperative. It would necessitate the schedul- ing of the Colonies with regard to their degrees of credit, and naturally give umbrage in some rases. In conclusion, the right hon. gentleman expressed a hope that the lion, baronet would be content with the discussion he had raised, for it had shown there was every desire in this country to uphold thwedit of the colonies, and that desire would have effect wherever there there was a practical proposal before the House. —Baron Dimsdale and Sir R. Temple followed, and then Mr. Evaws (Southampton) delivered his maiden speech in the House' and was -warmly greeted by his political associates. He opposed the eeesalution.--L-Sir Bamoz rowere. afterwards asked leave to withdraw the motion.—Mr. ANDERSON objected that the Govern- ment should first promise legislation on the subject, but eventually the motion was withdrawn by leave. ECCLESIASTICAL ASSESSMENT IN SCOT LAND.—MT. HUNTER called attention to the assessment of property in Scot- land for ecclesiastical purposes, and moved" that in the opinion of this House it is inexpedient that such lissessment should be maintained, and that in lieu thereof In equivalent annual assessment ot it be made for ssisting secondary education in Scotland."—Mr. FIRTH seconded the resolution.—Mr. JAMES CAMPBELL moved an amendm.nt stating that the House declined to alien- ate eeetes• assessments to secular uses.— Sir C. DATA 111.)1 seconded the amendment. —Sir G. TREVELTAN held that the resolution was one which was directed against especial ecclesiastical privilege, which lay outside the question of disestablishment and disen- dowrnent. He would suggest thattbe resolution should he altered so as to confine the assistance to secondary. education only, and in this Mr. lIVNTER concurred.— The Loan ADVOCATE characterised the resolution as a side-wind working in the lineof disendownaent. It was purely a political move. On a division there were— For the motion Against The result was received with Opposition cheers, re- sponded to by cheers from the Ministerial benches.— Dr. CAMERON described the amendment as of a reac- , tioriary nature, and insisted upon the House going to a division upon it. The Speaker took the chair at 20 minutes after twelve dclock. The Manchester Ship Canal Bill (which had come down from the House of Lords) was read a second time.

On consideration of the report of the amendments to the Libel Law Amendment Bill, Mr. LABOUCHERE moved an addition to one of the clauses giving the defendant power to obtain security as to costs from a plaintiff not domiciled in England, but it was rejected. A new clause was added to the Bill sanctioning the consolidation of actions.—Mr. SAMUEL SMITH carried his clause,amendedat the Attorney-General's suggestion, that the words should not be set out in the indictment in proceedings instituted against the publisher of any ob- scene and blasphemous libel. It was also decided that the publication by request of any Government or police document should be privileged.—Mr. .."II,DERSON moved that the clause providing that a plaintiff could not re- cover unless he showed special damages should be struck out.—Sir A..BOUTHWICH considered the clause most valu- able, and could not consent to its being struck out, es- pecially as its object was to protect respectable news- papers against the attacks of speculative attorneys and , plaintiffs.—Mr. ANDERSON moved that the question be ' put, and the closure motion being adopted the House ' divided on the clause, which was rejected.—The third reading was fixed for next Wednesday. MISCELLANEOII9.—The Reformatory Schools Bill was ordered to be read a third time, and the Distress for Rent (Dublin) Bill was reported. The House then went into committee on the Oaths Bill, and rejected Mr. Norris's amendment to exempt from the operation of the clause persons declaring that they had no religious belief. Soon afterwards progress was reported, and on the motion for adjournment Mr. JoHN MORLEy, amid loud Irish cheers, asked whether it was true that the Court of Exchequer •in Dublin had discharged the prisoners from Killeagh on the ground that there was absolutely no evidence of con- spiracy.—Mr. BALFOUR admitted that the prisoners had been discharged:; but he added—and the assertion provoked loud, laughter—that there was the clearest evidence of conspiracy punishable at common law, though they had no sufficient evidence of the particular kind of conspiracy punishable under the Crimes Act.— The IRBIL SECRETARY replied somewhat petulantly to ,Mr. Sexton, denying the report of his resignation, and the House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Duke of Buckingham, in the absence of the Lord Chancellor, took his seat on the woolsack shortly after .four o'clock MIScELLANEOUS.—The North Sea Fisheries Bill to pre- vent the sale of intoximntsto fishermen on board coopers was read a second time and passed. Lord CARNARVON asked if the Government intended to issue instructions refusing to allow the entry of foreign ships of war and transports carrying troops into our fortified ports.— Lord ELPHINSTONE replied that the subject was under the consideration of the Government; but it would not be convenient to the public service to say how far any result had been arrived at.—A return was ordered show- ing the amount of trade between India andthe colonies; the• Wine Duty Bill was read a first time, mad their Lord- ships adjourned at ten Minutes past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIMSDA.T.
The SPeaTlcei:l-ocoli-the-c—li.a-ii:;itiree Ore PAUPER _HALF-TIMERS IN FACTORIES. —n reply to

Mr. Lees, it was stated by Mr. Rercins that a pro- posal had been submitted to the. Local Government Board that children should be allowed to leave the work- house part of the day in order that they might work as half-timers in factories. It was, however, opposed to the principles of the Act that persons while maintained tin the workhouse should be employed in factories, thus competing with independent labour, and he oould not hold out any promise of an alteration of the THE ATE ELECTION.-Mr. M'Nnitm, was cheered'loudly on rising to ask why the Argyle and Bute Artillery Militia had been sent down to Plymouth at the time of the Ayr election.—Mr. STANHOPE replied that the militia were selected to train at Plymouth in December la,st,*and the order for their embarkation was issued on May 17. No application had been made asking for a change of arrangement, and he added that if any such application had been made it could not have been acceded to.—Mr. APNEita, asked if it was not the fact that there were no fewer than 200 Parliamentary voters in the regiment ; but on this point Mr. STANHOPE was not in- formed. TME IMPRISONMENT OF MR. DILLON, &C.-Mr. GLAD- STONE, rising amid loud Oppolition cheers, asked that a . copy of the record and depositions in the court of first instance and on appeal in the case of Mr. John Dillon, M.P., now sentenced to six months' imprisonment, should be laid on the table of the House.—Mr. BALFOUR remarked that such a course would be an extremely un- usual one, and he should be glad if Mr. Gladstone could give any special reason why it should•be taken in this case.—Mr. GLADSTONE was prepared to give the reasons, but said it would be the Speaker's duty to check him, therefore he would put the question on the paper.—The Chief Secretary was further questioned as te the Killeagh case, and, driven into a corner, promised to make an authoritative statement on the subject. SUPPLY, &c.—After another protest from Mr. Cmur.,- DEES, at the introduction of the ad valorem principal, the Wine Duty Bill was read a third time.—The House went into Committee of Supply, and on the vote of £1,410,000 for warlike and other stores, Mr. PIANBURY drew attention to the remarkable scandals at Wool- wich, and made some extraordinary revelations as to the ways of contractors and the character ,d the stores they supplied. The Gevernment were bound to show that the department was properly organised, and that time country's /parley would be well spent. He concluded by moving the re- duction of the vote by £l,ooo.—Mr. STANHOPE replied, admitting that defective stores had been sent in, and that he could not defend the system that had obtained at Woolwith ; but he said he had tried his utmost since he came into office to make the system of inspection of war- like stores independent and real.—The discussion was continued by Lord RANDOLPRCHURCHILL and other mem- bers. On a division the motion was rejected by 131 rotes to 96. The vote was agreed to.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. STANDING ORDERS.—Upon the motion of Earl CADOGAN to name certain of their lordships members of the Select Committee appointed to consider'the Standing Orders of the House, 'Lord HERSCAELL inquired whether the terms of the reference would give the Committee the power to examine into the advisability of ,appointing Standing Committees each session, somewhat similar to the Grand Committees of the other House, and to one or other of which alibills should be referred for consideration unless the House should otherwise order. lie thought that that .would be of great assistance in putting legislation into better shape.—Earl CADOGAN said that it would be unnecessary to enlarge the scope of the reference for the purposemamed.—The motion was agreed to. - BILL ADVANCED.—The National Debt. tSupplemental) Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at fi 0 p.m. 'HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 2 p.m. QUESTIONS.

A number of inquiries were addressed to Mr. Balfour, as topolice interference with, and intimidation of, street newspaper vendors in .Irefacd, and he replied that the police only interfered with those persons who caused obstructions.

The main question appeared in the name of Mr.'Flyrin. but Mr. Sexton and other Irish members put supple- mentary questions; and in the end the Speaker called several of the hon. gentlemen to order. Sir 'JAMES FKILMTSSON informed Dr. Farquharson that he hoped an arrangement might be Made with the .authorities of certain Swiss cantons, whereby English doctors might be enabled to practice in Switzerland.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Monday witnessed the completion of the third week of Mr. Bright's confinement to his bedroom. His doc- tors report him to be out of danger from the congestieu of the lungs. but he is still exceedingly weak. _ _

Mr. Angus Holden, the selected Liberal candidate for be Duckrose Division, addressed a large meeting at Driffield on Monday. Mr. Holden expressed his political views at large, and strongly denounced the Irish coercion policy of the Government. His reception was most cordial. Mr. W. A. Mc.Arthur, M.P., also spoke.

Mr. Michael Davitt, speaking on Suniay, at a meeting in county Kildare, said it was impossible to exaggerate 'he significance of the Ayr election. The sentence upon coercion and injustice in Ireland was written as plainly and menacingly by that event as was the writing on the wall at the feast of the Assyrian King. At home and Abroad this Coercion Government was rapidly losing credit, and the time was coming when Lord Salisbury would have to eat his words about 20 years' vigorous i:overninent of Ireland.

The Grand Committee on Trade met on Monday, Sir Matthew White Ridley presiding, and further considered the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill. Sir B. Samuelson moved an amendment to clause 13, giving the com- missioners power to order two or more railway or canal •tompanies to charge through rates for the conveyance of eaods. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach accepted the principle. and undertook that a clause embodying it should be in- serted in the bill. On clause 17, which provided for an appeal from the commissioners to a superior court, and thence to the House of Lords, a long discussion took place as to the desirability of permitting more than one Appeal. Eventually, on the motica of Sir B. Samuelson. the permission to appeal to the House of Lords was ~truck out of the bill, without a division. . THE ISLE OF THANET CONTEST. The writ for the election for the Thanet Division of Kent has been received, and Friday, the 29th inst., has been fixed for the polling. Mr. James Lowther, Conservative candidate for the Thanet Division of Kent, was publicly introduced to the constituency at a largely attended meeting held in the Amphitheatre, at Ramsgate, on Saturday night. Mr. Lowther, in the course of his address, said nearly twenty years ago Mr. Gladstone was returned to power specially to deal with the Irish question, and he succeeded in passing into law two measures which were nothing short of sheer robbery. The first was the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and the second was the confiscatioi, of proprietary rights in land which was handed over to the avowed enemies of Great Britain. He (Mr. Lowther) pointed out at the time that this policy was bound to prove a failure, and Mr. Gladstone admitted it to be so Mr. Lowther did not think there was any great demand for the Local Government Bill, and he doubted if the new article would prove better than the old one.—Mr. Akers Douglas, M.P., and. Mr. Penrose Fitzgerald, M.P.. also spoke, and a resolution was passed approving of Mr. Lowther's candidature. Mr. James Lowther, in his address to the electors, say- it will be his earnest endeavour to aid in securing the continuance of a firm and courageous administration of law in Ireland. Mr. Knatchbull-Flngessen says the, choice of electors will be confined to the adherence to a policv of reactionary Toryism or given from a new and bold departure on the lines of truly Liberal progressive principles, and in the concession of a generous measure of domestic self-government to Ireland.
AYR BURGHS ELECTION.-GRAND LIBERAL VICTORY. _ _
