A Scotch correspondent points out that it is an error to describe the new member its "Captain" Sinclair, and to vete that he had unsuccessfully contested the seat itt r.l!, Liberal interest against the late member. It was captain Sinclair, of Caithness, who opposed the late member in 1836. The newly-elected member is Mr. John of Grangemouth, a retired Free Church minister. Tie now enters Parliament for the first time, and is the .ifty-third new member who will have taken his seat in st. Stephen's since the last general election.

SIR W. HARCOURT AT STOCKPORT.-Sir W. Harcourt was the principal speaker at a great meeting of the Liberals of Stockport, held on Wednesday night, under the presidency of Lord Vernon. In response to an ad- dress which was presented to him, the right hon. gehtle- man delivered an important speech in which he discussed the political situation. Referring to the recent Liberal victories, he said that the enemy were shaking along their whole line, and all that Liberals had to do was to push their advantage with energy, with courage, and with confidence, and they would inflict upon the Tories a rout like that of 1880. The results of the Southamp- ton and Ayr elections, followed by the defeat of Tuesday night in the House of Commons, had had a sobering effect on the Government. The Liberal Unionists were beginning to think of their latter end. Southampton and Ayr were warnings, and the shadow of the division of Thanet was over them. Criticising with some severity Mr. Chamberlain's attitude, Sir William said that in the Liberal thermometer there was a lower depth even than the Whig zero, and it would be found that the Radical Unionists of Birming- ham were a good many degrees below that zero. What was now happening throughout the constituencies was this. Doubts and hesitation which kept men from the poll in the previous election had disappeared, and Liberals of all kinds who were real Liberals were return- ing to the old standard and the old leader. All attempts to set up a new and rival party had totally failed. He believed Mr. Dillon would suffer in his person for the knock-down blow which he administered to the Govern- ment at Ayr ; but imprisoning their political opponents was the coercionist conception of political argument and political justice. They might try to destroy Mr. Dillon, but he was quite sure that Mr. Dillon would destroy them. At the close of Sir William Harcourt's speech Mr. R. Wallace addressed the meeting, and a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone was unanimously passed.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Rev. Dr. 'fhicknesse, Archdeacon of Northampton, has been appointed Bishop Suffragan of Leicester. By the assembly for training of seven more regiments, the number of militia under arms in this country on Monday reached 50,000. The teasers at Messrs. Hartley's glassworks, Sunder- land, have struck work for an advance of Ss. a week. There are 250 men affected.

On Saturday, a boiler 'exploded on the tug Admiral, in the Tees, at Middlesbro'. The engineer was killed, and two other men were injured. At a mertinff of the Northumberland coalovrners, on Saturday. Mr. Burt, M.P., and the miner's delegates ap- plied'for 15 per cent. advance. The application was ad- journed for consideration. Orders have been received at the Royal Small Arms Factory, Enfield, for the manufacture of a large number of the new magazine rifles. About 400 men have been working overtime during the past week. The Bishop of Peterborough, speaking at Kettering. on Monday, on almsgiving to the Church, expressed himself as strongly opposed to bazaars and fancy fairs, which he thought most objectionable contrivances for raising money. MUTINY IN A CONVICT PRISON.-A revolt has taken place in the prison at Kovba, near Baku. Eighty-four convicts were concerned in the movement, and of these several were killed and wounded, while a few escaped. Nine soldiers were killed.

Two men, named Chapman and Partridge, married and with families, were accidentally drowned, near hultrock Lydney, Devon, on Saturday. They were fish- ing for salmon, when the current cut the sand from under them, and both were carried away. A third man narrowly escaped. During the last week nine persons have lodged com- plaints at the riornsey-road Police Station, London, that many ladies have had valuable sealskin and other jackets destroyed by vitriol, thrown by malicious youths in the streets by means of toy squirts. None of the perpetrators of the outrages have been arrested.

Mr. Gladstone has definitely promised to attend and preside at the second day's proceedings of the National Eisteddfod, to be held at Wrexham on the 4th, 6th, and 7th of September. The Prince of Wales has been invited to take the chair on the opening day, and if his arrange- ments admit of his presence, it is understood that His Royal Highness will consent.

THIS FATAL QUARREL AT TFIR BRADFORD WORKHOUSE.— On Monday-, at Bradford Police Court, Henry Sander- son, 54, an inmate of the Bradford Workhouse, was charged with having caused the death of William Mar- shall, an inmate of the Workhouse, by beating his head on the floor during a quarrel. The prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the assizes.

CARDINAL MANNING'S EPISCOPAL JUBlLEE,—Cardinal Manning will, in June, 1890, celebrate the silver jubilee of his episcopal consecration, and already a movement is on foot to present him on the occasion with a testi- monial in recognition of his services in the causes of religion, education, and temperance. A large and in- fluential committee of the clergy and laity has the project in hand. DEATH, OF LORD ROBERT GROSTENOR.—lnformation was received at Eaton Sall, Chester, on Saturday even- ing, that Lord Robert Grosvenor, son of the Duke of Westminster, died at Conbtantinople on Saturday morn- inc,. Lord Robert, who was 16 years old, was travelling in the East with a tutor' and contracted a cold when at Jerusalem. This was followed by an attack of typhoid fever, from which he died. The Duke and Duchess of Westminster are at Cleveland.

At Glasgow Police CA2urt, on Monday, 52 men were brought up charged with drinking in the Glasgow Argyll Club, on Sunday. The premises were unlicensed. The detectives, who had a warrant to enter the club, knocked at the door at night, pushed in, and at a signal 30 policemen surrounded the place, and arrested the occu- pants. Forty-four of them pleaded guilty, and were each fined 10s. The others, who pleaded not guilty, will be tried.

Sin Monett Mscxerare's Frs.—Curiosity has been exercised of late as to the amount of the fee likely to be received by Sir Morell Mackenzie for his professim al attendance on the late Emperor Frederick. Here is the very newest report, which, it is needless to say, contra- dicts all the others. He is to get a sum equal in English money to about £3,000 a quarter or any part of a quarter. His income in London.of late years is said to have been ever £15,000 a year. The Emperor is not the only patient he has in Germany. Some of his English patients even have travelled thither for consultation.

- DESTITUTION AND ATTEMPTRD SUICIDR.—At Manches- ter, on Monday, an old woman. named Mary Wilson, who was charged with attempting to commit suicide, told a terrible story of privation owing to the insufficiency of her remuneration at a costume factory. Her story was that for a week's work she only earned 2s. 2d., out of Which 6d. was stopped for cotton and hot water, and 6d. for a loan she had from the forewoman. She was rescued from the canal through the agency of a little fox terrier dog, which the owner discovered endeavouring to pull her out The magistrates suggested that the animal should be decorated with the Humane Society's medal, and discharged the woman. AN ENGLISHMAN'S "STRAIGHT TIPS." —An amusing instance of English audacity and French credulity is just reparted from Paris. -Just before the Grand Prix, an innocent-looking man, who casually remarked that he was the jockey Madge, took rooms at a first-class hotel. The landloed, in consideration of "straight tips,' which his guest at once confided to him, advanced him £2O, and provided his board free. The head waiter, too, slipped bank notes for large amounts into the horsey man's palm, and soon all the local unsophisticated turf votaries p rrd gold into the jockey's pockets in order to receive I. s tips. When the 'celebrated English rider" had netted a small fortune he decamped, leaving his vic- tims to discover the fraud. They lost heavily, having hacked horses which were "not in it." Warsaw° DAL—LANCASHIRE REGIMENTAL Elosotors. —Monday being the 73rd naniversary of the battle of Waterloo, the occasion was observed with the customary honours by the regiments which took part in the memorable fight, and in that at Quatre Bras two days previously. The only Waterloo officers now on the Pension List are General Whichcote, who received his first commission in 1811, and General the Earl of Albemarle, who joined the Foot Guards as an ensign only eleven weeks before the great battle; and the list of non-comtnissioned officers and men receiving the special Waterloo pension is now very small. The Lan- cashire regiments which decorated their standards with laurel, as having been at Waterloo, are the King's Own Royal I ~incaster. the East Lancashire, and the South Lancashire.

INDEPENDF.NT METHODIST CONFERENCE.—The eighty- third annual assembly of the United Free Gospel, or Independent Methodist Churches, commenced at Bolton onMonday ; Mr. W. Crumbiehuhne, of riolton, the retiring president, in the chair. There were ninety repre- sentatives present, the chief towns of Lancashire, Cheshire. Yorkshire, and Durham being repre- sented. The Connexional officers were appointed, as follow :—Mr. W. Crumhlehulme, Bolton, president; Mr. T. Worthington, Wigan, vice-president; Mr. R. Foulds, Colne. secretary; Mr. H. Kennedy, Southport, vice-secretary; Alderman Dyson, Oldham, treasurer: Mr. J. Settle, Boltqn, Connexional auditor; and Mr. W. Brimelow, Bolton, Connexional editor.—Last evening, a public meeting was held, when Addresses were given by Mr. Matthew Kennedy, Southport, on "True success; Mr. P. Worthington, on "Our church pouts-; " Mr. A. Roscoe, Bolton, " Our ministry ; " and Mr.. Bolton, Sun- derland, " How to increase attendance on public worship." MEMORIAL TO NEWSPAPER " SPECIALS."—On Satur• day, Lord Wolseley, who was accompanied by Lord Charles ' Beresford and other officials who served in the war in the Soudan, unveiled a memorial in St. Paul's Cathedral, to the special correspondents who fell in the cardpaign. The company then proceeded to the Press Club. where the visitors were welcomed by the president (Mr. Walker). Lord Wolseley referred in the highest terms to the personal qualities of Mr. Cameron, Mr. St. Leger Herbert., and other correspondents with whom he was personally acquainted. When men in time to come re”• ~red those to whom this Memorial had been erected, ..ey would say that. those had done well who built it tip to the memory of men who did their dirty to their employers. :Lnd to their country. Lord Charles Beresford also spoke in eulogistic terms of the correspondents whom he had met, SAD BOATING ACCIDENTS • FAHER AND SOst DROWNED. --,On Sunday night.. Et. Buchanan, of Ayr, his son. and hiS brother Archibald, were out yachting in Ayr Bay, and they left the yacht in a punt, with a can called Parker, to go ashore to bathe. On returning, the punt overturned. Roiert Buchanan took his son on his back to swim, and clung to the punt, which Archibald Buchanan towed safely ashore. Robert and his son however, never Teethed the shore alive, but sank.— Three young men. Their boat, however, was tinet half-way. Walsh and Murray Ivaelied ail island in an exhausted condition, white they were found on Monday, but their companiiins were all drowned.

A 14 my Srs.AmEn : Loss or LIFE.—The new paddle steamer Princess of Wales was proceeding down the Firth 4,4 Clyde for her trial trip on Saturday after- noon, and when near Wemyss flay she came into col- lision with the steamer Flalmoral Castle. The Princess of Wales was cut nearly in two about 50ft. trom the stern, and at, once commenced to sink. The steamer Adele went to her assistantie. and took her in tow for the purpose of running her ashore, hut when about 400 yards from the beach the tow rope had to be cut, and the Princess of Wales foundered, her boiler bursting as she went down. The crew, some of whom were slightly injured by the explcsion, were re.cued by boats, but two workmen to the service of the ntractors were drowned. The Princess of Wales was recently built by Messrs. Barclay and Curie, Glasgow, for service between Southampton and the Isle of Wight. The Balmoral Castle was little injured, and proceeded up the Clyde. She formerly belonged to the Currie line of Cape ateamers.

KNITTSFORD v. WARRIXGTON. - Played at Arpley on Saturday, and resulted in a decisive win for the home team by 77 runs. Jackson and Rycroft commenced the Knutsford innings to the bowling of C. G. Lawton and J. J. Crosfield, but so well did Lawton bowl that the whole side were out for the small total of 68, and with the exception of Monkhouse, who played a good defen- sive game, and scored above half the runs from the bat, the batting was very weak. The bowling of Lawton was first-class, and he kept a very good length all through the innings. His analysis was-19 overs, 8 maidens, 33 runs, 7 wickets. Clarke secured two wickets for six runs, but the bowlers were wellbacked up by bril- liant fielding. Podmore made a brilliantcatch in thelong field, and Wallington also secured two clever catches at slip. Warrington were first represented by Crosfield and Reynolds, but after a few overs Reynolds was easily se- cured at slip, making way for C. G. Lawton. The new comer did not seem at home with the bowling, and got hit about the fingers and body several times very badly. He was at length bowled for sixteen. and Clarke came in. After playing steadily for a few overs he scored six- teen (three leg hits and a cut) in one over of Sawyer's, the fifth ball being out of reach. Crosfield was unfortu- nately run out when he seemed well set. Podmore, although he only made seven runs showed perfect cricket and strong defence; and Fairclough and Myle- ehreest when together caused much amusement by their dodgy runs. Score :

The match between Notts and Lancashire was 014 Wednesday abandoned as a draw owing to the heavy rain. The weather was also wet at Birmingham on the same day, when the Australians resumed their match with an Eleven of England. As the Australians were anxious to get the match over they went out to field while it was still raining fast, and Turner and Ferris had to bowl with a greasy ball. Mr. Bainbridge was bowled at 77, but Mr. Thornton came in and, amidst loud cheer- ing, hit four 4's, saving an innings defeat. Soon after, however, both Mr. Docker and Slulton were bowled, and the innings closed for 99. Wanting seven runs to win, , Worrall and Boyle went in at 20 minutes past twelve, and, amidst heavy rain, hit off the runs in ten minutes, the Australians winning by ten wickets. At the match between Warrington and Knutsford, on Saturday, every bowler got hit about the body, and C. G. Lawton had his finger broken. Knutsford batted first, and only Monkhouse stayed against Lawton and Crosfield. Monkhouse made 33 not out, in a score of 68;. Lawton had seven wickets for 33 runs. Lawton received several blows on the body, and at last was ht on the hand. Clarke hit Sawyer for four 4's in one over, and left for 23. The match was won with three wickets down, and then the bowling was hit freely. Mylechreest made 21 not out, an I the innings closed for 145. On Saturday the Tyldesley cricketers were opposed by St. Helens Recreation. St. Helens, on a splendid wicket, started well, the first three wickets producing 53 runs; but, owing to the effective bowling of A. Broome, who took seven wickets for 22 runs, they were all disposed of for 75 runs. Tyldesley also commenced well, IV.Eckers- ley (12) and P. Woodhouse (13) being the first batsmen. It was, however, left for A. Broome to carry off the batting honours, this player following up his excellent bowling performance by tnaking 28 (not out), which ' really won the match for Tyldesley, who scored 81 runs. H. Allen, of Warrington, is riding remarkably well at present, and the consummate ease with wlaieli he won Friday's event at Widnes made him a popular favourite for Saturday's Open Mile, which he had little difficulty in securing, again followed home by Garnett, who, after falling a few yards from the tape, walked his machine in some five yards ahead of J. Hargreaves, who, by the way, was the only Liverpool rider able to secure a prize at the meeting. A great number fancied Allen ,for the double event; but, unfortunately, his axle worked loose, or I fancy he would have troubled Garnett before the finish. As it was, the latter had a very easy journey in the Three Miles, winning eventually by sixty yards from W. H. Stubbs and R. Jackson, of Manchester. Webster, of Warrington, would have been well up Vr a place had he not " croppered " after covering a counle of miles. S. R. White, of the Sefton and Dingle collided with Harry Green, of the North Liverpool 8.C., when trying to pass the latter on the inside. White ap- pears to be rather fond of passing his men on the inside, and perhaps his cropper last Saturday will have the effect of bringing him to his senses.—" Athletic News."

Mr. Condon, M.P.. was released from Cork Gaol, on Wednesday, after undergoing a month's imprisonment for advising persons not to pay the Constable Leahy tax. On Wednesday, as three men were descending the new shaft of the Roundwood Colliery, Wakefield, the bucket swerved, and two of the men were pitched to the pit bottom and killed. '

Mr. RITCHIE, however, fails by essaying the part of Mr. FACING-BOTH-WAYS; • be prates of "trust in the people," but when it comes to legislation, his trust is thrust aside. It , 18 not without its lesson that both these politicians Were beaten on Tuesday; Sir WALTER BARTTELOT. !as in a hopeless minority; and Mr. RITCHIE went down under a majority agaidst him of thirty. A :little later on MT. STANLEY LEIGHTON showed how, ,i.i ttle he had learned as a Tory by proposing to get ver the difficulty by substituting the Home 3cretary for the Joint Committee in the manage- ?flea of the police. As if the Home Secretary had Xot more than he could manage in the direction of the London police! Mr. C. GRAHAM gave the :death-blow to this ridiculous suggestion by ob- tierving that there were only two places in the kingdom where the police were in collision with ,be people—lreland and the metropolis—and in /both of these the police were under the direct con- ° ol of the Crown. Mr. LEIGHTON'S amendment .W 5 quickly negatived without .a'division ; and as -the bill now stands, the county police—from the Chief Constable down to the rawest recruit—will be under the control of the Joint Committee of Inagistrates and members of County Councils. la ut this is not satisfactory. "A system which," .8e Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT observed at Belper, excited first of all the most profound distrust of the popular vote, and in the next place erected a 'dual control over the police, was, in his opinion, absolutely unworkable, and would demoralise the Police force itself." The Liberals in the House of 'Commons must therefore continue their efforts to amend this portion of the Local Government Bill. They will have another opportunity when it conies up for the report stag; they have compelled the Government to yield on several points, and must Compel them to yield again. It is a merit in the Rinistry-such as it is-that they become virtuous on oftipulsion ; they dare not go before the country they have betrayed, and will do anything rather than dissolve.

THE FUNERAL of the late Emperor FREDERICK took place on Monday, and on Monday evening both Houses of Parliament unanimously adopted . -addresses of condolence with the Queen and with ,the Empress in the great bereavement they 'aye sustained. The language which was em- , Ployed on the occasion testified in the warmest

411(1 most direct manner to the true nobility of • character of the late Emperor. It is customary • .04 occasions such as this to hear sentiments ex- pressed of a formal and commonplace kind; the klulation is sometimes forced, if not insincere; but ill the case of the references to the late Emperor it was obvious that the speakers felt what they 414, and that too great a tribute could not be paid t° the ruler who will live in the memory of the People of Germany as Frederick the Good. In illoving the address in the House of Lords, the I'IRIME MINISTER said : It seems as though there was accumulated upon his head every possiblequalificationfor a life of glori- us, splendid, and peaceful usefulness. Great ex- Perience, proved aptitude and courage in war, a high reputation for culture and for a knowledge of the rors of peace, a deep and well understood sympathy all the highest and best aspirations of his People, the support of a Consort never surpassed in der ability, her affection, her constant enthusiasm for right—all these things seemed to fit him for a career of power, and of splendid capacity for good, \ career which might well have been as long as that his illustrious father. ia testimony of the highest kind; Lord GRAN- could not hope to add to such an eloquent 7 • but he went to the heart of the matter ' . he remarked say of the departed peat that they were hout fault seems to be vulgar, unmeaning flat- 07Y. It cannot be quite true; and yet, having had tortunitie- during the last 37 years in this coun- tP:t in Russia, and in Germany, of closely observing late Emperor, I could not, even if I wished, re- an error which marred his straightforward and 1,0,01 e character. tlat a splendid tribute this to the wisdom as as the goodness of the man! Mr. W. H. sitrit, in the House of Commons, after appropri- ;elY referring to the courage and capacity of the rince as a commander, added lie could face death with his men in battle, and knew how to care for the wounded and the sick L"r the struggle, and to see that order was restored c,.,111°11g the civil population. But these qualities are 401Inon as comp 'red with the fortitude which en- -2,11,e8 a man on whom a fatal disease has fastened. a'(id,g slow but sure progress from day to day, deerfully and uncomplainingly to endure long and evous suffering, and to go about his daily work Preined in the discharge of his duty by a sense of ~'evotion to his country. I'Learn to suffer without complaining" was the 'aaon which, it is stated, the late Emperor sought te impress upon the son who has succeeded him as ruler of Germany; and he showed by his life and hY his death that with him precept and example 'were one. It was fitting that Mr. GLADSTONE, the freatest statesman of the age, should pay the final Pbute, in the House of Commons, to the charac- 'er of the noblest Prince of modern times. In con- cluding a brief panegyric, he said:— tut one wish I think remains to us, and it is this -that the recollection of his great qualities, his Igular union of wisdom and valour—of wisdom ^rith virtue and valour—with his known attach- to the liberties of his country and his respect er its constitution whiv.di made him so secure a pardian of the privileges of the people no less ja'!ali of the honour of the throne, and all the win- tng personal qualities which in him showed forth, ttt Most beautiful and appropriate of all associa- 'oilB, of the extreme of gentleness with the highest lhood, and again the holy recollection—to which right hon. gentleman has referred—that he had flayed upon the I)ed of suffering a fortitude i3'etiter in degree than that of many a soldier, and ,thaps many a martyr—all these things constitute great and noble inheritance to the great German th2Ple. And we trust that that great nation, vi,...'Qugh long periods of strength, prosperity, and I.le, will cherish the recollection of the Emperor : pc, °ln they have lost as amongst the most precious ollsessions that can accrue to the lot of any people earth. Aft er this what more could be said? Lord '4ltrixurox felt that it would mar the effect to 4`llod any words of his own; but lie did that which oanY will think was far bettor; he thanked Mr. LkosroNE, " notwithstanding any political dif- :Nlicea which might unhappily exist," for "the I.leir3l eloquent expression of the feeling and senti- I:4 which prevailed in every part of the House." IIArTINGTON was softened; he felt, as all .tav e felt, that touch of nature which has made the qu world kin in sympathising not only with the eert, but with the Empros VICTORIA and the -°Ple of Germany. div.p: turn on the Home Rule Question (forgetting that letters from Lord HARTINGTON, MT. CHAMBERLAIN, and Mr. GLADSTONE, kept Ireland before the con- stituency). In short they see every reason for their defeat except the real reason, and that is, that in the Ayr Burghs, as everywhere else, where Liberal Unionists were previously returned, a change has taken place in the views of the electors. The Liberals who doubted if it were wise to go the full length of giving Home Rule to Ireland, and who thought that Coercion was not necessarily the al- ternative of Conciliation, now see that they were in the wrong; and, more than that, they are dis- gusted with those of their leaders who promised them that reform of local self-government should be effected in Ireland without recourse to Coercion. They could not believe, after observing how the Tories allowed the Crimes Act to lapse, that they would, withoutioause, force through a more strin- gent act; nor could they conceive that even Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL would, within two years, be under the necessity of telling the Government to their teeth that they had broken the pledges which they had made to the country. But the facts are before them; they are not to be ignored ; and the result is such a reaction as was shown at Southampton, and as is revealed in the election at the Ayr Burghs. The country is now ripe for the return of Mr. GLADSTONE to power, and every week, as things go, the Government get deeper in the mire. Let Liberals prepare for a General Election; "the readiness is all."

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Mr. John Dillon, M.P., is again sent to gaol— this time for six months! This is a disgrace—not to Mr. Dillon, but to the Chief Secretary for Ireland.

Yesterday, in the House oS Commons, Mr. John Morley gave notice of a motion condemn- ing the Government with regard to the im- prisonment of Mr. Dillon. Mr. Gladstone asked for a day for the discussion, and it is set- tled that the battle royal shall commence on Monday.
Well done, Ayr! As Burns has it— Auld Ayr, wham ne'er a town surpasses, For honest men and bonny lasses; [And Radicals amongst the masses.]

The conversion of a Tory and Liberal Unionist majority of 1,175 into a Liberal majority of 63 that z's victory! And yet, so completely are Cham- berlain and Co. out of touch with the people that they actually talked of the progress they were making in Sotland. There is progress, but it is not in the direction of the illiberal 'Unionists.

The poet Shelley was something of a seer. Could he have anticipated the plight of Liberal Unionism when he sang— We look before and alter, i* And pine for what is not? Our P.D. is not a seer; he waits for the event to come off and then states the issue in this way— Before. Said Joseph to Evelyn, "I swear You're certain to beat that Sinclair." After. Said Evelyn to Joe—" I declare— We've been building a castle in air !

We are in a position to contradict the rumour that the, committee of the Conservative Club pro- posed to run their flag half-mast high on receipt of the news of the Ayr election. Something of the sort has been talked of ; but it is felt—so many are the defeats of the Government and the Tory party—that if they hoist the flag half- mast high every time there is a disaster, they will never have to take it down—as Paddy would say.

Ladies who are tired of a single life need not "go to a nunnery," or to "Jericho ;" they must go to Japan. "In Japan, the rule which obtains in Europe is reversed ; there the males prepon- derate. At the last census there were 19,157,977 males and 18,711,110 females." We always did like the Japanning process; it gives such finish, you know.

According to the "Scotsman," the Earl of &a- field was at one time a bailiff; and vs in posses- sion of a house at Oamaru, New Zealtrnd,when the news reached him that he had succeeded to the earldom. There is nothing, of course, inappro- priate in this. The Peers have had possession of a certain House for many years. Their title is certainly of a questionable kind, and they have abused the opportunity so much that there is a disposition, all round, to make them clear out.

Saul, however, is now amongst the prophets; Lord Salisbury hits taken to reforming the House of Lords. His notion of setting things right with the addition of a few life peers is about equivalent to putting a fifth wheel on an old coach with the idea of fitting it to compete with a loco- motive. But his lordship is "only preten- ding," in the belief that it will keep the people quiet for a time. It will, but for a short time only.

The Rev. J. Lockwood will do well to Oress the matter of the necessity of dealing with what is alike a danger and a nuisance at Halton. Although the chairman of the -Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority declined to put the resolu- tion to take immediate action, he would not feel very comfortable if an accident were to happen as the result of leaving this bad thing alone. If the opinion of the Local Government Board requires to be taken, it were well if it were taken without delay. Delays are dangerous.

Excellent sport was to be had in the district on Saturday. There was an Athletic Festival at Newton, the twenty-fourth which has been hold in connection with certain employes of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway. The second day's sports at Widnes were also brought to an agreeable close, prizes being distributed to the successful competitors, amounting to nearly £2OO. There was admirable management both at Widnes and at Newton, and everything passed off well.

The Rev. J. A. Drummond, of Warrington, is sharing the frequent fate of curates. He gets a notice to quit—and a testimonial. There is no question as to his nsatilness and popularity ; and, this being the ease, perhaps somebody will ask the new rector why the old ctrate has to go. We say old curate, (though Mr. Drummond is a young man), for he is old in servict. He has actually been four years at St. Elphin's, and that, as things used to go in that parish, is an historical period of no mean length.

The loss of the lives of three Warrington ?en whilst working in a sewer at Widnes has given a shock to the community. As the inquest is not concluded it would be premature to express a full and definite opinion upon the circumstances of the catastrophe; but this much may be said—that the men who went into this dangerous sewer took their lives in their hands, and ran risks which men ought not to be called upon to run. Something, of course, will be done to ensure that such an acci- dent will not happen again. The stable door will be made secure now that the steed is szolen. There has been a strong muster of Warrington and Newton Volunteers for the camp life at South- port. It would be a good thing if the Govern- ment would let some of the thousands which run to waste flow in the direction of the Volunteers , Thy deserve better treatment than they get; for "one volunteer is worth twenty pressed men." The Rev. H. Siddall preached a capital sermon to the corps on Sunday, though it was a little odd to hear a clergyman quote the cynical saying at- tributed to Nat_oleon that "Providence is al- ways on the side of the strongest battalions."
"Mr. Balfour states that there is no foundation whatever for the statement published by the Dub- lin Daily Express' that he intenth resigning the Chief Secretaryship." The Government have
no such luck; Mr. Balfour will hold on; and his name will be worth, at the next general election, a hundred thousand votes —to the Liberal party.

Sir William Harcourt surpassed himself at Stockport, on Wednesday, which is saying a great deal. How charmingly he chaffed the Liberal Unionists! "There was a letter addressed to the faithful at Ayr—there was the epistle of Lord Hartington ; and there was the general epistle of Mr. Chamberlain. When Lord Hartington writes a letterto a constituency I have observed we generally win. When Mr Chamberlain writes a letter we always win."

This is how Sir William sums up the situation as regards the bye-elections. We commend the quotation to Liberal Unionists who are still in the wilderness. "There have been eight seats in which the representation has been changed, and in seven of these eight it has gone. to the Liberal cause, and only one has gone against us. Well, lam very willing to accept that proportion, and if we get it at the general election we shall do pretty well." Yes, there is no denying it—" We shall do pretty well."

In his speech at Newport in the autumn of 1885, Lord Salisbury said :—" I do not think local option is a bed thing where the thing to which it is to be applied is perfectly legitimate, and we have admitted that the closing of publie-houses on Sunday, where this is according to the views of the population, is a legitimate act." In view of this definite pronouncement, it will be interesting to observe how the Prime Minister will act on the question of Sunday closing as provided for in the Local Government Bill. Will he eat his own words ? We shall see.

The "Morning Post" is disposed to lecture the Tories on the defeat at Ayr. It makes a confes- sion we were scarcely prepared to hear when it says :—" We have become vague in discussing principles, and virulent in attacking persons. It is time to leave alone both a particular bill and a particular person, and go patiently and diligently to the root of the separatist question once more." Just so, but what is the root from the Tory point of view ? "There's the rub."

Can it be that Mr. James Lowther, the Tory candidate for Thanet, was at "the root of the separatist question" when ho said, speaking at Broadstairs, on Tuesday night, "there had been a great influx of Irish members of Parliament into the constituency—men who at one time where described by an authority as persons who were steeped in treason, and who were described as a nest of vipers. Yet the vipers had somehow got on to the Liberal platform." This is the style of a tear ago; but " Jimmy " was always behind the times. Somobody should remind him that Mr. Chamberlain (who is supposed to understand the root of the matter) suggested, at one time, that the chief " viper " (Mr. Parnell) should occupy the post Mr. Lowther once held—that of Chief Secretary for Ireland.
Lord Rosebery was in a happy vein at Wil- lis's Rooms, on Thursday; and he roused the feel- ing of his audience when he referred to Mr. Dillon. He said : .

Mr. Dillon is in prison to-day—(criesof " Shame") —but I greatly doubt it he would exchange his dun- geon for any place in the land, because, in the long intervals for contemplation which by the favour of the present Government he will enjoy during the next six months, he will know from the bottom of his heart that his imprisonment is doing more to forward the cause of Irish autonomy—(loud cheers) —than he co,uld do even by his eloquence outside the prison walls. (" It's a blackguard shame all the same !") Every great cause has its martyrs, and Mr. Dillon is the martyr of this cause ; and I doubt if he regrets it. (Hear, hear.) This is a matter of common sense. Home Rule is not an end, but a means,—a means by which the Irish leaders tell us, and by which we believo we can attain to what we have never yet possessed—a loyal, prosperous, and contented Ireland. (Cheers.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1888.

1! GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT RIINCORN.—OR ; Monday evening, a labourer named Peter Acton jumped • into the Bridgewater Canal near Mr. Lello's tannery to I rescue a boy who had accidentally fallen into the water. , The boy's life was saved by Acton's prompt action. This, it appears, is by no means the first time he has ' been iastrumental in saving life, as he has rescued several people from drowning. It is to be hoped steps will be , taken to obtain for him the medal of the Humane Society. WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, Moou-LANE.---The anniversary services were commenced in the above place of worship on Saturday evening last, when Mr. D. M. Jenkins, of Liverpool, preached a most impressiver ser- mon to a very large congregation. On Sunday morning and afternoon the services were conducted by the Rev. Mr. Oliver, of Holrvell ; the evening service was com- menced by Mr. Josiah Thomas, of Liverpool, and the sermon was preached by Mr. Oliver. There were large congregations throughout the day, and the eloquent dis- courses were most attentively listened to and • appre- ciated. Satisfactory collections were made. On Monday evening a lecture' entitled "The importance of little things, was delivered in the chapel by the Rev. Mr. Oliver. There was a good attendance. Mr. D. H. Jones, of Runcorn, presided. PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Luke Holmes, auctioneer, High-st., conducted a sale of property at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance. A lot of property, comprising the dwelling-house and shop, No. 41, Regent-st., in the occupation of Mr J. Canning; the dwelling-house and shop adjoining in the occupation of Mr. William Fletcher, and six dwelling-houses, situate and numbered 2 to 12 inclusive in Cross, was offered. The property is held under a lease for the residue of a term of 1,000 years, and the gross annual rental of the property is £lOO. The lot was knocked down to Mr. Thomas Irvine at £1,250. The dwelling-house, with outbuildings, situate in Cock and Hen-lane, Runcorn, in the occupation of Mrs. Mar- garet Nickson, also changed hands at £3lO. Mr. John Frodsham, being the purchaser. Messrs. Linaker and ' Linaker were the salicitors in the matter.

BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN —A picnic party, composed of the members and a few friends of this society, paid a visit to Delainere Forest on Thursday. They accomplished the journey in a couple of brakes belonging to Mr. Peck, of Bridge-st., and thus had an opportunity of viewing on the way, one of the most fertile parts of Cheshire. Arriving at Forest Lodge the house of Mr. Walker in the heart of the woods, the party partook of lunch, and then divided into smaller parties to pursue pleasure according to their oWn sweet wills. The forest was glorious in all its wealth of sum- mer raiment, and there was much to interest and delight the naturalist, the botanist, and the amateur photogra- phers who were present in strong force and obtained some excellent negatives. A capital tea was afterwards provided in the large room of the lodge. Mrs. T. Hand- ley dispensed the refreshing beverage with an unstinting hand, whilst Mr. A. Lightburn and Mr. • T. Lydiate proved themselves proficient Hi the art of using the car- ving knife. The return journey was safely completed by about half-past ten, a most pleasant 'day having been spent by all.

. . JUVENILE THIEVES AT IVIDNES.—SL Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, John Mulligah (8), Wm. Glynn (10), and Moses Bates (10), were charged with having sometime bAween 4 p.m. on Saturday and 9 a.m. on Monday, stolen five pigeons, valued at .55., the property of Alfred Midwood, son of Mr. Joshua Midwood. The pigeons were secured in a stable in Ditton-road on Sat- day afternoon and on Monday morning the building had been broken open and the pigeons stolen. The pri- soners, in answer to the charge, said "We were all to- gether in the cote. A fine of 5s was imposed in each case.—William James Rimmer (9), of 5, Water-at., was charged with having. on Tuesday, stolen a cucumber from the hot house of Mr. Horabin, jun. 15, Albert-st., square Halton View. A of glass had been broken in order to effect the theft. The prisoner was found with a cucumber in his possession, which he said he had found near the hospital. He was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch rod.—Michael Garbutt (14) was charged with stealing a jacket. worth 7s 6d, the property of Henry Richards, bricklayer, 50, Bridge-st. On Friday afternoon, Richards was employed at the works of the Widnes Metal Company, and placed his coat in a shed. A few hours afterwards it was missing. In the street afterwards Thomas Buenos, labourer, Pear-st., Widnes, saw the prisoner with the jacket, and he threatened to give him in custody. The prisoner dropped the jacket and ran away. The prisoner, who had been several times previously convicted, was sentenced to 14 dap' imprisonment, and four years' confinement in a reforma- tory school. SUDDEN DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORN RESIDENT.—Mr. William Bennett, boat maker, Devonshire-square, died very suddenly on Monday night. For a few days pre- viously he had complained of having a cold, but he went about his duties as usual and nothing serious was ap- prehended. About nine o'clock on Monday night lie re- turned from the Post Office and lay down upon the sofa. He was suddenly struck with an acute pain in the head, and Dr. McDougall was summoned and did all in. his Power for the sufferer, but without avail. Death took place in about a quarter of an hour in consequence of Ithe breaking of a blood vessel in the brain. Mr. Ben- nett. who had attained the age of 135 years, was one of the few old residents who were born in the town, and he was held in respect by large numbers of his fellow- townsmen. For upwards of 30 years he had acted as Dock Postman, and his punctuality and regularity was proverbial, and he had earned from Government the highest stripes for good conduct. Although be had been entitled to a pension for some years he laboured on to the last. His mortal remains were interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Lea, the post- master, and nearly the whole of the other officials fol- lowed their dead comrade to the grave as did also the boatmakers and other tradesmen in the town. The mourners, included Messrs. Wm. Roach, and Edward Key (sons-in-law), W. Handley, William Rushton, S. Bennett Stringer (Wilderspool), James Bennett (Bootle). Samuel M'Carraher (Rock Ferry). all nephews, and others. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. A. P. Watson. A large crowd assembled in the Ceme- tery to witness the ceremony.

ST. , HELENS JUNCTION ATHLETIC SPonTs.--he annual sports under the auspices of the St. Helens Junction (L. and N.-W.) Cricket Club will be held at St. Helens Junction, to-day (Saturday.) About 350 entries have been received, including some of the best athletes in Warrington, St, Helens, Liver- pool, Manchester &c. An excellent programme has been provided, and an afternoon's good sport seems ensured.

THE BEECHAM PILL CASE. —ln the Chancery Division .if the Righ Court of Justice, on Saturday, before Mr. tist ice Stirling, motion was made for judgment in the cage of Beecham v. Pritchard. His lordship some time ago granted an interim injunc- tion to restrain the defendant from displaying on pill boxes the words "Beecham's Pills," or other matter calculated to deceive the public into the be- lief that the pills he was offering for sale in Liver- pool and the district were manufactured by the plaintiff. Counsel now stated that no appearance had been made for the defendant, and he had now to ask his lordship to make the interim injunction Perpetual. He further 'gated that the plaintiff waived his claim for damages, and only asked for the costs incurred.—His Lordship granted a per- petual injunction, with costa.

MILITIA INSPECTION AT ALTCAR.—The officers and men of the 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment, at present under canvas at Altcar range for their 29 days' training, siere inspected on Thurs- day by Colonel Tweittyman, commanding 18th and 40th regimental districts. The inspecting officer expressed himself highly satisfied with all he had seen in connection with his visit to the camp. The battalion drilled admirably well, and it would give him great plepsure to make a favourable report of the corps to headquar- ters. The officers of the regiment present were Colonel 0. Nalley (in command) Lieutenant- Colonel Fletcher, Major W. Joynson, Major Black- burn, Major Woodcook, Captain Joynson, Captain Hall, Captain Eckersley, Captain Tarbet, Captain Heap, Lieutenant Horly, Lieutenant Oliver, Lieut. ISkeffington, Lieutenant Lewis, Lieutenant Buckle, LieutenankJames, Lieutenant Davies, Lieutenant Shaw, Lieutenant Ward. Major and Adjutant J. Ritchie, Quartermaster Howes, and Sergeant-major Logan. The field state showed that there were pre- sent on parade 23 officers, 33 sergeants, and 607 rank and file. The camp will break up this (Satur- day) morning, when the Aen will be conveyed to Warrington by special train.

FIRE AT ACTON GRANGE.—lnformation WRS re- ceived at the.fire station, Warrington, shortly after four o'clock on Monday afternoon, of an outbreak of fire at A,,ton Grange. With commendable promp- titude Superintendent Turner and six of his men. with the manual engine, were' on their way to the scene of the fire. On arrival at Acton Grange they found a cottage over which the flames seemed to have obtained complete mastery. The efforts of the brigade were accordingly Mainly directed to saving the adjoining cottage, and in this they were suc- cessful. The two tenements are known locally as Cockfight Cottages, and the one which has been burnt down was occupied by a farm labourer named John Jackson. The origin of the fire is unknown, but it is supposed to have been caused by a spark from the chimney falling on the thatched roof, as that was where the flames were first observed. Assistance was readily lent by neighbours, and most of the furniture was safely removed from the cot- tage before the fire had made much way. Some difficulty was experienced by the firemen at first, as they had to go a distance of over 200 yards to the Bridgewater Canal for water. The cottages are the property of Sir Richard' Brooks. The damage, which is estimated at £lOO. is covered by insur- ance.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchase all kinds of in- ferior manufactured spectacles, which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deanagate, and 44, Market-at., Manchester, 143, Lord-st., Southport, .and 60, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his "Per- fection" Spectacles, which he adapts at either of the above addresses at 7s 6d per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on application.---Adrot WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY AT FARNWORTH.—The annual sermons in aid of Farnworth Wesleyan Sunday School were preached in the chapel on Sunday by Mr. E. Lyon, L.L.D., of St. Helens. In the afternoon a children's ser- vice was conducted by Mr. J. J. Cook, also of St. Helens. There were good congregations at each service, and the collections amounted to over £lO. THE RENOWNED RUNCORN RELISH is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which render It of most valuable assistance in the ingestion of food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road, Runcorn.— Advt. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Whilst following his , employment at the Works of Messrs. Sullivan and Co., James Devaney, aged 65 years, labourer, of 30, Cross-st. met with a serious accident. The sleeve of his coat be- came entangled in the machinery of a revolver, and his arm was dreadfully mutilated. He was conveyed on a stretcher to Widnes Accident Hospital, where it was dis- covered that a compound fracture of the left fore-arm had been sustained, and Dr. O'Keeffe successfully per- formed the necessary operation of amputation. The patient is favour ably 'progressing. HALTON PARISH CHURCH.—On Sunday the F and G companies of the Earl of Chester's Rifle Volunteers at- tended Divine service at Halton Parish Church The companies mustered a little over 50, besides about 20 of the band, with which they were headed. The Rev. J. Lockwood, as acting chaplain, met the volunteers on the borders of his parish and walked with them to the church, which was crowded to excess. The Rev. Dr. Bartle, of Birkdale, Southport, preached a sermon from 1 Corinthians, ix., 24 and following verses. In the evening service was also held in connection with the Queen's Accession, and music of a special character was rendered. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The anniversary of the establishment of these schoolswas celebrated in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday. The preacher was the Rev. W. L. Watkinson, of Harrogate, and at both morning and evening service large congregations assembled to listen to his eloquent and convincing dis- courses. In fact at the evening service forms had to be placed in the aisles to accommodate the worshippers, and many were even then unable to gain admission. Under the leadership of Mr. John Birkett, the scholars and choir rendered specially selected hymns and anthems in capital style. Mr. Grice presided at the organ. The collections for the day amounted to £45. The sacred edifice was again crowded on Monday evening when the Rev. Charles Garrett preached an eloquent sermon, and the collections in aid of the school were brought up to a total of £62.

HONOURS Fon RUNCORN PUPILS.—The pass list of the Royal kca.demy of Music for this year includes the names of the fbllowing local pupils who have succeeded in satis- fying the examiner, Mr. Arthur O'Leary. Honours (junior division) : Mary Adelaide Smith, 14, pianoforte; pisSed :•Marianne Frances Rogerson, 14, pianoforte; and Maud Mary White, pianoforte. Miss Isherwood, of Stanley Villas, has been the tutor of the successful pupils. UNJUST WEIGHTS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty , Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Heesom, of Devonshire- place, was summoned for being in possession of unjust weights. Siiperintendent Hollingworth said he visited the defendant's shop on the 13th inst., and out of twelve weights he found a 41. b. weight three drachms light, and a 21b. weight two drachms light. The others were cor- rect. In May Mrs. Heesom brought eight weights to the police station, and these two had probably been over- looked. A fine of 6d and costs, 9s 6d, was inflicted.

ALLEGED DISEASED MEAT FOIL SALE AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. G. Pil- kington and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, a butcher named Geo. Maddison, who keeps a stall in, the Market Hall, was summoned by the Local Board for having, on the Ist inst., exposed a quantity of diseased meat for sale in the Market Hall. 'Mr. Mearns, solicitor, St. Helens, ap- peared for the defendant, and requested that the case should be adjourned for a week. in order that an im- portant witness might be summoned. The case was adjourned. TIRE ABSENT DEFENDANT AT RUNCORN .—Geo. Lancaster, commercial traveller' Stanley-villas, was summoned to the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. Contrary to their usual practice, the Bench heard the case in the defendant's absence, and imposed a fine of 2s 6d and costs, 10s 6d. Superintendent Hollingworth said a Ship Canal labourer would not object to paying 108. but when he had not appeared in answer to the summons, and a warrant was granted for his apprehen- sion, he fled in fear of the consequences. A CONSTABLE ASSAULTED BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES.— Ann Corrigan, a middle-aged woman, was brought be- fore the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with haying been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaul- ting P.C. Bruce. On Saturday night the woman was creating a distufbance in the street. She made use of most profane language, and as she would not go home she was taken to the police station by Constables Bruce and Ingham. In the office she kicked Bruce on the back. The prisoner, who was an old offender, was fined 5s and costs in each case, or fourteen days' imprison- ment. _ _

A DESERTED WIFE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, Ann Wal- ker, about 35 years of age, was charged with sleeping out on the previous night.—P.C. Houghton deposed that he found the woman asleep in a closet in Davies-st., and he took her to the home of a relative, who, however, re- fused to take her in. The woman had only been released from gaol that day and she had abused and threatened her brother.—Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner had been deserted by her husband in consequence of her misconduct, and he had since joined the Salvation Army. On promising to go to the workhouse, of which she had been an inmate, the woman was discharged. TRESPASSERS ON THE RAILWAY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Lee, 37 Oakland•st.; William Naylor, 15, Frederick-st. ; James Mason, 3, Dock-Bt. • and John Owen, 3, Dock-st., were summoned by the London and North-Western Railway Company for having trespassed on the railway leading to West Bank Dock on the 31st May.—Mr. Preston, of Liverpool, said the line upon which the defendants were trespassing was one of the most dangerous portions of the London and North-Western system. The defendants pleaded guilty, with the exception of Lee. who said he had been sent to the docks by his employers at the Liver Alkali Works. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed in each case. ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN. Yesterday. at Runcorn Police Court, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley. a youth from Manchester, named William Thomas Belcher pleaded guilty to having on the 15th June stolen hammers, screw drivers, chisels, planes, &c., belonging to Mr William Farrrll, builder and contractor, and also several similar articles belonging to Samuel Barrow, an apprentice. The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month.—Samuel Bailey, a navvy, was charged with having on the 15th inst. stolen a coat, valued at 15s, belonging to Henry Peacock, a ship canal labourer, who lives at Duckett's lodging house. Whilst Peacock was washing himself the prisoner walked away with the coat, and was apprehended by Inspector O'Donnell with the coat in his possession. He pleaded guilty and was sent to gaol for a month. SCENE AT A RUNCORN BOWLING MATCH.-0/1 Monday afternoon a large number of spectators assembled on the bowling green of the Bridge Hotel, Runcorn, to witness a match between W. Rhodes, of Runcorn, and James Gor- nall, a noted professional of Liverpool. The game, which was 101 up, was for a stake of £2o—£lo a-side. Gor- nall conceded 10 points start, and could never get upon terms with his local opponent, who bowled in splendid style When a stoppage was made for ~tea the scores stood at—Rhodes 76, Gornall 51. The latter complained that the green was not in proper condition, and being re- fused the roller and mowing machine of the proprietor, he borrowed a machine from an adjoining green. The partisans of Rhodes refused to allow Gornall to make use of the machine, and an amusing scene occurred, the contending factions struggling for possession of the machine. Afterwards Gornall gave up the game, and Rhodes having made the necessary 101, received the stake. STUBBS' FURNITURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliantTgloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottle§, Id., 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road, Run- corn .—Advt. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORIC.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, the following persons were sum- moned by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school :—Harriat Holland, 13, Cierrard-st. ; James Carr, 30, Pear-st. ; Denis Malone, 36, Pear-st. ; George Rotel!, 2, Dock-st. ; 'Agnes Holden' Old Marsh; James Houghton, 39, Bridge-st. ; John Clegg, back James-st. P. Garvey. 23, Davis-st., West Bank: Thos. Robinson, 6, John-st., West Bank Thomas Billingtoa, 7, Bridge-st. ' • William Malson, 14, Catherine-st. ; Mat- thew Murty, 66, Elizabeth-at, Moss Bank; Charles Mc- Kenna, 14, Elizabeth-st. ; Patrick McPartland, 15, Bryn- st. • Catherine Garmley, 4, Davis-st• ;. John Doyle,, 18, Catherine-st. ; W. Case 14, Davis-st., and Geo. Culley, 34. Kent-st. The usual fine of 5s was imposed in each case. It was stated that in the case of George Rozelle, the lad was the son of the late Dr. Hines. He would not go to school, and his mother had no control over him, whilst his stepfather took no pains to send him. Mr. Danby said he had applied three times Ur have the boy sent to an industrial school, but on each occasion the Bench had refused.—Their worships decided to give the boy one more chance. THE ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM THE ALEXANDRA HOTEL; WIDNES.—On Monday, at,-Widnek Police Court, William Dickson, a youth, was charged with having, on Sunday the 10th inst., stolen the sum of £2O 54 6d. belonging to Thomas Gerrard, of the Alexandra Hotel, and one of the proprietors of the Alexandra Theatre. The prisoner had been employed as a barman at the hotel., On the day in question he left the house at half-past two and should have returned iii' time to re-open the premises at six o'clock, but he did not do so. That evening Mr. Ger- rard missed a parcel containing over £2O, a portion of the takings at the Theatre, from his bedroom, and sus- picion falling upon the prisoner information ayes given to the police. On Saturday night, the 16th inst., P.C. Thompson apprehended the prisoner in Stanley Park, Liverpool He denied stealing the money. That morn- ing (Monday) Mr. Gerrard ordered his wife and servant (Sarah Sparks) to make a thorough search of the house, and the latter found the parcel of money between some , linen in a drawer in the prisoner's bedroom. There was nobody in the prisoner's room after he left on Suns day.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and he wak, corn- itted to take his trial at the Quarter Sessions. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN MISSIONARY.—FIom the " Wynberg Times "(South Africa) we learn that on the 16th May an event interesting to the public of Run- corn took place at Wvnberg. There was a large gather- ing at the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel to bid farewell to the Rev. S. H. Ravenscroft, son of Mr. Samuel Ravens- croft, of Runcorn, who was then about to remove to Harrismith, O.F.S. Mr. Ravenscroft has been a mis sionary in Africa for eight years. The Rev. R. Ridgill, who presided, said that he was losing one who had been to him like a son, and addresses were delivered by the ministers of the various denominations. On behalf of the stewards and congregation and the Sunday school Mr. Ravenscroft was presented with several addresses, a purse containing 40 guineas, a handsome travelling bag, and a framed photograph of khe teachers and scholars. Mr. Ravenscroft acknowledged the gifts in an appropriate speech, in which he referred to the extension of church work that had taken place in Wynberg during his five years residence there. He should never forget7Wynberg, for it was there he made his first home. Ile should never forget that building, for he was married there and his three children had been baptised there. And he should never forget their kindness to him and his family. A MIDNIGHT MARAUDER AT NALE.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, a tramp named John Welsh and a boy named William Shiels (13), were charged on remand with stealing about 7 lbs of beef and a dish, the property of George Rowe, of Ciss Green, Hale, on the Ist June. They were further charged with stealing an axe and other articles the property of Richard Lewis, of Ditton Lodge.—The charge was withdrawn against Shiels, who was called as a witness. He said he lived with his parents at Wellington-st., Liverpool. On Friday morning,thelst inst., he went to a house in Richmond row to see; some lads who went to the same school. Welsb,who was lodg- ing there, asked him to go to Manchester with him and said he would get him a pair of boots. Witne'sl consen- ted and they started to walk the distance. They begged on the way. At Ditton College one of the clergy gave Welsh something to eat and drink and a singlet. That night they slept In a barn at Hale. At two o'clock next morning they left the barn, and the prisoner tried the stable door of a large house, but it was locked. They took the axe and other articles produced. They then went in the direction of Liverpool, and the prisoner took the piece of beef from a safe at another house. • Welsh 'L had told him to say he was his son.and that if any police- man came along he was to go on the other side. He de- scribed what would become of him if he did not do this.-- The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. •
