AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF ENGINEEDS.—The thirty-seventh annual report of this society states that there are 142 members who belong to the War- rington branch, 38 who belong to the Widnes branch, and 72 who belong to the St. Helens branch.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES FOUNDRY.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES FOUNDRY.

At the Widnes Accident Hospital, on Wednesday- Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an in- quiry into the circumstances of the death of James Monagan, who expired on Sunday evening from in- juries received at Widnes Foundry on Monday the 11th inst. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, appeared on behalf of the firm, who were also represented by Mr. B. Brown and Mr. S. Robinson.—Miss Downie, the matron, said the injuries were all in the bead, and the patient never recovered consciousness up to the time of the death.—Geo. Hide, Venston- terrace, Birchfield-road, Appleton, said he was a labourer for the Widnes Foundry Company. The deceased started work on the 7th inst. On the 11th inst. the deceased was working on a travelling crane, which was about 17 feet 6 inches above the ground. The crane, which was worked altogether by hand, hud just been removed from the middle of the "runners" to thg end where the deceased fell. Witness was on the crane at the time, with his back towards the deceased, bet hearing some boards fall he walked to the end, and saw a workman picking up the deceased. The two boards were used for standing upon when winding up. The sides of the bearers were protected with an iron rail, but the ends were open. Had the ends been similarly protected there would have been less likelihood of a man falling off. The deceased was quite a stranger to him, and he did not know whether he was subject to fainting fits.—By Mr. Knowles: A man could always grasp the rail if he wished. He never considered he was in any danger himself while working at the crane. It would be his own fault if he met with an accident.—Mary Monag- han, of 31, Dolman's-lane, Warrington, said the deceased was her brother, and he was 17 years of age. He had always been in good health, and was not troubled with dizziness in the head. She did not know why he did not gain admission to the army.—Joseph Jones, do, Attewell- st., said he had worked at the Widnes Foundry for seven years. During that period of time the crane had been in use. The deceased ferupon some iron plates. From the position in which he was the deceased must have fallen off from the end of the bearers. The deceased did not need to II) within three feet from the end. If a rail was put at the end it would interfere with the working of the crane. He never knew an accident occur from that crane before.—After a brief consultation, the jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and suggested that there should be more protection at the end of the , bearers.—Mr. Knowles said the lives of the men were of the first importance to the firm, and they would only be too pleased to do anything they possibly could consistent with trade. (Hear, hear).

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The annual meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. P. Speakman, H. White, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn, J. Meadoweroft, P. Smith, W. Mellor, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, H. J. Griee, E. Marshall (see.), and M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

The Secretary took the chair and intimated that the first business was the appoifitment of chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr. P. Speakman said that according to seniority and the practice of the Board, Mr. Taylor had a claim upon the office of chairman, but with that ex- treme modesty of which they knew he was possessed Mr. Taylor had declined to accept the position for this year. Mr. Lake had also fio desire to take the chair, and he had much pleasure in proposing that Mr. Fisher be ap- pointed chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Fisher was peculiarly fitted to occupy that important position, be- cause he had, as chairman of the Finance Committee, done the Board and the ratepayers great service.—Mr. Dobson seconded the proposition with much pleasure, and it was supported by Mr. Once and Mr. Lightburn, and carried unanimously.

div.head: THANKS TO MR. DOBSON.
div.p: THANKS TO MR. DOBSON.

Mr. Speakmais proposed that the best thanks of the Board be tendered to Mr. Dobson for the services he had rendered in the chair during the past year.—Mr. Imison seconded the proposition, remarking that Mr Dobson had conducted the business of the Board most admir- ably, and had shown that he was possessed of the dis- cretion and tact which were requisite for the propercon- duct of public business.—Mr. Hankiason seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Dobson, in responding, said he trusted they would continue to work amicably together for the general good of the town. He wished to convey his thanks to the officers for the assistance they had rendered him during their • term of office. He hoped they would be long spared to retain the full confidence of the Board. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST CHOLERA.
div.p: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST CHOLERA.

A special Board meeting was then held to consider several questions. Mr. Dobson occupied the chair, and in addition to the members previously mentioned Mr. Pritchard was present. The first business was to con- sider the following recommendation of the Health Com- mittee :—(1) That application be made to the Liverpool Port Sanitary Authority to carry out on behalf of thel Runcorn Riparian Authority the provisions of the I Cholera Regulations of July 12th, 1883, in regard to cholera found on Runcorn-bound vessels passing through the Liverpool Customs Port and Port Sanitary District. (2) That the Liverpool Port Sanitary Autho- rity he invited to concur in Runcorn appointing, under the Cholera Regulations, the Liverpool Port Medical Officer of Health to carry out the several provisions of the Cholera Regulations in regard to cholera reported to him by the Customs, or otherwise, as found on board a Runcorn-bound ship, precisely in the same way as he would deal with cholera found on board a Liverpool- bound ship; the Runcorn Authority paying all legitimate expenses incurred in such action. (3) That the sanction of the Liverpcol Port Sanitary Authority be obtained to the fixing of the Sloyne as the most suitable place for the mooring or anchoring of Runcorn-bound ships certified to be infected, and that the approval of the Chief Officerl of Customs of the said port be obtained, to the fixing of such place. (4) That the proposed agreement be ter- minable on six months' notice being given by either authority.—Mr. Lightburni in moving the adoption of these recommendations, pointed out that while in 1887 , there were 99 deaths from cholera in Calcutta, which was the home of the disease, there had been during the corresponding period of 1888 no less than 182 deaths, so that there was a tremendous increase. What safeguards had they to prevent cholera-stricken ships reaching Runcern ? In the first place, all foreign vessels of what- ever size, an_d alLEnglish vessels of 99 tons register and , over, were boarded ,ley a: pilot, whose first duty was to ascertain if there wattsickness on the ship and report to the authorities at Liverpool. Secondly, the customs officials made similar inquiries ; and thirdly, the captain was liable to a heavy fine if he did not fly a flag intima- ting that he had disease on board. These precautions might seem sufficient, but the proposed regulations were made at the request of the Local Government Board. The average cost of attending to a cholera-stricken ship would be £l4 or £l5, but this sum could be recovered from the captain or the owners of the ship.—Mr. Grice seconded the metion.—A long discussion ensued, and the Chairman remarked that had some of the younger mem- bers witnessed the ravages made by cholera 47 years ago, they would never grumble at paying £l5 or £2o.—Mr. Smith protested against such a remark. The young men were quite as capable as the old men of looking after the interests of the town.—The Chairman said his remark had been misunderstood.s.—On the suggestion of Mr. Lake the word " sanitary " was substituted for " ri- parian "in the first clause, and in clause three, after "Runcorn bound ships "was added" And ships in dock at Runcorn."—The thotion was then carried.
THE WEAVER TRUST.

A letter was read from the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians who asked the Commissioners to support the Guardians in their protest against the proposal of Mr. Brunner to divert from the county fund any payments made by the Trustees of the Weaver in order to benefit the salt trade of Northwich. The report of the Clerk to the Guardians was also read.—The Law Clerk said nearly every public authority in Cheshire, with the exception of Northwich and Win.sford had concurred in the action of the Runcorn Guardikns.—Mr. Smith moved that the subject be referred to the next monthly meeting, and that in the meantime each melhher be provided with a 'printed ropy of the communication.—Mr. Imison secon- ded the motion.—Mr. (Mee said the simple question was whether thn surplus revenue derived from the river Wea- ver should be paid to the county fund for the reduction of the county rate, or' whether, as Mr. Brunner proposed, it should be devoted to compenlation for subsidence of land in Northwich. Let those Parties who were interes- ted in the business pay all the damages arising from their carrying on that business.—Mr. Imison stated that as sensible businessmen they ought to know what they were supporting and advocating. Although en the face of it it looked reasonable that the pumpers shouldpay for sub- sidences, yet an inquiry into the ancient history of the Weaver Trust and a consideration of the original inten- tion of the gentlemen who formed the Trust might lead to a different concliedon. If the members had more time fer consideration they might come to an intelligible opinion upon the question.—An objection was raised to the printing of the report, and Mr. Flankinson suggested that the Clerk to the Guardians should be asked to sup- ply the members with spare copies.—Mr. Smith said if the ratepayers objected to pay a few shillings for such an important matter, he would have the report printed for the benefit of the members himself. (Laughter.)— Mr. Smith's motion was carried.
THE 'RATING OF MACHINNRY:

A letter was read from the Newcastle-upon-Tyne Union requesting the Board to petition against the Bill intro- duced into Parliament to exempt machinery from rates. —The Law Clerk said that if that Bill were passed it would reduce the assessment of the works of the Run- corn Soap and Alkali Company by 50 or 70 percent., and the same with the firm of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele. This would be a very serious matter for the other ratepayers of Runcorn.—Mr. Smith proposed that the important question be referred to the Finance Com- mittee, and the motion was carried. There was no other business.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY "AnrEL."
That the Liberal demonstration at Winnington Park was a great success; and that the Runcorn contingent enjoyed themselves greatly on Mr. Brunner's steamer "Success, " and the barge Nn. 7.” _

That the captain of the steamer, who has been in the employ of Mr. Brunner for many years, is a. staunch Tory, and no:, at all afraid of giving expres- sion to his opinions. That this is one advantage of worldng for a Liberal.

That the petition against the imprisonment of Mr. John Dillon and Mr. O'Brien is being signed most willingly by the inhabitants of the division; and Mr. Handley will have the pleasure of forward- ing a monstre roll to Mr. Brunner for presentation to the House of Commons.

That the "young members" of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners are coming to the front, and that that is where they ought to be. That Mr. Smith, like the celebrated Pitt, does not consider it a crime to be a young man. That Mr. Imison has evidently some views of his own about the Weaver Trust, mid is quite capable of expressing them. That further investigation will strengthen hira in the opinion he pronounced at the last meeting. That Mr. Fisher will make an admirable chairman of the Board.

, That Mr. Taylor, who was offered the post, is suffering from the effects of an accident, and is confined to his room. That he has the sincere sympathy of his fellow- townsmen, who hope he will quickly resume his private and public duties. That the blinding of the New Catholic Church is about to be commenced, and that Dr. Castilda is to be congratulated upon the successful result of his energetic labours That he may quickly raise all the money he needs is the wish of the devotees of more than one reli- gious denomination. That things are very quiet in Widnes. and that the shopkeepers are complaining of bad trade, al- though the works are all in full swing. That the publicans receive by far too large a pro- portion of the Ten's earnings, and the legitimate traders are thus defrauded of their due share. That there are several streets in Widnes where the inhabitants are so poverty-stricken through their improvident habits that a certain doctor will not permit them to have medicine except upon •• cash terms."
That if some of these people were more tem- perate; they would have less need of the doctor, and would be able to pay for his services when they needed him.
DRUNKEN BURGLARS AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. George Pilkington, at-Widnes.Police Court, on Tuesday, Anthony O'Brien, aged 19 yeats, and Mark O'Brien, aged 24 years, both of 38, Mar- garet-st., were charged with having, between 10 p.m. on Sunday, the 17th inst., and 6 a.m. on Mon- day, the 18th inst., burglarious/3' broke into the Ship Inn beerhouse, Victoria-st., and stolen two pairs of boots, a silver watch and gold albert, a I quantity of tobacco, a cashbox containing £5 in money, a number of bottles of porter, lemonade, and many other articles, the property of William Jones, the landlord, and William Passey, grocer. Mersey-road, who is a lodger in the house. It appeared that the prisoners were frequent visitors to the inn, and were there on Sunday night. At ten o'clock the house was properly secured as usual. Next morning it was discovered that the back kitchen window had been almost completely forced out, and the door was open. Lying on the floor of the kitchen was a vest and a cap, Which were recognised as belonging to the prisoner Anthony. A search revealed that the articles mentioned in the charge had been stolen. Later, Mrs. Jones went to O'Brien's house. Mark came to the door. He was very drunk, and did not appear to have been in bed at all. She said, "Tell Anthony that our house has been broken into, and that his cap has been found inside; and if he wants to clear himself he must come at once." When Anthony came to the inn lie stated that Mark and himself had been wrestling on Sunday night in the entry at the back of the house, and somebody niust have thrown his cap over the wall. Afterwards he said he had not been near the house at all. During the morning the mother of the prisoners brought the missing watch and chain, and stated that she had found them hidden under the sofa in the kitchen.—The prisoners were then apprehended by P.S. McGregor, and were now remanded for a week.

div.head: ALLEGED BRUTALITY TO A WIFE AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE ALLEGED BRUTALITY TO A WIFE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Dug- gan was again brought up on remand charged with causing grievous bodily harm to his wife Julia on the 25th May.—Mrs Duggan was called, and her de- positions taken when it was feared that she would die, were read over. She alleged that she was not in'her right mind when they were taken, and de- clared that her husband was innocent of the charge.— Thomas Dodd, labourer, of 12, High-st., deposed that he lived next door to the prisoner, and about midnight on the date in question, he heard a great noise in the prisoner's house. There was also a thumping sound as if someone was being battered against the wall.—Mary Dodd said she heard a woman moaning. She had heard several rows at the prisoner's house, but none so bad as this last one.-Michael Ryan, labourer, 31, Hutchinson-st., said the prisoner was a great friend of his and he went to see him on the morning of the outrage. There was blood on the kitchen floor, and also upstairs. The woman was lying on the bed unconscious. The prisoner said his wife had got drunk, and, falling down, had cut herself. He replied "Now be careful, Jim, it looks as if you had been beating her." He then put a quilt over Mrs Duggan.— Maria Gilmour, wife of Daniel Gilmour, 18, Hope-st., also gave evidence.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed that when he arrived at the house he found Mrs Duggan suffering from two wo Inds on the head. One was a clean cut wound at the lower and back part of the head, about 11- inches in length, and penetrated the bone of the skull itself. He thought that this wound could not have been caused by a fall except from a great height. Her fore- head was very much swollen, and there were some skin wounds on the cheeks which appeared to have been caused by finger nails. Her whole body was covered with bruises. The loss of blood must have been great. The woman complained of excruciating pains in the stomach, and peritonitis setting in, her life was in danger. On the 27th May he thought she was going to die. He was present when her depositions were taken, and she was perfectly aware of what she was saying. The wounds could not have been self-inflict'd.— P.S. Clarkson and P.C. Thompson were also called. The latter found on the mantlepiece of the house a knife, the handle of which was covered with blood.—The pri- soner said "Surely you don't think I would hit the woman with a knife."—The prisoner now stated that his wife had done something to herself once before. He was not guilty; she did it all herself.—He was committed to take his trial at the next Quarter Sessions.

div.head: MORE RUFFIANISM AT WIDNES.
div.p: MORE RUFFIANISM AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. ICGaskell, jun., Michael James Keegan, Richard Rawlinson, and James Tobin, young men of corner-boy type, were charged with various offences—Keegan with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting and resi.ting P.C.'s Field and Cummings; Rawlinson with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting Constables Field and Holbrook; and Tobin with committing a breach of the piece and assaulting Constables Field and Cumminzs ; also with damaging the trousers of Field to the extent of IS. P.C. Cummings stated that on Saturday night from half-ost nine to ten o'clock the prisoners, along with 20 or 30 others, were walking about Waterloo-road and neighbourhood "wanting" to fight with anyllody they met. About a quarter to ten Tobin was cautioned about his conduct, but he refused to go home, and witnass was taking him into custody, when he was knocked down. Tobin kicked and struck athim, and also attempted to bite him. Keegan then struck him on the head with the buckle end of a strap, and ran away. There was a great crowd assembled, and there was much confusion; in fact, almost a riot. Tobin kicked witness on the leg, and struck Fiel4 on various parts of the body, besides damaging his trousers with his wooden leg.—P.C. Field gave corroborative evidence, and stated that he was struck by a stone thrown by Keegan. He was surrounded by a mob, and had to draw his staff in order to fight his way out.—P.C. Maitland deposed that when he went to the assistance of the other constables they were surrounded by a most unruly crowd. Field and Cummings appeared to be exhausted. Keegan shouted, "It'll only be seven days or a month, and can do that standing on our heads."—Sergeant Clarkson and Constable Holbrook also corroborated.— The prisoners alleged that they were apprehended with- out cause, and accused Field of being intoxicated.—ln- spector Keighley and Sergeant Clarkson coritradicted this accusation.--Superintendent Johnston informed the Bench that in March last Keegan was sent to gaol on similar charges, and in April Rawlinson was sent to gaol for assaulting the police.—Tobin was sentenced to three months' hard labour, Rawlinson to two months' hard labour, and Keegan to three months' hard labour.—John Hayes, a member of the same gang, was sent to gaol for a month in default of finding sureties to be of good be- haviour for three Months, for creating a breach of the peace on Sunday.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CONNEXION.—At a sitting of the Primitive Methodist Conference at the Prince's-avenue Church, Liverpool, on Friday, the conference fixed the stations of the itinerant preachers. The following were appointed in the district :—St. Helens, James Causland and Miles Dickenson; Warrington and Widnes, Walter Gra- ham; Earlestown, Richard Robinson,

div.head: – A DESERVED- WORD OF PRAISE. (Front the " Woodbridge Reporter.")
div.p: - A DESERVED- WORD OF PRAISE. (Front the " Woodbridge Reporter.")

We have always been very particuler about mak- ing editorial comment upon the wares of advertigers who make use of the columns of our paper. Shen we know of anything that ta worthy of special men- tion, we are frank enough to say so, but until We are satisfied we cannot endorse them. This is es- pecially the case with the large number of proprie- cçj which are placed before the public through the public prints. We blow there is a pre- judice ogainst the use of what are known as un- authorised proprietary medicines, and in many cases the prejudice is well founded, but there has lately come under our notice a case which, upon investigation, we have decided to give to our readers. Many of them will doubtless remember the severe illness of the little three-year-old son of Mr. Robert H. Durham, of 3, Warren Hill, Woodbridge, and his re!' arkable recovery. One ycar agf,r) last March, the Mile f,ellovr was taken ill 'with dropsy. Large water sacs formed over his eyes, his legs were swollen to the size of a full-grown man, and his whole body puffed up to an alarming extent: Said Mr. Durham to the writer:—" For eight weeks he was under the doctor's care, but without any beneficial results. During this time he was confined to his bed, his stomach would retain no food, and we were com- pelled to keep him wrapped up in blankets and close to the fire, in order to keep him warm and alive. His water was heavy with albumen, and frequently after boiling it became as hard as the white of a cooked egg. Several doctors were consulted, but all agreed that he could not live. I finally decided to give him \Varner's Safe Cure. which I was informed could be had of all chemists, and the immediate result was an increase in the flow of water. We continued giving him the Safe Cure, and the dropsy gradually disappeared, his appetite returned, ond he was brought back to health." In verification of what Mr. Durham had said, we were informed by Mr. Edward J. Eaton, M.P.S., of the Pharmacy, Woodbridge, that the case came under his personal notice, as he supplied him with the Warner's Safe Cure. Said Mr. Raton "The doctors had given upon all hopes of the boy's recovery, as dropsy had set in, when he was put upon Warner's Safe Cure, and was soon running around, to the surprise of all his friends. I have sold large quantities of this medicine, and know of lots of people who have derived great benefit from its use." As we said in the beginning of this article, we are not in the habit of commending patent medicines, but when we meet a case like the one above narrated, we believe it to be our duty to let the public know of it, and to place the credit where it properly belongs.

WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS. The sports were continued on Saturday afternoon, in the Showfield, Farnworth, and as the programme of events was of an attractive and high-class character there was a large attendance of spectators. The weather in the latter part of the afternoon was all that could be desired, though in the morning and till after mid-day the sky was extremely gloomy and threatening. Speak- ing generally the sports were very successful, and not a little of this success was due to the admirable arrange- ments and management of the committee and officials. The committee was composed of the following gentlemen: Messrs C. E. Barlow, Dr. Booth, A. F. Brundrit, W. S. Callaneler, J. Carr, H. W. Deacon, A. Deacon, D. Forster, W. W. Gossage, T. C. Haddock, W. B. Longton, W. H. Longton, Dr. MacLennan, Dr. McDonnell, Dr. McCam- bridge, Dr. Mangan, Dr. J. A. Nealon H. Rawcliffe, G. E. Sayce. H. S. Timmis, and J. R. Wylde. Officials :- Judges, Messrs F. H. Gossage, and C. E. Barlow (Widnes A. C.), Messrs Abraham and Ramsdale (N.C.A.A.) ; clerks of course. Messrs J. Carr, W. S. Callander, W. W. Gossage, H. Rawcliffe, G. E Sayce, H. S. Timmis, and J. R. Wylde ; field finance committee, Messrs Haddock and Brundrit and Dr. Cambridge; handicapper, official time- keeper, and referee, Mr. Walter Platt; starter, Mr. T. Wilkinson; secretary, Mr. J. W. Davies. The pro- gramme included two of the Northern Counties A. A. championships, namely, for putting the shot, and for the one mile fiat race. For each of these events noted members of the New York A.C. competed the first-named being won rather easily by G. R. Gray, of New York,. but E. C. Carter, the other representative of the United States seemed to be very much off colour and was easily beaten in the half-mile event. The following is a list of results:- 120 YARDS FLAT RACE HANDICAP (open).-N.C.A.A. limit 12 yards ; 73 entries, 12 heats, first only to compete in trial heat. First prize, pair of oxidised plaques in plush frames, 'Much Ado about Nothing" and " Merchant of Venice," value £lO lOs ; second, case of salt cellars and spoons, value £4 4s ; third, breakfast cruet. First heat: 1. H. N. Flewker, Mid- land A.C., 21 yards start, time 12 seconds; Second heat: 1, G. Ratcliffe, Warrington F.C. 9 yards; time, 12 2-5 secs. Third heat: 1, H. Braggs, Sefton Harriers, 71 yards ; time 12 3-5 secs. Fourth heat: 1, J. Bowker, Chester, 10 yards; time 122-5 secs. Fifth heat : 1, H. W. Barlow, Stoke V.A.C., 41 yards: time, 121-5 secs. Sixth heat: I,F.W.Staveacre,Manches- ter A.C., 5 yarns; tiro., 12 sees. Seventh heat: 1, S. Barlow, Fairfield L.C., 8 yards; time, 12 1-9 secs. Eighth heat: 1, A. S. Airey, Kersall C.C., st yards; time, 12 1-5 secs. Ninth heat: 1, G. T. Wainwright, Runcorn F.C., 81 yards; walk over. Tenth heat: 1, W. Parker, Manchester A.C., 81 yards ; time 12 1-5 sees. Eleventh heat: 1, J. Kean, Liverpool, 6i yards; time, 12 1-5 secs. Twelfth heat: 1, G. Millwood, Sal- ford Harriers, 71 yards; time 12 secs. Semi-finals :-First heat: 1, Staveacre ; 2, Flewker ; 3, Braggs and Ratcliffe, dead heat; time, 12 1-5 sees.; in running off the dead heat Bmggs won. Second heat: 1, Parker; 2, Wainwright and Kean. dead beat; time, 12 sees. Final heat: 1, Parker; 2. Stave- acre; 3, Flewker ; time 12 secs. Won by about a yard, second and third being separated by half-a-yard. NORTHERN COUNTIES A. A. CHAMPIONSHIP PUTTING Tim SHOT (open).-First prize, N.C.A.A. silver medal; 2nd, silver medal. Only It. A. Greene (Manchester A.C.) and G. R. Gray (New York AG) competed in this event. Gray, who, physically, is a model athlete, threw, without apparently any great effort, the shot 43ft. 2in., to Greene's 401 t. 2in. and con- sequently was declared the winner. It was subsequently as- certained that the shot weighed half-a-pound less than its proper weight. ONE MILE Btcycys: RACE (open, N.C.A.A. limit, 150 yards.) -Ist prize, case of six solid silver saltcellars and spoons, value ' £8 8s; 2nd prize, case of silver-mounted carvers (five pieces), value £4 4s; 3rd prize breakfast cruet -First heat : 1, It G. i Garnett, Warrington C.C., 130 yards; 2, H. Allen, Warrington C.C.. 115; 3, J. E. Feay, Manchester A.C., 65; time 3 mine. 15 4-5 secs. Second heat: 1, J. Hargreaves, Liverpool A.C., 125 yards; 2, E. Bramall, Stoke, 135; 3, S. R. White, Liver- pool, 140; time 3 mins. 23 secs. Final heat: 1, Allen; 2, Garnett; 3, Hargreaves; time 3 min. 13 secs. In the final of this race Garnett led the way till the last lap when Allen who rode with good judgment spurted ahead and kept this position :despite the strenuous efforts of Garnett. This latter rider un- fortunately came a cropper when within a few yards of the tape, but, notwithstanding, he succeeded in gaining second place. NORTHERN COUNTIES A.A. His breast wears the Cross of the Order Pour le Merite and the Iron Cross. Below these lies a small laurel wreath wound around with scarlet ribbons. tci the Emperor by the Empress Victoria after tti: battle of Woerth, and fondly preserved by him. At the foot of the bed a number of beautiful fresh wreaths an lying, sent by the nearest relations, the regiments. and Am- bassadors. The reason the Emperor's face is so beautifn' and lifelike is t,,at by the wish of ,he Empress Victoria an' the Emperor William he v-^ a cabalmed. Only injectio.aa of a nreservin,g fluid were maue yesterday. Very few admitted to the touching presence. At three tl-m peror was photographed. The Empress NI" jvafia had expressed a wish that this should not be dr ' ..ne, but when this morning she saw how beautiful her 'husband was in death, she gave her reluctant consen%, This afternoon, the body was placed in the coffin, - Anti borne through the :zround-floor apartments of the -en-called Jasper Gallery. where a service was read b-ji Court Chaplain Perseus. at which only the meml-ers of the Imperial Family and the Impels' Houierotd were present.

div.head: LYING IN ST -ATE.-AN EAGER THRONG.
div.p: LYING IN ST -ATE.-AN EAGER THRONG.

BERLIN, SUND.-N-MllT.—Friedrichskron, to-day, sva swarming wil soldiers, there being probably 20,00 n men of all exn" quartered around the castle. Two hun- dred ext'.4 constables also were sent out, to-dav, from and an enormous crowd was assembled at thw Cte waitirig for admission. At half-past 12 the gate was opened, when there was a wild rush to get in Women screamed, and it was not until very energetic efforts on the part of the officers in command that the crowd was reduced to a semblance of order. Eventually, however, the crowd was formed into double file, and in this order people were con- ducted over the grounds and across the terrace where the Emperor used to sit during the last days of his life. Thence they entered the Jasper Gallery, where the body lies guarded by GrenadieTs in State uniform. POST-MORTEM EXAMINATION.—CANCER ESTAB- LISHED.

BERLIN, SUNDAY. The post-mortem examination of the remains of the late Emperor, which was executed by Professor Virchow, at the Emperor William's com- mand, was confined to dissection of the neck, larynx, and lungs. In place of the larynx, which was found to have been completely destroyed by suppuration, there was a cavity almost the size of a clenched fist. Sir Morell Mackenzie stated in the report which he has drawn up by command of the Emperor, that the disease to which lii s late Majesty succumbed was doubtless cancer of the larynx, and observes that diagnosis was rendered very difficult, as the disease attacked the cartilage of the larynx at the outset, and afterwards developed it- self chiefly in the lower portion of the cartilage. The National Zeitung publishes the follcwing state- ment on the Subject f-•-•-" The examination proved that the larynx was competely destroyed by cancer and putrid bronchitis. There was also inflammation of the

finer ramifications of the bronchite, into which putrescent particles had entered. The whole larynx was suppurated and presented a soft limp mass, scarcely any trace of the cartilaginous structure remaining, and in place of the larynx a large cavity had been formed. There was nothing, however, to show that a perforation existed of the walls separating the trachea anl the cesophagus. The choking sensation from which his Majesty suffered during the last few days of hi, life, and which were at- tributed to suoh perforation, appear to have been due to the collapse of the larynx, owing to the destruction of the cartilage, thus permitting small quantities of the liq lid nounshment which was being administered to How into the trachea and lungs. The direct cause of death is attributed to paralysis of the lungs. The examination occupied one hour. THE FITNE.RAL.—IMPRESSIVE SCENES.' _

POTSDAP.E. MONDAY Monsr,- —A second mortuary service was held at the Castbz. of Friedriehskron, last evening, attended by the Emperor, Empress, the Dowager Empress, and the Imperial family. The coffin was then sealed, and placed in the shell which conveyed the remains of the Emperor William. The route from the Castle to Friedenskirche was lined with funeral torches and crossets. burning. BERLIN. MONDAY Moannln.—Prince Bismarck. General

Von Moltke, and the few foreign princes who have arrived to attend the funeral of the late Emperor, left Berlin for Potsdam, this morning. The railway station was closed to the general public, who had assembled in vast crowds outside to witness the departure of the illustrious mourners. At Potsdam, the railway station is closed to the public use, and at both places strong forces of soldiery and police are keeping, order. The Palace of Fried rich.irron is enclosed, like a fortress, with deep cordons of troops drawn up at every entrance. The bells of every church in Berlin are chiming forth funeral peals, and at Potsdam and in the neighbouring country the sante honour ic paid to the memory of the dead Sovereign. At nine o'clock punctually the Minis- ters, bearina;the insignia et the deceased Einperor and of the realm of Prussia. took their assigned places round the coffin of their late master in the Jasper Gallery. Half an hour later the official representatives and court officials entered, followed by Prince Bismarck and Count Von Moltke. Within a few minutes of the arrival of this seltrfirt procession, the limperial family and the foreign princes came into the gallery and fell silently into their arranged places. The choir of the Church of the' Twelve Apostles then intoned Bach's two hymns, "Soon Thou callest me to higher iC)FB, which this world cannot give," and "Jesus, my I rust and my Saviour in life." Court Chap- lain Roerrel then approached the coffin to bless the corpse, and offered up a fervent prayer, whilst the whole assembly chanted the hymn, "If I am to die, do Thou not leave me." Amidst impressive silence, the coffin was then raised from the catafatcon by twelve commanders of the twelve regiments of which the Emperor Frederick was Colonel-in-chief, and was be them borne to the hearse, being preceded by the Ministers of State, with the Imperial insignia. Eight majors and colonels of regiments stationed in Berlin took 'each a rein of the horses attached to the funeral car, and the procession immediately left for the Eriedenskirche Just before the service commenced the Empress Augusta was wheeled in in an arm chair, and took bp her station next to the Emnress Victoria, the Grand Duchess of Baden, and the Hereditary Princess of Saxe Meinimien. The procession moved forward to the heat of muffled drums. The Knights of' he Order of the Black Eagle walked on each side rif the car, close behind which was led the late Emperor's charger. Next came the Emperor William, Prince Henry, the King of Qaxony. the 'Prince of Wales, and the Grand Duke of Radon, and following them the other Princes, the foreign distinguished mourners, the late Emperor's Ministers, the deputations from foreign regiments, members of-ti e Federal Council. the Presidents of the Reichstag and Prussian Net, and deputations from various German towns. The Generals of the army who took part in the procession were headed by Field-Marshal Count con Moltke, who walked alone in front, carrying the Marshal's staff. Special attention was attracted by the eroup of the late Emperor's physicians, including Sir Morell Mackeazie wearing the 'blue sash of the order conferred upon him ‘tfy the late 'Emperor. Escorts nf the Garde du Corps and the dragoons of the guard preceded and closes:l the cortege, which reached the Friedenskirche at half-past eleven. No funeral sermon was delivered in the Priedenskirche, in accordance with the Empress Victoria's instructions and the wishes expressed by the late Emperor Frederick. His Majesty did not leave any written instructions re. glinting the arrangements for his funeral. Prince Bis- marck was not nresent at the funeral ceremony, his health being shaken by recent events. DL Roegel repeated the burial service, and pronounced the benediction. The mourners left after a volley had been fired, and the Empress Victoria before departing approached the coffin and bending over it took a solemn farewell-of her deceased consort

div.head: SYMPATHY IN GREAT BRITAIN.
div.p: SYMPATHY IN GREAT BRITAIN.

Nearly all the members of the Cabinet called at the German Embassy, in London, on Saturday, to leave their condolences on the Emperor Frederick's death ; among the first to call being Mr. Balfour. There was a continuous stream of carriages at the Embassy during the morning, many of whose occupants inquired as to the health of the Empress Victoria. Lord Salisbury has despatched a message of condolence to the widowed Emprest, in the name of the Government. The Queen ordered the court into mourning for six weeks, as a mark of respect to the memory of the late Emperor Frederick, commencing from Saturday. For the first half of the period, this will be full mourning: and for the latter half, semi-mourning. A funeral service was held on Monday in West- minster Abbey. Among those present were the Nether- lands Minister, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Mr. Gladstone, Lord Henniker, Lprd Manners, Lord Arthur and Lady Hill, Lord Edward and Lady Cavendish, Mr. White, United States Charge d'Affaires, and others. Funeral marches were played, and the Dean gave an address, referring iti,a feeling manner to the loss sus- tained by Gertnry and the civilised world through the Emperor Frederick's death.

THE FEELING ON THE .CONTLNENT. VrENNA, SATURDAY.-1 he Emperor Francis Joseph re- ceived the news of • the blperor Frederick's death with tears in his eyes, and exclaimed, "Now are his sufferings at an end.'' The Court has been ordered into four weeks' mourning. .

PARTS, SATCRDAY.—AII this morning's journals eulogise the Emperor Frederick's memory, and the Repribtigers Franc:Liss says :—" Europe will witness the accession of William the Second not without uneasiness."

BERNE, SATERDAY„—At the sitting of the National Council, to-day, the President paid a high tribute to the qualities of the late Emperor Frederick, and invited the Assembly to pass a vote of sympaty and condolence.

div.head: NEW EMPEROR (WILLIAM II.)
div.p: THE NEW EMPEROR (WILLIAM II.)

"He will certainly be a distinguished man, and pro- bably a great sovereign. Prussia will perhaps have in him a second Frederick the Great." Such was the fore- cast which a shrewd observer made five years ago of the young man whom Fate has raised to greatness be- fore his time, and who is to-day Emperor of Germany. That he will play a conspicuous part in the drama of European history is a conviction which has been im- pressed upon all who have had opportunities of observing the intelligence, the high spirit, and the independecce of the young qovereign. It. will be of interest, therefore to recall what preparation he has had for the work o' government upon which he has entered. First and fore- most, like his grandfather, he is a soldier every inch of him. The late Emperor, his father, was credited with too deeply Liberal a spirit, and with too entirely pacific intentions, to be altogether a favourite with the army. tut the new Emperor adores the army, and is beloved by it in return. He has been through the strictest discip- :ine, has held numerous commands, and well tinder- :,.tands the minute military administration of a German officer-

it would be vomplete mistake to suppose that the Emperor's training has been entirely military. For eighteen months the Emperor studied at Bonn. He rose every morning at 5 or 5 30, and dined at mid-day—his dinner being small and short. Two courses of meat, some vegetables, and dessert were his ordinary bill of fare. The Emperor himself ate very little, drank only wine and water, and for the rest looked on at his com- panions dining, talking all the while with much intelli- gence or listening with bright interest. On days when he " entertained " the dinner would be somewhat more elaborate, and the young Prince always corrected with his own hand the French of the menu. For, like Frederick the Great, he is a French scholar. His French tutor at Bonn, it is especially interesting to know, was a former editor of the Figaro, M. Anted& Pigeon. Thanks, too, to his mother, he is a good English scholar also; and can converse with ease in French and English. His mornings were devoted to lessons at home; his after- noons to lectures at the University. During his eighteen months at Bonn he went through the courses of law, history, chemistry, and political economy. He was also diligent in "private reading," and is said to have read widely both in French and English literature. But, needless to say, the Emperor did not abjure outdoor exercise.

Like all persons of hot-headed and somewhat self- sufficient disposition, eays the New York Tribune, the new Emperor is as soft as wax in the hands of a clever and clear-headed woman. In his particular case the woman happens to be an American lady, the daughter of a New York banker, of the name of David Lea, who in 1864 was created by the Emperor of Austria a Princes' von Noer in her own right on the occasion of her mor- ganatic marriage with Prince Frederick of Schleswig- Holstein. The Prince died of apoplexy, and the beautiful young,American, after only six months of married life, thus found herself at barely 25 years of age free to marry again, a Princess of the Austrian Empire in her own right, and one of the wealthiest women in all Europe. She took up her abode at: one of the most fashionable of German watering-place, where her beauty, her wealth, her cleverness, and the touch of romance hi her history soon caused her to be surrounded by a crowd of suitors of every degree and nationality. Among the most promi- nent and desirable of these was a Count IValdersee, who, besides being a member of one of the ancient fami ins of Prussia, was a great favourite both of the King and of Count Bismarck, and generally regarded one_erf the most prominent !tali officers of the'artny. Toivara Arrn4 of 1866 a marriage took place between the Gaunt and the widow. who shortly afterwards pro- ceeded with her husband to take up her residence at Berlin. Aided by his charming wife's cleverness and wealth, Count Waidersee became an important per- sonage in the Prussian capital, A favourite of Field- Marshal von Moltke, and maintaining his intimate rela- tions with the great Chancellor, he gradually got to be looked upon in the light of the latter's representative on the head-quarters' staff. He greatly distinguished him- self during the Franco-German war '; and when, a couple of years later, increasing age and infirmities forced Von moitke to ask for a deputy, General Count Waldersee was nominated to the post, with the rank of Quarter- master-General of the Imperial German Empire. His wife's salon had meanwhile become a power in Berlin, and was the rallying-place of the Chancellor's patty, as opposed to that of the anti4lismarckian Court factions. When, in 1881, Prince William (the present Emperor) married Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein, the power ad influence of the Waldersees still further in- creased, for 5' 'virtue Of her first marriage Princess von Noer is a grand-aunt of the Royal bride. The latter, who is neither attractive nor clever, dd not meet with much kindness at the hands either of the Prussian Royal Family or of the Imperial Court Her mother-in-law, who is one of the mos,t talented and clever women in Europe, is intensely intolerant of stupid women and . Princess William was only too glad to seize the helping hand held out to her by Count Waklersee's wife, and to avail herself of the relationship which existed between them to turn to her for guidance and advice. Few per- sons were better qualified than Countess Waldersee to act the part of mentor to the young Princess among all the pitfalls of the Berlin Court and society. Nor was the result long in making itself felt. The Princess has be- come completely subject to the will and direction of her clever relative, and Prince William (the new Emperor) was nat long in following his wife's example, and is now almost as subservient as the latter to the talented American.

The wife of the Emperor Frederick has al ways (iii- played a marked antipathy towards Count Waldersee's wife, whom she regarded as a parvenu, an intrigante, and even as an adventuress. It is due to theinthience of Countess Waldersee that both Prince William (the new Emperor) and his wife have displayed such marked favour to the well-known Court Chaplain Stoecker, the leader of the "Judenhetze " movement, who is Probably the bit- terest and most openly avowed of the enemies of the late Emperor and the Empress. Pastor Stoecker is the editor of a religious weekly paper, the Ecclesiastical Review, arid in the number issued on the 10th of December last lie actually had the audacity to write in an editorial article, signed with his name, the following cruel sen- tence :—" Let us pray every day and every hour for our Rot-al Family, and in particular for the old man (Kaiser Wilhelm) and for the young man (Prince William) of this race of heroes. May God in his mercy grant that the terrible punishment which has overtaken the sick Prince (the late Emperor) bear f liit, and may it bring resignation te his mind and peace to his conscience" It should be added that the Emperor Frederick has frequently expressed his strongest. disapproval of Pastor Stoecker's participation in the "Judenhetw," and re- peatedly, though unsuccessfully, urged Kaiser Wilhelm to deprive him of his Court Chaplaincy. The late Em- peror, whose liberal and brood-minded tendencies are well known, is of the opinion of Frederick the Great— namely, that everybody is entitled to seek eternal salva- tion in his own way, and he has even gone so far as to be present with his wife at the solemn inauguration of a Jewish synagogue in order to show how thoroughly he disapproved of persecution of the Jews. _

This will suffice to show great is the influence which Counted Waldersee wields over the new Emperor and Empress of Germany. During the past few months court has been paid to her such as was paid to Md me. de Maintenon during the latter part of Louis XlV.'s reign. Now that the young Williatn has succeeded to his father's crown, and the Crov it Princess has become Em- press, the role of the .fair American may become a com- manding one, and the "power behind the throne" vested in the person of Mary Lea, Princess of Noer and Countess of Waldersee:

Prince William (born January 27th, 1859) married, at the age of 22, the Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Flolstein- Augustenberg. The Princess is a niece of Prince Chris- tian and a daughter of that granddaughter of tile late Duchess of Kent. Adelaide Hohenkthe, whom the Queen would not alio* to marry the late Emperor of the French when he proposed to her. The ceremony took place ,at the Babelsberg Palace. On May Bth, 1882, 'a son—Frederick William—was born to the Prince and Princess William. The other children of the marriage are—Eitel Fritz, born in 1883; Adalbert, born in 1834; and another son, August William, born in 1807. It was thu.s given to Emperor William, as it is rarely given to Sovereigns, to behold three successors to the throne in the direct line. An authentic anecdote, that illustrates the sim- plicity of German life, is told of the birth of the first- born of Prince Wlllican's family. His father. the Crow7l

Prince, was pacing up and down outside his son's palace, somewhat perturbed and meditative, when sud- denly a window was thrown up, a head was thrust out, and a 'mice exclaimed, in a tone of mingled surprise and jubilation," Papa, it's a boy!" littiousiAtioN BY THE NEW EMPEROR. The proclamation, which was published in the Official, Gazette on Monday, is an address by the King to the nation, in that simple, hearty form which is peculla3, ' the Hohernollerns when they speak to their peoplA. Emperor recalls the fact that the grave ha.d scar:. ..seifrtifted upon the Emperor when the Emperor Fretieritck,stras called away. The latter had borne bis hard. 'ae with heroic and Lristian resignation, and rem lir ..1 faithful to his kingly duties. In the fete Months tO:lortedto him he had exhibited all the e,oblo.toolities, 61 his mind and heart. His virtualfdlils victories wpon the battlefield will be rentehitered as long as German hearts beat. He (William IL) had taken, over the Government look- ing up to the King of all kings. He prayed God that he might, after the example of his father, be to his people a just and element mince, foster piety and the fear of God, guard the peace and promote the welfare of the land, be a helper of the poor and distressed. and a firm guardian of the right. Might he ever think of his kingly duties in unison with his neople, who in good and evil days stood true to their Kings. He counted upon their fidelity in the conscious- ness that he would return it heartily, as the true Prince of a true people, both equally ready .for sacrifices for the Fatherland. Fmm his conzeiousness he derived the con- fidence that God would lend h:m strength and wisdom to discharge his kingly office for the welfare of the Fatherland.

" Truth" says :—Among the many different ac count of the new Emperor's physical blemish that I have seen, it is curious that there is not one which is correct. The left arm is not deformed, but withered, or rather dwarfed ; the nerves which vitalise it were subjected to great and prolonged pressure during birth, so that their conducting power (nerves are like °telegraph wires) was destroyed. Hence the muscles of the arm were paralysed, and became wasted from want of use, and the limb did I not grow with the rest of the body. The responsibility of this rests with the German doctors who officiated on the occasion, a fact which partly explains the Em- press Victoria's distrust of native talent. She insisted on Dr. Gream presiding at all subsequent ceremonies of the same kind, and outraged Teutons have never forgiven her for this affront to German "science."

The reasons for the applica- tioti. cot powers to make this canal is stated in the eroartiNe to the Act. "it is there set forth eit IN legally orthodox Phraseology, that "the said river (Weaver) between Frodsham bridge and its jnnction with the river Mersey near Weston Point, the direct navigable course to and from the said port of Liverpool,is not Only wholly unnavigable at net p tides, but, by reason of sand banks and heaps of stones laid to support and protect lands against the said river, is rendered dangerous and difficult to navigate, to the manifest injury and inconvenience of the trade on the said river Weaver, which can most effectually be remedied by making a navi- gable cut or canal from the said river Weaver, in the township of Sutton-by-Frodsham, to the said river Mersey at or near a certain place called Weston Point." THE ELECTION OF THE WEAVER TRUSTEES. Reference is from time to time made, in a more or less public fashion, to the non-representative character of the Weaver Trustees, and in the Act of 1807 we find provision as to the mode of filling up vacancies on the Trust, It is there stated that in case of death or refusal to act on the part of a Trustee, any nine or more of the surviving Trustees at their general annual meeting, "or the major part of them then assembled," may from time to time, by instrument in writing under their respective hands and seals, nominate and appoint some other person or persons, possessing the needful qualifications, to be trustees in place of those that have died or refused to act. These new trustees from the time of their appointment have the "like power and authority in all things relating to the matter" as if they had been appointed by the Act of Parliament itself.

div.head: AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
div.p: AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 23.-THE WEAVER AND ITS NAVI-
GA.TION.

Amongst others interested in the navigation of the Weaver, and protected by Act of Parliament against any ill effects upon the navigation that may result from the making of the Ship Canal, are Messrs. Rigby, of Sutton Mills, near Frodsham. The canal company are, during the construction of the por- tion of the canal between Eastham and Weston Point, to make provision for the passage across the canal to and from the Weaver from and to the navi- gable channels of the estuary of the Mersey, of all vessels destined for, or coming from, Sutton Mills. After the completion of the canal, all vessels bound for, or coming from Sutton Mills, are to be permit- ted to enter or leave the canal from or to the Mer- sey free of toll. In case the company fail to pro- vide the necessary facilities for the passage between the Weaver and the Mersey, the vessels will be at liberty to enter the canal at Eastham and pass along it free of dues and tolls to the Weaver, or, on the other hand, proceed from the Weaver to the Mersey at Eastham. At the present time there is a navi- gable channel of the Weaver running close past the south side of Messrs. Rigby's mills, whicn is used as a landing berth, and it is laid down that, if, by reason of the works of the canal company this chan- nel should be silted up or madb less deep than here- tofore, the company must forthwith, after being served with notice in writing by Messrs. Rigby or other tenants ot the mills, by dredging or other- wise remove such silting and restore the landing 'Perth to its present depth. The company will also, from time to time, have to pay to Messrs. Rigby, or other tenants of the mills, full compensation for any loss or damage which they may sustain by reason of the works or defaults of the company, either by stoppage or diminution of, or interference with, or delay in the passage of vessels to and from the mills during the construction of the canal. STAFFORDSHIRE "PROTECTED."

Though having no direct concern with the Weaver and its navigation, we may, perhaps, at this stage as conveniently.as at any other briefly glance at another section of the Ship Canal Act, which has for its object" the protection of the North Stafford- shire Railway Co., and of traders using the Trent and Mersey Canal." We there find that if, by the construction and maintenance of the new canal the present waterway for the carriage of traffic between the Trent and Mersey and Canal and the port of Liverpool be interfered with or interrupted, the Ship Canal Co. must at all times permit the free passage of boats and barges between the point near Runcorn Gap where the Trent and Mersey Canal, by means of the Bridgewater Canal, communicates with the Mersey, and the entrance to the canal at Eastham. Upon the company acquiring the Bridge- water undertaking, they were thereupon and there- after to "maintain such works, and provide and maintain such plant and appliances, and afford such accommodation and services at Runcorn, for the transport, haulage, wharfage, dockage, and ware- housing of traffic passing to or from the Trent and Mersey Canal on and over the Bridgewater Canal or the river Mersey as will render the transport of such traffic at, on, and over such Bridgewater Canal and river respectively, at least as cheap and convenient in every respect as it now is, and the company shall not be entitled to demand, or receive for or in res- pect of, all or any such works, plant, and appliances or accommodation or services, or of the use of the Bridgewater Canal or the river Mer- sey," &c., by boats and barges conveying traffic to or from the Trent and Mersey Canal, any dues or tolls higher than were, at the date of the passing of the Ship Canal Act, 1885, demanded by the Bridge- water Company. Further, if during ehe construc- tion of the canal or any temporary works the navigable access from the Mersey to the Bridge- water Docks and basins at Runcorn shall by reason ' of any act of the company be obstructed or ren- dered less deep than heretofore, the company, on receiving notice in writing, must remove or remedy the obstruction and pay to the /North Staffordshire Company and the traders on the Trent and Mersey Canal full compensation for and indemnify the North Staffordshire Company against all loss or damage occasioned by any such act. The notice above referred to may be served by. the North Staffordshire Railway Company or tlieir agent at Runcorn, the President for the time being of the North Staffordshire Chamber of Commerce. the Secretary for the time being of the Staffordshire Potteries Manufacturers' Association, acting under resolution of the members of the Association, or from the Secretary for the time being of the North Staffordshire Ironmasters' Association. For the protection of manufacturers of and traders in North Staffordshire pottery ware, &c., using the Trent and Mersey Canal, the following provision has been inserted: "All vessels destined for the Bridgewater Canal, at Runcorn, whose cargo consists only of flint, felspar, china - stone, china - clay, pot- ters' ball - clay, bones or bone-ash for use in the manufacture of pottery, or the manu- facture of earthenware. or china, and not exceeding four hundred and fifty tons gross register, and not carrying more than five hundred tons may enter the river Mersey and pass along work No. 1 (that is the canal between Eastham and Runcorn) on the pay- ment of half the ship dues prescribed by this Act, and such cargo, if destined for the Staffordshire potteries shall be liable only to half the tolls pre- scribed by this Act."

div.head: 'THE WEAVER NAVIGATION.
div.p: 'THE WEAVER NAVIGATION.

The present Weaver Navigation had its origin in an Act passed in 1720 "for making the River Wea- ver navigable from Frodsham Bridge to Winsford Bridge in the County of Chester." The preamble to this Act sets forth that " the making of the River Weaver, alias Weever, alias Weyer, navigable for boats, lighters, and other vessels from Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, to Winsford Bridge, in the same county, will not only be bene- ficial and convenient as well for the carriage of salt and cheese (the great rnanufuctures and products of the said county) as of other goods and merchandises to and from the towns adjacent, but will employ the poor, and be the means of preserving the high- ways of the said county, and will very much tend to employ and increase watermen and seamen and b 3 for the good of the public. An Act to amend the above-mentioned Act in various particulars was ob- t Lined in 1759, during the reign of George the Second.

EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE PORT. New ground has been opened out near Boston Wood and a steam navvy started in the cutting. This will connect the work. Mangs of men, totalling over 1,500, are now in one continuous line from Eastham to Elles- mere Port. At Eastham rock has been struck in the cutting at a depth of 35 feet ; another lift of about 15 feet has to come out, which will all be rock. Thiswould naturally be supposed to be against the work, but really it will be a great saving to the contractor, who can utilise the stone thus got on the spot, in the building of walls and embankments. The brickyard is complete and the kilns burning. A large amount of good brick earth is found here which will be sufficient for all the bricks needed. The cutting on the Ellesmere side of the brook is, with the exception of about ten feet on the top, all rock, and the contractor estimates that in this cutting alone there are over half a million tons of rock to be ex- cavate& From this cutting the canal will again run into the estuary past Ellesmere Port Docks, wherea most difficult piece of work has to be done, in fact, a large wall or embankment requires to be built in the river, and the contractor, whilst building it, will have to keep a passage open for vessels using the docks. The hospital at Ellesmere Port, which is provided by Mr. Walker for the use of the Eastham and Ince sections, is now opened. During the first week it was opened there were no less than four accidents and one case of sickness, one broken ankle, one back injured, and one broken arm. The hos- pital is constructed to hold twenty beds in the men's ward, and eight beds in the ward for women and children.

INCE. The work near Ince up to the present has been mostly soil stripping, rail laying, and bridge building. Now, however, there are two cuttings opened and two steam navvies are placed in position in each. At the first cut- ting near Stanlow Point there are also three cranes and two locomotives at work. Near each of the bridges a fire pump is placed, charged, ready for use in case of fire. This section is connected with Eastham by telephone. MOORE, Sze. The work at Moore continues to be pushed on with the greatest possible speed, and the cutting over Walton Common is being visibly lengthened. In this cutting ' there are two steam navvies of the American type at work, and they keep the locomotives busily engaged dragging away the tip-waggons laden with the excava- ted soil. Another navvy is now on the ground ready for being put in use. Pumping operations are going on at Walton. The soil that has been so far met with here has been of a sandy and yielding nature, and the navvies have had very little difficulty in dealing with it. The cottages built in this neighbourhood for the men are now all occupied, and they have a very Knnfortable and homely look. The hospital has been completed. This section—number five—is under the charge of Mr. J. R. Walker, who resides at Bell-house farm. THE HUTS AT MOORE AND NORTON. At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday, certificates of occupation were granted with respect to the eight Ship Canal huts at Moore and one at Norton.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT MOORE. On Thursday morning a Ship Canal navvy named Wm. Shadbolt, who was about forty years of age, and who was employed on the Ship Canal works at Moore, died at the Infirmary at Warrington. From a report that has since been made to the borough police, it appears that on Sunday the deceased was sitting on a gate at Moore when he accidentally fell off and injured his back. Later on in the day he was conveyed to the Warrington Infir- mary, where his injuries were attended to by the House Surgeon, Dr. T. Smith. Despite all that could be done for him, however, he succumbed from his injuries on Thursday. The Coroner has been communicated with, and in due course an inquest will be held. BARTON. The erection of premises for storing dynamite and other combustibles is now being proceeded with about a hundred yards from the banks of the Irwell, near to the aqueduct at Barton. A bed of red sandstone has there been met, and dynamite is about to be used for blasting purposes, the contractor (Mr. Walker) having obtained the sanction of the county justices. The utmost activity now prevails on the section between Mode Wheel, Weaste. and Stiggin's Islands Salt Eye, Barton, as may be gathered from the fact that between the places men- tioned ten locomotives, five steam navvies, and upwards of 1,300 men areat work. Huge embankments have been formed the whole distance, and shortly it is expected the railway from the latter place on to Salford will be complete. The bed of the Irwell, where it takes a cir- cuitous course near Stiggins Island, is being utilised as a "tip." The difficulty.of land purchase in Flixton dis- trict has now been removed, and latterly men have been at work on the Flixton side of Hulme's Bridge, and at Irlam, where the canal will pass through the Rev. R. Martin's (vicar's) glebe land. The erection of the chapel in Cawdor-st., Fatricroft, for the use of the nav- vies, is now almost completed.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, ttc.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, ttc.

"My Friend and my Enemy" is the title of a capital story by Mr. Paul Blake, author of "The Two Chums," "School and the World," &c. It is published by Messrs. Griffith, Farren, & Co. in their Boys' and Girls' Library series, and is a handsome well-printed volume. The writer is a practised hand at story-telling, for he never for a moment lets the interest flag. It is due to him to say that the incidents are not unduly sensational, and yet there is no lack of lively adventure. All, young or 'old, who dip into the pages of 'the book will get in- terested in the fortunes both of the "Friend" and ' the "Enemy." The tone of the writing is through- out healthy and stimulating. The story is specially illustrated, and comprises thirty-two stirring chap- ters; it is a good book far a good boy. Messrs. Macmillan & Co. have issued a volume of "Selections from Tennyson, with introduction and notes by F. J. Rowe, M.A.. and W. T. Webb, M.A.," which is likely to become popular with the general reader as well as with the student. Tennyson is not like Browning in requiring a special Society to make his meaning clear; but there are passages that touch a hundred things that cannot be known to everybody, and it is just these allusions that reguire explaining, and that render a poem all the more attractive when they are explained. The general introduction describes and illustrates the poet's characteristics as a reciter; and the notes elucidate the selections generally. These notes are so full as to serve even juvenile readers. It is to be hoped the publishers will find the venture so successful as to be induced to issue Tennyson's poems right through in this form. Referring to the lines in " The Revenge ' " And a chizen times we shook 'em off as a dogthat shakes his ears When he leaps from the water to the land" we are told that "em" in this case is the old objective plural of "lie," and is not a contraction of "them." But the editors are wrong as to this note, for the poet refers to the Spaniards as being shaken off and not the Spanish

- dickens's Dictionary of London, 1888, is also published by Messrs Macmillan and Co., and is from the pen of Mr. Charles Dickees. It is a wonderful compilation, for. while nothing is missed, everything may be readily found. The section maps—fourteen in number—are of themselves worth the shilling that is charged for the volume.

Dickens's Dictionary of the Thames is a work similar to the last referred to; it does for the whole of the valley of the_Thames what the other does for the metropolis. The tourist, angler, and yachtsman may learn 'all about" the royal river from its source to the Nore. There are maps and plans to aid the text where required, So that the hand book may be said to be perfect in its way. In the English Men of Letters, edited by Mr. John Morley, we have Cowper by Mr. Goldwin Smith. Cow- per has written much that is getting somewhat out of date, but he has also written much that will never cease to be a treasure to humanity. The lines on his mother's portrait will move the common heart as-long as language endures. Mr. Goldwin Smith furnishes, as might be ex- pected of him, a most attractive biography. He gives a

vivid picture of the condition of England during Cow- per's career, and shows in what way the poet helped in that spiritual reformation, the effects of which we feel in a large measure to-day. The reader will find from this interesting volume that Cowper could write charm- ing letters as well as charming verse. The English Illustrated Magazine contains a continua- tion of the a Glimpses of old English Homes," Eridge Castle being described and Flustiated for the current month. Part I is given of a series .of illustrated articles on " Pagodas, Aurioles, and Umbrellas," and, amongst other things, there is a further supply of "Coaching Days and Coaching Ways," which is so good, both as to text and illustrations, that it is to be hoped, like Tennyson's brook, it will "goon for ever." Messrs. Cassell and Co. have issued a shilling number with a happy title. It is called Summertide, and is pub- lished as the Little Folks Holiday. Number for 1888. It contains as many as eight complete stories, and a large number of original drawings—some of them full page— besides an out-of-doors play, and oddities, riddles &c. There is, too, given with the number a large coloured plate of C. Burton Barber's painting entitled " Picka- back."

"The Life and Times of Queen Victoria" is comple- ted with part 24, and contains, amongst other illustra- tions, remarkably fine portraits of the late Emperor Frederick and the Empress Victoria. We have received the first part of Casseß's History of Protestantism, by the Rev. Dr. Wylie. It is handsomely and profusely illustrated, and will be completed in 36 parts. With part 1 there is presented a fine coloured plate suitable for framing. It is from the picture by Sir 0. W. Brierley, and represents Admiral Sir William Win- ter, in the Vanguard, engaging two large galleons of the Spanish Armada, July 20, 1588. That Radical Parson," by Hydra, is published by Mr. Walter Scott as one of Mawson's Northern Tales. It is a vigorous sketch of life in a northern town; the charac- ters are well drawn; and, though they will strike Londoners as exaggerations, we can testify that there is plenty of original material quite as raw and peculiar. The story shows the difficulties which beset the path of the clergyman who fights the battle of the poor; and it wilr be the means, we trust, of inciting others to follew a noble example. "The Emperor Frederick 111. and the Crown Prince, with biographical notices of the Empress Victoria and Prince Bismarck," is the title of a, shilling volume just published by Mr. Walter Scott. It is sure to have a large sale, for it abounds in moving incidents and stirring details; and is illustrated with admirable portraits of the leading personages. The *titer of ,the 'work is Mr. Joseph Lawton, who 1/1 on the staff of the "Liverpool Daily Post." It should be added that the • biograph is brought down to the death of the Emperor Frederick, andthe accession of William 11. , A supplement to the " Graphic " containing reproduc- tions of the pictures of the Royal Academy Exhibition for this year is likely to be treasured, as it is a finished piece of work, and printed on beautiful paper. It will enhance the reputation of the "Graphic." and doubtless add largely to its circulation. The Ladies' Treasury for June contains a very pretty coloured design for embroidery for tidy or for a cushion for bamboo wicker chair, notes on dressmaking, millinery, cookery, &c., and numerous sketches, and stories.

div.p: i/FIERE are very few men in England who are naturally more hearty and healthy than James Braddock. He is a gamekeeper, and lives at Jepson's Clough, Adlington, near Macclesfield. He is stoutly built, alid until two years ago we may say he never had a week's illness in the Whole sixty years of his life. One day this summer (1887) he was found at home, and in the course of the talk that sprang up, Braddock told the follow- story, which we print because it will interest many besides himself. Re said: "Perhaps you have already heard about my case, and if so, it's 110 use my telling it all over again." "I heard it alluded to in Manchester," was the answer, "but I should like tO hear it from your own lips." "Well, sir," said James, "I'll run it over for you. I've told it lots of times, aild it's always done good to somebody. It was two years ago this summer that I was taken very bad with indigestion. How ill I was, and how I finally got cured, is no news to the people in this part of the country, sir Scores of them came from far] and near to, see me and talk to me about it. I first 40ticed a dull feeling all over me, and my appetite failed so I could eat 40thing without just forcing it down, sir; and then it lay like a heavy weight °/). my stomach. Food used to make me feel strong for work and exercise, blit now it seemed to do me no good at all. My mouth tasted bad, and when looked in the glass I saw .my skin and eyes had a yellow colour, and People said I was dreadfully bilious, my liver was out of order, and my blood ql full of poison. And so I believed, for my head ached and my legs and 4rins ached, as though I had some manner of fever hold of me. I took pills, 41d a hundred other medicines, but they only made me feel a little easier for day or two, and then I was worse than ever. "After a bit, sir, I began to be short of breath, you know, and had to sit clown and rest, when once I could tramp all day without being tired or once retching a long breath. I couldn't make out what was the matter with me k' whatever had brought it on, but I kept on getting worse, and that much I Was sure of. My heart would flutter and get weak and faint in my breast,

So it went on, sir, and neither my friends nor the doctors appeared to understand what was ailing me. "One day I was taken with such a queer spell, it almost scares me to think back of it.
