LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT NORTH WICH.
MR. BRUNNER,, M.P. ON LOCAL GOVERNMENT
AND THE WEAVER TRUST.

On Saturday afternoon last, about 4,000 persons assembled in Winnington Park, the residence of Mr. J. T. Brunner, to protest against the compensa- tion clauses and other provisions of the Local Government Bill. Liberals and temperance workers formed part of the demonstration, which was a great success in every way. No part of the division was unrepresented, and large numbers from Run- corn and Northwich were conveyed to the scene by boats on the river Weaver. The Runcorn contingent were attended by the Weston Church Brass Band. About four o'clock a long procession started from the Bull-ring, Northwich, and, led by the Winning- ton Crescent Brass Band, marched to the meeting place. Under the shadow of the trees in front of the hall, ra platform was improvised, and Mr. 11. Bratt, of Northwich, took the chair. On the plat- form were Mr. and Mrs. Brunner, Mr. F. Stevenson, M.P. for Eye. Mr. T. E. Ellis, Mr. T. Hardy (United Kingdom Alliance), Dr. Ilewitt, Messrs. George Slater. John Thompson, F. J. Thompson, John Bur- gess, James Williams (Middlewich) ; and Messrs. T. Handley, W. Handley, tied T. Clegg (Runcorn). The meeting exhibited the utmost enthusiasm, and "our member" and the other gentlemen were greeted with loud cheers. At the outset, Mr. Brun- ner announced the magnificent victory at Ayr maid much excitement, an I in response to his call three ringing cheers were given for the "Grand Old Man' The Chairman delivered a brief address, and then Mr. Brunner, who was received with loud cheers, moved "That this mass meeting of temperance refor- mers and Liberals "—and, he remarked, there was very little difference between the two—(hear, hear,)—" re- joices at the withdrawal frdin the Local Government Bill of the provision for the compensation of publicans and brewers, in face of the moral uprising of the "people against creating a gigantic vested interest in a traffic which works such injury and ruin upon the social wel- fare of the people—(hear, hear,)—but condemns the withdrawal of the clauses which confer upon County Councils the power ofs„losing public-houses on Sunday and transfer the licensing powers of the magistrates to the County Councils; and further condemns such reac- tionary proposals in the bill as the introduction of alder- men into County Councils, and the dual control of the police by a joint committee of the County Council and the Court of Quarter Sessions.' tie said it had been very clearly shown that the proposals of the Government to compensate brewers and distillers would have entailed upon the people of this country a debt to those classes equivalent to an enormous addition to the National Debt. Whether they were in the habit of taking beer or were ab- stainers they would be better off if they had fewer public-houses. Did it not follow from that fact, then, that the insistence by the Government upon their paying for that with on their part for their own welfare and the welfare of their neighbours, entailed an enormous tax upon them? The resolution went on to condemn the withdrawal of the clauses which confer upon county councils the power of closing public-houses on Sunday. He was entirely disin- terested upon that questior, and meant, as he had meant ever since he stood before them as a candidate for their favours, to act in that matter according to their wishes, and if it be their wish, and he believed it was, that the power should be given to county councils to close public- houses on Sundays, he was going to vote for it. (Hear, hear.) He did not mean to say that he considered the proposal a perfect one, but it was far better than the present system. (Hear, hear.) Finally, the resolution condemned the re-actionary proposals of the introduc- tion of aldermen into county councils, and the dual con- trol of the police by a joint committee of the county council and Court of Quarter Sessions. He never in all his life saw the use of an alderman, and in their own neighbourhood these aldermen—for there were to be aldermen in every district council and county town—would be a most mischievous lot. He was perfectly satisfied that in almost every district of the kingdom the new-fangled proposal of aldermen in the local boards would entail upon the ratepayers the ex- penseof enlarging the offices. (Laughter). They did not want those aldermen for any purpose whatever, and if they saw that they were not only going to be useless but ex- pensive he claimed their votes against them. (A Voice ; "They are only robbers.") Now, with regard to the dual control of police by the magistrates, the Court of Quarter Sessions, and the county council he asked what would be the county council It was going to be the magistrates over again, for there were very few men, as they knew, in Cheshire who had the time and the money to spare to go to Chester to sit on those county councils once a month, except the class from which the magis- trates were drawn. Only those men had got the time and the money to spare, and since the Government de- clined, in the usual Tory fashion, to permit poor men to have their expenses paid when they were called upon to serve their neighbours upon thcir muty mucus —to permit their railway fares to be paid —it was perfectly clear that only men of leisure and means would be able to get into the county council. As square-headed men of business, they must, if they wanted a thing well done, put it into the hands of one body to manage it. They might depend upon it, that just as England and France made a hash of it when together they tried to manage Egypt, and as in many a case in our history where two bodies had been put to manage one thing, so they would find that where the magistrates sitting in quarter sessions and other magistrates sitting in county councils were to manage the police between them, they would make a hash of it. (Hear, hear.) There was no better way of maintaining order amongst any population than to give the manage- ment and the preservation of order into their own hands (Cheers.) As long as :,the management of the police was in the hands of an irresponsible class, always in the hands of the rich, they were always in danger of having conflicts between the people and the police. He urgect that the victory of Ayr had been an answer to the Government, not only upon its proposals with regard to compensation, but it had been an answer, and a straight answer, to the Coercion Act. (Hear, hear,) Speakers had gone from London to speak to the people of the Ayr burghs, the most respected, the most honoured. (Cheers.) And he said that the declaration of the voters in the Ayr burghs had been a direct and utter condemna- tion of the policy of the Government which condemned such a man as John Dillon to prison. He shook hands with John Dillon less than 40 hours previously, and he very much feared it would be the last time he should shale hands with him. (A voice : "I hope not.") His friend John Dillon was a man of delicate fr,ame, a man whose health had already been broken by the cruelty of the laws—(" Shame ")—and he sadly feared that such a punishment as had been proposed to be inflicted upon him, of six months' imprisonment, with all the hardships they could impose upon a murderer and a pickpocket, will end his noble life. ("Shame." and a Voice : " What rascally work.") He said he was much obliged to his friend Mr. William Handley., whose kind thought had prompted him to pro- pose that they should have an opportunity of signing a petition to the House of Commons upon that subject, praying that the House of Commons would take such measures as should in the name of equal and just law and common humanity prevent the sentences of im prisonment from being carried out. (Hear, hear.) They would be invited to sign that petition at the close Of the meeting, and he hoped they would do so. He proceeded to observe that Mr. Gladstone had said in his letter to Lord Hartington two or three days before, that by the help of the Liberal Unionists the Government had been able to impose upon Ireland a law insidious and cruel, and an administration of the law worse than the law itself. Be wished to enforce what Mr. Gladstone had said by an incident which came before the House of Commons. The House decided that the secret inquiries were to be held in the ordinary places, where the magistrates met. Now, what did the rascally policemen in Ireland do? Instead of having the inquiry before the magistrate him- self, they employed a detective, thereby escaping them- selves from an infringement of the law. He did not know whether he ought, on an occasion of that sort, to allude to a matter which was somewhat personal to him- self, but his reputation amongst them for fairplay was so important to him that he asked them to forgive him if he introduced something which had nothing to do with the ordinary business of that meeting. It was this. He asked a question of the President of the Board of Trade the other day with regard to the tolls on the Weaver, and with regard to the surplus from the Weaver, and he said that to his mind it was a wrong thing that the workers in one trade should be taxed for the benefit of the whole county. (Hear, hear, and "Shame.") He was proud to say that whenever he had spoken upon that question he had found the Runcorn people so fair-minded, so generous, that they agreed with him without a dissentient voice that the suffering caused in the salt district by the subsidence of the ground ought to be compensated by the surplus funds from the Weaver. (Hear, hear.) He had calculated that if the sur- plus funds of the Wea.ver, £15,000 a year, were no longer paid over to the coanty, in the year 1896, when the cattle plague rate would come to an end, the debts which would then be chargeable upon the county would be £BOO a year. That came to a farthing a head for a year, and he asked his friends who had come from Runcorn whether they would not allow that they should be charged each a farthing per head in the year in order that the suffering, the undeserved suffering to the pro- perty owners and the tenants in Northwich, Marston, Anderton, and Winsford should be compensated. He asked them whether of their fairness and of their generosity they would consent to help him in bringing it to an end. (A Voice: "The pumpers ought to pay for it.") Certainly the pumpers ought to pay for it. He was one of the biggest amongst them, and he said that the pumpers ought to pay; but it was an unfair thing to ask the people in the salt trade to pay more than they were paying now until they had given them the surplus which belonged to them. (Hear, hear.) In concluding, he said he had again to declare his unalterable fidelity to them. (Hear, hear.) He trusted they had found him always on the same side, and that the work he had done

div.head: latttrs to tht Vittor.
div.p: latttrs to tht Vittor.

"BELLEROPHON" AND HIS QUOTATIONS. Sir,—He who excuses, accuses, and it is evident from the characteristically ill-natvred excuse in his last letter that "Bellerophon" is beginng to be rather shamefaced over his muddy quotations. But it is the misfortune of some people that they cannot do without that of which they are rightly enough ashamed. The skunk without its mal-odorous fluid would be the most defence- less of animals, and " Bellerophon " deprived of his unsavoury quotations would be simply "naked to the world." There is only one way in which he can hope to keep his head above water, and that is by using the peculiar talents with which nature has endowed him. He has as keen and infallible a scent for a piece of literary offal as a vulture has for carrion, and if he once becomes ashamed of using this faculty his "occupation's gone."—Yours, Sze.,
CADMUS.
Warrington, June 21st, 1888.

FOUL AIR IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—Allow me to call the attention of yourself and, I hope, of some of your readers, to what I may call the insanitary condition of one or two of the smaller streets in the town. Going through Haydock-st., early one morning this week, I was almost suffocated by a smell, the most awful, I think, my nostrils were ever ac- quainted with. In a moment I thought of the alleged gas leakage, and fully expected that I had discovered the cause of the embarrassment of the Gas Committee. But reviving somewhat, I found that it was only the houses, yards, or something else very near to me, which smelt most abominably. There might be a quantity of coal gas in the air, but there was also something far worse. Now, sir, is it wise, with the smallpox so near, and the hot weather upon us already, to have this state of things in a crowded part of the town ? I believe there are a nuisance inspector, and two assistants, em- ployed by the town to discover the cause of such matters, and to find remedies for them. Could one of them wend his way through Haydock-st.about 8-30 some morninghe might find some way of lessening the annoyance. There are other streets also in the town that are not pleasant at times. In one small side street (Jolley..) off Legh-et. there is a most dreadful aroma of what I should think is bad fish. I was assured by a resident that it was healthy. To my uneducated nostrils, however, it was only extremely disagreeable.—Yours, etc., ANTI-AROMA. Warrington, June 21st, 1888.

div.head: WESLEY/LNISM AT GOLBORNE.
div.p: WESLEY/LNISM AT GOLBORNE.

Sir,—My attention has been called to a letter from "Wesleyan" in your last issue. lam sorry your corres- pondent had not thd courage to publish his name, and also that, ere he "rushed into print," he was not careful to make himself thoroughly acquainted with all the de- tails and bearings of the case upon which he writes. ' Had he...done this with a mind free from prejudice, he', would have escaped the mistakes into which he has fal- len, and avoided the misconceptions, misrepresentati misjudgments, and unfair conclusions which his epistle reveals. It is unfortunate that he has spun a misleading letter out of the imperfect knowledge implied in such phrases as " I am told," "it is said," "I am informed." Tongues do not always say "the whole truth, and no- thing but the truth." Information may be partial. A sincere man may unwittingly think and believe what is untrue and unfair.

I beg to inform "Wesleyan"-1. That the " unpleasant- ness 'does not involve a "settlement with ministers" ; not being a question of ministers versus people. 2: That have not the " authority " with which he and others credit me, not being "superintendent of the circuit." A man cannot use what is out of his reach. 3. That I shall probably survive blame for not doing an impossi- bility. 4. That the proposal which " Wesleyan ' says was repudiated with scorn" was an equitable one; inwartial men being' judos, That all that natiaTice Coma et prevent the breach, consistently with fairness to all parties, has been done; unprejudiced men again being the judges. 6. That the "beautiful new school" and the "oran in the church" are "monuments of the work" of others, as well as" the im- portant members" who "have left the church." Against the ratter I will not pen a word, but could cheerfully write in their praise. 7. That all the resources provided by Wesleyan laws for the defence of right and the re- dress of wrong are not exhausted; and these are at the command of "Wesleyan." 8. That it is just possible that others may be as conscientious as " Wesleyan " ; who, from his lofty altitude of superior conscientious- ness, is ready with a supply of pity for those whose faculty for discerning right and wrong may appear to him to be not so healthy as his own. 9. That I shall take no notice of any further newspaper correspondence upon this matter; but will gladly put the whole case before "Wesleyan," if he will "come out of his shell."—l am, sir, yours faithfully,
JAMES BENT, . Wesleyan Minister.

Earlestown, 20th June, 1888. A SOUTH AMERICAN FARMER'S HOLIDAY. On the arrival of the 11-45 train from Liverpool to London at Warrington Central station on Monday night, a respectably-dressed middle-aged gentleman was seen to jump from a Pullman car on to the plat- form when the train was in motion. The conductor of the train told the local officials that he thought "the gentleman had the horrors," and the man was taken to the Inspector's office and there detained. A doctor was st nt for, and, after seeing the man, ex- pressed the opinion that he was insane. In conse- quence the railway officials took him to the police- station, where he was not locked up, but was simply "detained for safety." Next morning he was con- siderably better, and was brought before the magistrates on a charge of having, while apparently of unsound mind, attempted to to leave a train while in motion. He stated that his name was Thos.Clinstian,and Mr Rigby,stationmaster at the Central, informed the magistrates that when at the station the defendant said that he was a • farmer in South America, and that he had come over to England for a three month's holiday. A first-class ticket for London, and some valuable documents, wJre found upon him. When before the Bench defendant explained that he came from Douglas on Monday afternoon, and all that lie had to drink was a little brandy and lemonade in Liver- pool, and a bottle of soda water that he had in the train, which he obtained from the guard. He be- came, as it were, insane, and could not account for the drink having had such an effect upon him. As Mr. Rigby did not press the charge, it was with- drawn, defendant paying what expenses had been incurred.

div.head: FELONY BY A WARRINGTON SERVANT.
div.p: FELONY BY A WARRINGTON SERVANT.

Phtebe Dickinson (18), a respectably-dressed young woman, described as a domestic servant, was charged, at the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, with having on the previous day stolen from the house of Mr. Charles S. Burgess, 7, Egypt- /A., a diamond ring, value £lO. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable, stated that defendant was the daughter of William Dickenson, a tailor, who lived on Pinner's-brow. On the 7th - inst, she called at Mrs. Burgess's and applied for a situation as nurse, asserting that she had never been in service before, but had lived with an aunt in London. She was accepted, and on Wednesday, the 12th of June, she entered upon her duties. All seemed to go on right until Friday afternoon, when she went upstairs to dress, and shortly afterwards left the house, saying that she • was not gong to stay there to be "sauced." An hour or two afterwards, Mrs. Burgess, on going to her room, found her diamond ring missing. Information was given to the police, and at a quarter to eleven the same even- ing P.C. Monaghan apprehended the prisoner at the Hop Pole Inn. She at first denied the theft, but subse- quently produced a pawn ticket for it. It was after- wards discovered that she had pledged the ring for 25s at the " Tower' pawnshop, Bridge-st., where she told the assistant that it was an engagement ring, giving her name as Martha Hall, Clifton-terrace, Latchford. She displayed some cunning in the matter, for, after pledg- ing the ring, she bought another one for 7s, telling the assistant I cannot go home like this; I must have a ring of some sort or he'll find out. Prisoner had been in the habit of assisting at the theatre, and fer some time, when in service at the "Millstone Inn," Gelborne-st.,

, used to sing to amuse the company. Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour, and the ring purchased by her, together with 13s ad in money found upon her, weri erdered to be returned to the proprietors • ot the pawnshop.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1888.

met with their approbation. He could promise them after all the many tokens of kindness that he had received at their hands that with all the strength that he had he would work for their interest in the future. (Loud cheers.) Mr. F. Stevenson, M.P., supported the resolution, and after dealing with the various points, he referred at length to the Allotments Act. In conclusion he urged them not to rest contented with what they had already attained, but to do all they could to spread the light of ,Liberalism and of justice, and to get those principles in which they believed carried out in practical legislation. (Cheers.)

Mr. T. Hardy spoke on the temperance aspect of the question, observing with regard to the compensation clauses that he was taking part in the funeral service of the most impudent and absurd proposal ever made in the name of a civilised Government, and he did so without any live of their resurrection into life. (Applause and laughter.) He was very glad to hear that the ninth clause of the bill was not to be allowed quietly to drop, as there were many Conservative members of the House of Com- mons who were quite prepared to agree to the closing of public-houses on Sundays, Christmas Day, and Good Friday. The temperance party had been charged with aiming at the confiscation of the property held by brewers and licensed victuallers. They did not plead guilty to the charge. Public-houses were a necessity for public convenience; they had been for long enough, and they would remain so to the end of the chapter. It was only , against public-houses that were a nuisance that they entered their protest against. (Applause.) Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P.f who had a most cordial recep- tion, said it seemed to him% hat between the Ayr elec- tion and the speechos that afternoon her Majesty's Gov- ernment had been knocked and battered out of all recog- nition. (Laughter.) They had never had much admiration' he thought, for the qualities of the present Government of her Majesty, but he thought they must confess that they had learned and practised one art exquisitely and consummately, and that was the art of climbing down. (Renewed laughter.) He mentioned a number of propcsals the Government had introduced and then abandoned. When a general election came ' Toryism would be wiped away altogether, the carcase of Unionism would be swept from the House of Commons and from the country. (Cheers.) Mr. 3.0. Bmndrith, of Northwich, speaking on behalf of the united temperance workers of the town and dis- trict, expressed sympathy with the movement, and sup- ported the motion. On being put to the meeting the resolution was unani- mously carried amid loud cheers. Mr. Brunner read a letter he had received from Mit- chelstown askingrhis co-operation in getting up a testi- monial to William Gould as a mark of his appreciation of his conduct on the memorable 9th September, 1887, at MitcheLstown, where he distinguished himself by gal- lantly defending the rights of public meeting. Mr. Brunner said he should be heartily glad to shake Wm. Gould by the hand, because he was a right manly fel- low, and he was going to respond to that circular in a way that he trusted would be' agreeable to them. If ever, when they were holding a public meeting in Ches- hire, the police attacked them without saying before- hand "This is an illegal meeting and we want you to go home." he would tell them that if they broke the police- men's heads they were in the right. (Hear, hear.) Wm. Gould did that and he was going to help to get up a tes- timonial to him for it, He proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Bratt for presiding. Mr. G. E. King seconded the motion, which was sup- ported by Mr. T. Clegg, of Runcorn, and carried, and the meeting dispersed.

RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also pre- sent the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, and J. Lockwood; Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Stokes, Hadfield, Bran- dreth, T. Hewitt, W. Hewitt, Whitlow, Parr; H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk.) DANGEROUS PROPERTY AT HALTON.—THE CHAIRMAN DECLINES TO PUT A RESOLUTION.—The iv. J. Lockwood. in accordance with notice previously given, moved the following motion :—" That in the opinion of this Authority the condition of the highway leading from the village of Halton to the Northwich-road at the turning opposite to Messrs. Gamon and Rowe's business pre- mises constitutes a nuisance and is highly dangerous to the travelling public, and that this Authority in con- junction with the Daresbury Highway Board proceed to abate the nuisance by the removal of the debris from the land where the nuisance exists, and to properly fence the same, and that the cost of so doing be charged to the township of Halton." In moving the resolution Mr. Lockwood described the property as dilapidated and dangerous, and he also mentioned cases in which acci- dents had happened to children and others.—The Chair. man did not see what jurisdiction that Authority had in the matter.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said that the great difficulty was as to the ownership of the property but whatever might happen he should now feel that he had done his duty as guardian for Halton.—Mr. Hadfield said if they moved in that matter they might afterwards be brought up on a charge of trespass. Mr. Lockwood wanted to get rid of his responsibility, but he (Mr. Had- , field) did not see why he should try to throw the respon- sibility on that Authority.—Mr. Aaron seconded the pro- position, and remarked that three of the owners of the property were known, but another one was missing and he had left this country forty years ago, and was then thirty years of age.—Mr. Hadfield thought the owners ought to take the responsibility of removing the danger. —The Clerk remarked that that Authority had power over a dilapidated building which was dangerous.—The Assistant Clerk said he should suggest that they take the bull by the horns and make the building so that it would not be a danger to the people of Halton and the travel- ling public at the cost of the township of Halton.—ln answer to a question, Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspec- tor) said the building had been a danger for a long time, but he could not say as to whether that Authority could interfere.—Mr. Brandreth : Put the motion,—The Chair- man said he would not put that motion on his own res- ponsibility. Let the Highway Board take the iniative. —The Rev. J. Lockwood said the Clerk had said it was right to move the resolution.—The Chairman said the I officials were divided as to what could be done. He (the chairman) did not want them to enter on a thing that could not be carried through. It was not a nuisance in- jurious to health.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said the Act of Parliament laid it down that any nuisance might be brought before that Authority.—Mr. Hadfield: The ruler of the meeting is the Chairman, and if there is any dispute he is the one to rule what must Ise done.—The Rev. J. Lockwood: I think the Local Government Board is the final authority.—The Chairman: I feel so sure that if this resolution were passed we should get into some trouble that I decline to put it. Let the Local Government Board say whether I am right or wrong.-.- The Rev. J. Lockwood : Then you refuse to put it ? The Chairman: I decline.—The Rev. J. Lockwood : Well it shall be referred to the Local Government Board.— The matter then dropped. OVERTON PUMP.—The Inspector reported that the water from the village pump at Overton was being largely used for other than domestic purposes, and after some discussion he was instructed to put a lock on the pump, and put the key in possession of those who re- quired the water for domestic purposes. This was all the business.

RUNCORN BOARD OF OUARDIANS. , The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, and /. Lockwood; Messrs. Mclntyre, Speakman, Once, Aaron, Stokes, Jones, Hadfield, Brandreth, W. Whitlow, Parr, T. Hewitt, Joseph Hall, T. Foster; H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk.)

THE WEAVER TRUST.—The Clerk reported that letters had been received from Neston and Parkgate Local Board Chorley Cheshire) Local Board. Marple Local Board, and Altrincham Union, stating that each of these Authorities was in favour of the proposed petition to Par- liament against any interference with the Weaver Trust which might affect the contribution of that body to the county rates.—On the motion of Mr. Hadfield, seconded by Mr. Brandreth, the seal of the Board was attached to a memorial to the above effect.

RELIEF SUPERVISION COMMITTEE.—This Committee re- commended that the collector be instructed to make in- quiries as to the ability of relatives to support children who may be in the house, and that he be directed to ap- ply for authority to take proceedings in any case where proceedings are necessary, and that some remuneration be fixed by the Board to be paid to the collector for un , dertaking prosecutions and for the duties connect° therewith.—The Rev. J. Lockwood, in moving the adop- tion of the report, said the collector had supplied them with a list of 18 children whose parents were contribu- ting towards their support in the workhouse.—Mr. Speakman said the question of sending children who had parents that ought to provide for them with a home out of the house had been raised by the master of the work- house, who found that if something was not done in that direction they should very soon want a new wing to the workhouse. Some parents seemed to be under the im- pression that if they paid towards the support of their children in the workhouse they could not be compelled to take the children out, but he was glad to learn that that was not so, and he thought people outside ought to know it.—Mr. Once said the subject had been, 'brought for- ward because a man who was going to be married again wanted to send his children to the workhouse. (Laugh- ter.)—After some further conversation :the Rev. J. Lock- wood gave notice of motion to the effect that the collec- tor be paid 5s per case brought by him before the magis- trates.

THE CHILDREN'S TIM/LT.—The Workhouse Master re- ported that upwards of seventy of the workhouse chil- dren went on the Monday of the previous week to South- port, in the care of the matron, school teachers, and three adults. They left Preston Brook about nine o'clock in the morning and on reaching Warrington were accommodated with two special carriages. At South- port the day was spent in an enjoyable fashion. At two o'clock they all partook of an excellent dinner at Haye's restaurant, and later in the day of an equally excel-

ent tea. By special arrangement with the railway com- pany the return journey was commenced at 7 o'clock, and the workhouse was reached a little after 10. all well pleased with the day's outing, and without accident. The Master also reported that in addition to the sum an- nounced at the last Board meeting Mr. W. C. Jones, of Oaklands, had sent £5. He (the Workhouse Master) proposed, with the consent of the Board, to put any balance that might remain after the expenses of the treat had been met in the bank in the name of the Chair- man of the Board to form the nucleus of a treat fund for future years. This was all the business of public interest.

FRODSHAM.. SCHOOL SERHOWS.—On behalf of the Sunday School Fund of the United Methodist Free Church, Helaby, ser- mons were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday afternoon and evening, by Mr. C. Hibbert, of Denton. The collections amounted to £l5 7s 110. Cnusca PARADE.—The 2nd (Earl of Chester's) Volun- teer Battalion Cheshire Regiment attended Divine service at the Parish Church, Frodsham, on Sunday morning, when the vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, preached. The officers present were Captain H. Harrison, Lieutenant T. B. Ashton, Sergeant-Instructor Evans, together with 2 sergeants, 1 bugler, and 44 rank and file.

Permission has been granted by the Russian Govern- ment for women to become chemists. A fire causing damage to the amount of about £4,000 occurred on Wednesday at the premises of Messrs. James Pendleton and Co., iron-founders, Dale-st., - Liverpool. A despatch from St. Paul de Loanda, of Wednesday's date, gives some very interesting particulars of Mr. Stanley's expedition. It is said that the great explorer has been severely wounded in an encounter with natives.

A FISHING FLIET DESTROYED: GREAT Loss OF LIFE. —Some shipwrecked French fishermen, who have been landed at Leith, report that the recent storm did an appalling amount of damage to the fishing fleet off the coast of Ireland. They believe that some 30 or 35 ves- sels and no fewer than 400 lives have been lost. This, however, needs verification. A fishermen of 34years' Iceland experience, says he never saw such a terrible storm.

"THE TRADE" ON LOCAL OPTION.—A large meeting of the principal brewers and wine and spirit dealers was held in London on Wednesday, under the presidency of Lord Burton, to protest against the retention in the Local Government Bill of anything favourable to local option, and to enforce the right of the " trade "to com- pensation. Lord Burton hinted that he could not con- tinue to follow Mr. Gladstone if compensation was de- nied to men whose trade had been sanctioned by succes- sive Parliaments.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town hail, on Tuesday. Mr. Bradsha,Tv presided and there were present the very Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs F. Heyes, R. H. Davies, J. B. Imison, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing the month of May there were 250 persons summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act and 48 were prosecuted before the magistrates and convicted. There were 120 applications for the payment of School fees, and fees were recommended to be paid in 113 cases.—The Committee recommended that the salary of Attendance Officer, G. R. Joynson, be increased ac- cording to the scale of the Board from the first of July, that officer having completed nine years service. The minutes were passed on the motion of Dean Fine- gan.

PRIZES TO WCPIERS. The School Management Committee reported that Mr. R. Holden Davies having expressed his willingness to give prizes to those pupil teachers who had distinguished themselves in the annual Scripture Examination they beg to recommend that the best thanks of the Board be given to Mr. Davies, and that his offer be accepted. Adopted on the proposition of Dean Finegan. SITES AND BUILDING COMMITTEE. On the recommendation of this committee it was re- solved that the tender of Messrs. Jones and Sons. dated May 15th, 1888, be accepted for the new latrines, drains, &c., for the Warrington-road Schools, and that the fol- lowing tenders be accepted for the painting, cleaning, repairs, &c., required at the various Board schools : Messrs. D. Lea and Son, for Warrington-road School, and Mr. C. J. Sutcliffe for ,the Simm's Cross and West Bank Schools.
The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Davies.
FINANCE.

The Finance Committee rmended the payment of accounts amounting to £592 19s 11d, and reported that the receipts amounted to £1,154, including school fees £143 7s 10d. It was recommended that the Board be empowered to obtain p, loan of £4,000 from the Public Works Loan Commissioners for the additional accommo- dation required at Simm's Cross, Warrington-road, and West Bank schools, and the necessary furniture and fit- tings, for 30 years at 3i per cent. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

div.head: ELOPEMENT FROM WIDNES.
div.p: ELOPEMENT FROM WIDNES.

During the past week an elopement has taken place in Widnes which has caused no little sensa- tion among those who happen to know the facts. It appears that about six months ago a dashing-look- ing young fellow, who had previously served in the army, came into the town to commence work at one of the works there. He took up his abode in the neighbourhood of West Bank, a very populous part of Widnes, with an elderly lady, who had rather a good-looking married daughter, whose husband was employed at the same works. The two men got very friendly, and as a result they, together with the young wife, were to be seen often walking out. Nothing would then satisfy the military looking man but that he must change his residence and live with his mate, a matter which was at once agreed to by the latter, never for a moment sus- pecting what was to be the outcome of their friend- ship. The affection between the landlady and the lodger, however, seems to have grown very strong, for on the husband returning from his daily toil some few days ago he discovered that the woman of his choice had eloped with the lodger, taking the youngest child and leaving an elder one to comfort him in his distress. Some time ago, it seems the false wife had a sum of money left her, which was deposited in the bank. She has, however, with- drawn this and taken it with her. The deserted husband is much upset by the conduct of his better half, and swears vengeance if he should happen to find the runaway pair.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from' page 6.) TETELWALL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from' page 6.) TETELWALL.

During the week operations have been considerably extended on this section of the canal, and men are now at work on the Warrington side of Morris Brook, and on part of the site of the future Latchford Locks. The steam navvy in front of Morris Brook farmhouse con- tinues steadily at work, and makes very evident progress from day to day. Between this point and the river at Thelwall the other steam navvies are in constant opera- tion, the larger of the two " Jubilee " navvies having been repaired and again put to the work of excavation, which during the last few days it seems to have been carrying on very satisfactorily. It is estimated that about 40,000 cubic yards of earth are displaced each week on this section. The finishing touches are being put to the 4th row of navvies' huts, and these, like the other, will soon have their full complement of inhabi- tants. The comfortable-looking wooden hospital at Cedar Lawn is now occupied by Dr. Burn, who has charge of the patients. Hitherto they have been few in number, and none Of them have suffered from any very severe injuries,

CADISHEAD. Operations have now commenced at Cadishead. Much trouble has been met with ; the company haying to set- tle with so many small owners trustees, and executors, and Pendleton.Corporation.low gangs of men are busy removing the top soil in the fields opposite Mill Bank Paper Mill. Here the course of the canal is within 150 yards of the High-road, leading from Manchester and Liverpool, on the Lancashire side of the river, and much work has to be done in the vicinity. At Rixton a start has been made with the second draw. Water is found to bo a hinderance, and the machines sink in the slutch made by the water, rendering the clay soil soft. Below thelWarburton Bridge-road we find all the first draw has been removed, showing the canal width and course, and two steam navvies are at work. Steam pumps are also busy at work, drawing water from wells sunk to a depth ,of nearly sixty feet. A trestle bridge is being thrown across the river Mersey to connect the lines with the Lymm section. PATRICROFT.

The erection of the iron church in Cawdor-st., now familiarly known as "The Navvies' Mission Church," is proceeding rapidly towards completion, and will be ready for use in another week or so. The provision of the church is mainly due to the exertions of Mr. L. P. Nott, of Eccles (son-in-law of Mr. Walker, Ship Canal contractor), a gentleman who has taken much interest in providing for the spiritual wants and needs of the men engaged on the Eccles and Barton section. The church will seat close upon 600 worshippers. Mr. Bird, formerly employed at Swinton in the capacity of mis- sioner to the navvies there during the construction of the new line of railway from Pendleton to Hindley, is in charge of the mission on the Burton and Eccles section, and has already held a series of special open-air services on Sunday.

div.head: UPSETTING A SANKEY POLICEMAN.
div.p: UPSETTING A SANKEY POLICEMAN.

On Wednesday, at the Ceunty Petty Sessions at Warrington, a case was heard in which Fred. Moly- neaux, a respectably-dressed young man, described as a photographer from Manchester, was charged in custody with having, on the evening previous, rid- den a bicycle on the footpath at Liverpool-road, Sankey, without using a lamp; and with having also assaulted Police-constable Dugdale, of the County Constabulary, damaging his uniform to the amount of !Is. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the de- fence, and pleaded guilty to the first charge, but not guilty to the second. From the statement of Dugdale, it appeared that that officer was, at about ten o'clock on Tuesday night, in Liverpool-road, Sankey, when he saw Molyneaux riding a bicycle without a lamp. Witness shouted to him to stop, but the bicyclist, quickening his pace, came towards witness, and, turning the machine against him, caught witness on the leg with the pedal, and knocked him down. The constable added that both machine and rider went over him, he was bruised and cut, and his trousers were torn. Molyneaux was in consequence detained. In answer to Super- intendent Weir Dugdale said that Molyneaux acted deliberately, and, replying to questions put by Mr. Browne, he denied haying seized hold of the bicycle. in addressing the Bench for the defence, Mr Browne 'aid that his client was in a respectable position as a photographer in Manchester, and was the photo- grapher to Her Majesty's Commissioners of Prisons for the Manchester district. In that capacity he had the honour, if honour it could be called, of photographing the notorious Jackson. On Tuesday he had been to Liverpool, and, as he was tired, he was riding slowly, lie alleged that the constable got hold of the bicycle, and pushed him over. A constable had no right, Mr. Browne said, to stop a bicyclist, or to apprehend him for not using a lamp. The Bench fined Molyneaux 5s and costs for riding without a lamp, 20s and costs for the assault,, and ordered him to pay for the damage to the police- man's trousers.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Union Work- house, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present :—Mr. J. Kenwright (chairman), Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. J. Lowe, J. Burchall, J. Birchall, W. Twist, J. Buckley, W. Middlehurst, J. Ranson, W. Tyrer, J. Whalley, J. Leatherbarrow, R. A. Graves, J. Fisher, E. Birchall, T. Eatock, C. B. Johnson, E. Syder, W. Daine, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) RELIEF.—The Master reported there were 498 inmates this week, 499 last week. and 465 in the corresponding week last year; 66 vagrants had been relieved against 65 in the corresponding week last week. THE FIRE BRIGADE.—Mr. Tyrer said he hoped none of the members of their fire brigade who attended the de- monstration at Ashton-under-Lyne misconducted them- selves.—The Clerk said they did not. Mr. Hale had informed him that he thought they would have taken the first prize if they had had their engine with them. A NEW HEARSE.—At a meeting of the Visiting Com- mittee, the Chairman, Mr. Leatherbarrow, and Mr. Jos. Birchall were deputed to purchase a new hearse for the workhouse. THE WORKHOUSE ALTERATIONS.—The Local Govern- ment Board wrote asking if the Guardians were intend- ing to spend any money beyond the sum of £3,220, the amount of a contract accepted by the Guardians, in carrying out the alterations at the workhouse.—The Clerk said there would be the architect's fee, and per- haps some extras. He promised to inquire, and report to the Local Government Board.

SENDING BOYS TO SEA.—MT. Charles Jeffs, managing director to the Great Grimsby Ice Company wrote, stat- ing that by the kind permission of the governors of the Liverpool Industrial Schools, he had chosen eight lads belonging to the Prescot Union, for sea service, and they were all willing to go. In regard to religious matters the boys would be left to their own inclination, and they would be supplied with a complete outfit. The lads would go to sea for two months on trial under the care of the Board of Trade, and if willing they would then be bound apprentices until they were 21 years old.—The Clerk said some six or eight weeks ago there was an ap- plication for a boy to besent to a fishing boat at Grimsby, but the committee thought it undesirable to send any boy to the fishing business.—lt was decided that the ap- plication be not entertained. . . . . .

- A SINGULAR REQUEST.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. W. H. Williams, of the Van Mines, Llanidloe,s,stating that Mrs. Margaret Russell, late an inmate of the Pres- cot Union, was dead, and as he had about £3O of her late husband's money in hand, he wished to know what sum was claimed by the Guardians for her maintenance. It was decided to leave the matter in the hands of the clerk.

APPLICATION FOR I,NCR.EASE OF SALARY.—Mr. Alfred Pennington, relieving officer, Sutton district, applied for an increase of salary, and his letter was referred to the Finance Committee. THE CLERK'S OFFICE.—The Clerk stated that he and the Workhouse Master had been unable to find accommo- dation for office purposes during the &Iterations, and he asked permission to use a portion of the Board-room while the alterations were being made.—Mr. Burchall moved, and Mr. Lowe seconded, that the application be granted.—Carried. _ _

TER REVISION OF PAUPERS' LISTS.-Mr. Middlehurst referred to the recent revision of the list of outdoor paupers, and said it had shown that the relieving officers were doing their duty in an efficient and admirable manner.

CONTRACTS. - The Board then considered the tenders for the supplies to the Workhouse during the next six months and the following were accepted': Flour, &c., L. Swift, College-st., St. Helens; groceries, J. Povev, Church-st., St. Helens; butter, cheese and eggs, 'J. Collins, Market House, St. Helens; wine and spirits, Messrs. Mee and Rogers, Prescot : linen and woollen dra- pery, J. B. Pratt, Prescot ; coals, R. Evans and Co., Haydock ; ironmongery, J. Jarvis, St. Helens; earthen- ware, H. Webb, Church-st., St. Helens; coffins, J. Cra- ven, Westfield-st. ; milk and fresh butter for twelve months, Mr. W. Rarnsden, Widnes.
A GIFT.—The Workhouse Master acknowledged with thanks a present of illustrated papers for the use of the inmates from Mr. W. L. McClure, Whiston.
This concluded the business.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

- - - -- The Emin Pasha Committee profess to attach little importance to pessimist reports respecting Mr. Stanley published on Friday morning. A London correspondent states that the Government will make the question of dropping all the licensing clauses, including those relating to Sunday closing, a vcte of confidence.

The weather in London yesterday was more like that of November than of June. A phenomenal darkness hung over the City, necessitating the use of gas in most of the business establishments. Mr. John Albert Bright wrote yesterday to the secre- tary of the Rochdale Liberal Unionist Association intima- ting his intention ot withdrawing from the position of candidate for the borough at the next election. The ill- ness of his fatter is given as the reason. FATAL ACCIDENT AT FLEETWOOD STATION.—On Friday morning John Singleton, whilst assisting to paint the inside of the roof of Fleetwood Railway Station, fell from the scaffold to the platform, a distance of between 30 and 40 feet, and was killed on the spot. The deceased is about 30 years of age, and leaves a widow and two children.

THE THANET VACANCY.—The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of the Isle of Thanet Division of Kent, caused by the death of Colonel King-Harman (C), took place yesterday at Ramsgate, when Mr. James Lowther (C) and Mr.Knatch- bull-Hugessen (G. L) were duly nominated. The polling takes place next Friday. I EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY.—TIIO middle-aged man who was travelling on Saturday night to Nantwich from Chester, where he had been an inmate of the Infirmary, and who was injured by the large glass lamp of a third- class carriage falling out of its socket and alighting on his nose, almost severing it from his face, died on Thurs- day night in the Chester Infirmary. A GHASTLY DISCOVERY IN A LIVERPOOL TUNNEL.—A , ghastly disco very was made on Friday morning in the tunnel between Lime-street and Edge Hill, Liverpool. ' A platelayer going to work found a headless body on the metals, and a search being made the head was also discovered. The body was afterwards identified as that of Evan Davies, joiner, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, who had been work- ing at the hotel in Lime-street fixing the electric light. How he got into the tunnel is a mystery. MEETING OF LIBERAL UNIONISTS.—OR the invitation of the Marquis of Hartington, a meeting of the Liberal Unionist party was held at one o'clock yesterday, at their offices in Great George-st., Westminister, to con- sider the action of the party in respect to the withdrawal of the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill and other matters. Lord Hartington presided, and there was a large attendance of members. His lordship said the meeting had been called in view of a possible division that afternoon upon the 9th and 10th clauses of the Local Government Bill. The first of these clauses, which was to have the support of the Opposition, set up Sun- day closing. Now, considering that the licensing clauses, as a whole, had been dropped by the Government, in deference to divided opinion, he (Lord Hartington) con- tended that it was inconsistent to ask Parliament to pro- ceed to restore them piecemeal. Mr. Chamberlain fol- lowed, and generally supported the views expressed by Lord Hartington. Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild and Mr W, S. Caine were amongst the subsequent speakers, and at the close of the discussion it was decided unani- mously to support the Government in abandoning the ninth clause. A suggestion was further made that the Government should be asked that an opportunity should be given for the consideration of the Sunday Closing Bill, and that, in the event of the House affirming the seconding reading of that measure, the Government should see that the measure was carried through.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS,
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS,
Th. House met ;.-t 4-oreloeV. __ _

MiscEttaNnous.—Earl Mprro called attention to the compotion of the electorate to which the appointment of minigters to vacant parishes in Scotland had been en- trusted by Parliament under the authority of Scotch Church Patronage Act, and moved for a select commit- tee to consider the provisions of that act.—The motion was negatived.—Replying to Earl de la, Warr, Lord KNIITSFORD said that the new constitution had been found most acceptable to all classes at Malta, and the working had been efficient.—The North Sea Fisheries Bill passed through committee; the Customs (wine Duty) Bill was read a second time.

The House adjourned at eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair shortly after two o'clock. THE DrLung PAPERS.—A number of private bills hav- ing been advanced a stage the Speaker read the official notification of the confirmation of the sentence on Mr. John Dillon, M.P.—Mr. SEXTON inquired whether the letter of the County Court Judge would appear on the votes of the House, and the SPEAKER replied in the affirmative.

THE ALLEGED EVICTION OF A DYING MAN.-Mr. W. REDMOND put a long question to the Chief Secretary for Ireland as to the eviction of a dying man on the pro- perty of Mr. Fardross, Clogher.—Mr. A. J. BALFOUR re- plied that there was no reason to suppose that the death of the man was hastened by his eviction. ^The ohl man was carried out of the house because his family refused to remove him. (Derisive Opposition cheers.)—Mr. REDMOND asked whether the attention of the right hon. gentleman had been called to the statement of the parish priest, that the man was in a dying condition when he was carried out of the house in spite of the protests of his friends ?—Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said he knew nothing of the priest's evidence. He had already stated that the man's own family refused to carry him out. (Loud Op- position cheers.)—Mr. REDMOND asked whether the right hon. gentleman would order an inquest to be held and prosecute the sub-sheriff for manslaughter, of which he was undoubtedly guilty ? (Cheers.) He would call attention at the earliest opportunity to the death of this man whose death undoubtedly lay at the door of the Government. (Loud Opposition cheers.)—The SPEAKER: Order, order.—Mr. REDMOND: This man is dead; he was cast out; and you talk about law and order.—The SPEAKER: Order, order.

THE KILLEAG4 CAM—Sir WH. HARCOURT, On behalf of Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, put a question as to the conduct of the magistrates in the Killeagh case, who re- fused the application to state a case to the Court of Ex- chequer. Was the Lord Ljeutenant satisfied as to the "legal knowledge" of these magistrates, and were they to be allowed to continue in their present position? (Op- position cheers.)—Mr.PALFOUR said these magistrates were certified as being competent by Lord Spencer in 1883. (Ministerial cheers.) THE IRISI POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.

div.head: FTTOPOSED VOTE OF CENSURE.
div.p: FTTOPOSED VOTE OF CENSURE.

_ Mr. JOIN MOSLEY, when questions were over at three o'clock, rose, amid loud Opposition cheers, and said : Mr. Speaker, at the opening of our proceedings to-day you read from the chair a letter announcing to the House that Mr. John Dillon, a member of this House, had been sent to prison for sit months. I wish to give notice that I shall submit the following resolution: 'That in the opinion of this House the operation of the Criminal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act, 1887, and the manner of its administration, undermines respect for law—(loud Opposition cheers)—estranges the minds of the people of Ireland. and is deeply injurious to the common in- terests of the United Kingdom." (Prolonged Opposition cheers.) _ .

Mr. GLADSTONE, who was greeted with 'loud and pro- longed Opposition cheers, said: I beg to give notice that on Monday I shall ask the First Lord of the Treasury to appoint a day for the discussion of the resolution of which notice has been given..

Mr. W. H. SMITE: I have listened with attention to the notice which the right hon. gentleman has given. I feel that it is one which challenges confidence in the Govern- ment. (Opposition cheers.) It will be only right to respond to it at once—(Ministerial cheers)—and I ha.veto say that the Governmen• will place Monday at the dis- posal of the right hon. gentleman. (Ministerial cheers and counter Opposition cheers.) THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL

Mr. CLANCY asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether there was any foundation for the rumour that the Government intended to drop further clauses of the Local Government Bill, and whether if that was so a full statement would at once be made instead of by in. ? (Opposition cheers and laughter.)—Mr. W. H. SMITH said he was not aware of ,the rumours to which the hon. gentleman had alluded. He consequently was unable to reply to the question. The Government had already given notice of their intention to drop certain clauses in the bill, and to that intention they adhered. If it became necessary to drop any other clauses—(loud Opposition laughter)—in consequence of the prolonged discussion on the bill—(" Oh, oh," and " Hear, hear ") —it would be quite time enough when the occasion arose to make the announcement to the House.—The House went into Committee on the Local Government Bill.— Mr. CHAPLIN moved an amendment to clause 8, having for its object the witlaolding from the county councils, until such time as the Government think fit to transfer the powers now exercised by the Board of Trade.—Sir. W. HAncourr opposed the amendment.—Mr. RITCHIE said the Government had come to the conclusion to sup- port Mr. Chaplin's amendment —After a long discus- sion, Mr. CHAPLIN moved the closure; ayes 298,n0e5316. —The amendment was afterwards carried by 306 to 224. Mr. RITCHIN then moved certain consequential amend- ments, and they were agreed to,—Mr. MIINDELLA moved to omit the words" or education department" from the clause, in order to prevent School Boards being handed over to the County Councils.—Mr. !tire= said they proposed to accept Mr. Chaplin's amendment excluding School Boards and Boards of Guardians from the clause. —The amendment was withdrawn.—An amendment moved by Mr. CHANNING, exempting School Boards from transfer to County Councils, was agreed to.—Mr. CHAP- LIN proposed that the exemption should also apply to Boards of Guardians.— This was agreed to. The clause was still under consideration, when progress was reported. _ _ _ _
A new writ was issued for South Longford, and the sitting was suspended. _ _ _
The House resumed at nine o'clock.

DISESTABLISHMENT IN SCOTLAND.—Dr. CAmmori moved that in the opinion of the House the Church of Scotland ought to be diaestablished and disendowed. The Preshy- tenan Church of Scotland did not embrace more than

45 per cent, of the population. Its connection vn State, so far from having consolidated and united it, been the cause of every secession that had place, and he failed to see why a section of a should continue to monopolise national subeidieS, to interfere in :purely social: affairs.—Mr. seconded.

RHYMES IN TIE DIALECT. " SAINT MONDA'." For Saints ov o sooarts ther's odd days set apart, Them omanack chaps hes 'em o off bi heart; But ther's one saint as sumheaw gods splattered o'er t' chart; That's t' patron o' th' siotches—Saint Monda! He's a gret deol o' followers, o' every class, Un th' mooast on 'em's atreytbacks, as ,squander ther brass. It's a pity! For mony a true lad un breet lass Hey gotten th' slutch thro' Saint Monda'. Ther's labourin' fooak ov o classes, un swells, Hey a quare way sumtimes ov enjoyin' thersels, For th' records o' th' Mice Coosa a sad history tells O'er t'doins ut th' shrine o' Saint Monda'. Ther's lots o' clatnd childer,,un ill-treoted wives, As hoe mated wi' misery o thro' ther lives, Know weel as ther's freawns, blows, an unbuttered Thro' t' brass thrown away o' Saint Monda'. Ther's cobblers un snips, wi' one X welly smoored, Thor nooases seem reight to brun hnyles thro' a booard ; Heaw they gabble un swagger when they con affooard To fuddle un honour Saint Monda Then, tiler's t' brokken deawn swell, wi' a grey seedy cooat, As hoe managed to bleed, fro' sum quarter, a zooate, He '"stan's Sam" like a foo', teemin' t' stuff deawn his throoat As meks him keer nowt for Saint Monda'. Un wed thriftless hussies, o in a low way, While th' husband's ut th' factry, un t' childer ut play, They'll meet, join, un gossip o'er hot rum un taY, Un backbite ther friends o' Saint Monda'. While o's i' full blow, wi' a quate leerin' grin, Sum Scotchmon n th' hunt for his "shulluns " drops in, Then for th' order he gods leaves a" saxpence" for gin— He pushes his trade o' Saint Monda'. Ther's slum-corner cadgers, bi th' jerry shop end, Lookin' eawt middlin' keen just to drop on a friend As is willin' a tooathry breet shillm' to spend To swill o ther throoats o' Saint Monda'. After loysin' th' clay!s wark for cowd ale, on tort neat, Yo'll see 'em zig zaggin', un brawlin' i'th' street; Sum's like brokken stoo's balanced up o' odd feet, Yet ther leawd ther praise o' Saint Monda'. Foo's mek thersels ill, un oft loyse a good shop, Thro' skulkin' ale-heawses,suppin' cowd slop; To gad howd out, they'll run tiler best clooas into pop, Un swallo' respect o' Saint Monda'. Iv sitch-like wur thrifty, un sowber, un wise, Un th' snares o' ronk laziness lamed to despise; This world w;,d be breeter, un shape tort' a rise Fro' th' blot every week brings—Saint Monda! JACK 0' ANN'S.
